pages.text:
Hello, hello, hello    Good God, any God

This book is an exploration of spiritual and religious beliefs throughout mankind's history. It investigates the reasons for such beliefs and considers whether there is evidence for a God, of any sort. In the process, besides religion, it examines other knowledge sources - philosophy and science.

The author, Nigel Blackmore, was born a Protestant and as a boy regularly attended Sunday School. A family switch to Roman Catholicism saw him briefly become an altar-boy in a Catholic church. He attended a Catholic, Christian Brothers, grammar school in Bristol, and later was married to wife Jane by his gentle grandfather-in-law, Edmund Morgan, an Anglican Bishop.

chapters.title: First of all
chapters.summary: The very beginning, the Big Bang, who/what started it? Adam & Eve, Discworld's Great A'Tuin, a space-turtle. Stephen Hawking and the blue touch-paper.

pages.text:
Chapter 1

First of all

In the beginning, there was a flash and a BANG, or perhaps first a bang and then a flash. The laws of physics had not yet been invented so sound might have sped past light, before light established its relative supremacy. The bang was a very big bang; the most gigantic bang there has ever been. Imagine an indescribably decibelic loudness. It was that big.

Well, that's what you might surmise had happened if you've heard of the Big Bang theory without studying it more closely. You would be excused for thinking that an enormous explosion took place, excitingly flinging the stuff of galaxies, stars and planets in all directions - the Big Bang. Disappointingly there was no bang. Those kill-joy cosmologists say so, despite this they still call it, confusingly, the Big Bang.

[Figure: Collage of the six days of creation, headed '1 2 3 4 5 6 days' and 'Job done': Doré's engraving of the creation of light, Dürer's Adam and Eve, Charles R. Knight's leaping dinosaurs and the Blue Marble photograph of the Earth]

Many of these scientists say that at the very beginning there was just an infinitesimally small, dense and hot object - something far smaller than an atom, impenetrably dense and much hotter than any star. This object, a singularity to be precise, started to expand. In fact, it did blow up, but like a balloon rather than a bomb. So, our universe began to ever increase by rapid, incredibly rapid, inflation; even faster than the speed of light. It was also a silent event. No one heard any puffing, despite the blowing up. No one saw anything either. There was no one to hear or see, except maybe Him. If there was a Him at this singular moment in time, some 13.8 billion years ago.

That is one account of universal origin. It has widespread support in the scientific community. But some religiously vectored people claim it is an invention of the godless and not the true explanation. These Creationists think the whole process started just 6,000 years ago and was both speedier and simpler. "Let there be light and there was light." They say that He said that.

HE followed on with a week's hard work. Unpaid too. There were no unions then. On the penultimate morn of His evolutionary week Adam burst forth. Eventually that day there was Eve. Did the universe start like this?

Alternatively, was this how it all began?

[Figure: Big Bang timeline diagram]

Did this almighty cosmic motion,
Come from a simple Godly notion,
Or was it of science, a natural thing,
That physics, and quantum did bring.

Prof. Stephen Hawking said: "It is not necessary to invoke God to light the blue touch paper and set the universe going." If so, what lit the blue touch paper?

Sir Terry Pratchett, hugely renowned author of the legendary Discworld series, appears to back both the Big Bang and Creation angles in one of his Discworld stories. He wrote of the Great A'Tuin, a 10,000 kilometers long space turtle, rendezvousing with its own kind in the depths of space. The different sex space-turtles engaged in an almighty big bang, with procreation firmly in mind. Well, if not in mind exactly, somewhere else quite vital in space-turtle reproductive anatomy. A thing so big, it's only detectable with astronomical rather than anatomical instruments.

[Figure: The world on four elephants and a turtle, as pictured in 1877: an engraving of the Hindu image of the Earth]

Terry does not receive the recognition he deserves for this, a version of the "Great Theory of Everything" (footnotes should shorten this to "Big Toe" theory). What Terry thought though about the origin of the universe is not clear. He did say in a 2010 interview: "I have no truck whatsoever with Genesis." On the other hand, he never claimed the Discworld to be more than fantasy. A pity that, some of us would like the chance to meet Granny Weatherwax, Captain Carrot, Mustrum Ridcully, Commander Vimes and the rest.

[Figure: J.B.S. Haldane, 1892 to 1964, mathematician, neo-Darwinist (photograph c.1914)]

The universe is not only queerer than we suppose, it is queerer than we can suppose.

J.B.S. Haldane, 1892 to 1964
Mathematician, neo-Darwinist

Setting aside space-turtles we have two beginnings in the frame, the Big Bang and Creationism theories. There are many others. But one beginning is enough. Two beginnings are more than enough. That is, if you are mathematically inclined. Philosophers would argue the point. Theologians wouldn't. They have faith in their certainty and certainty in their faith. Artists can picture any beginning, so they trump everyone else.

But the beginning is only the start of what we are about here. Was there a Him? Was He then and is He now and will He be forever and forever? That is the great God question we will explore. It's the question above all questions. An easy question to ask. The hardest to answer. A question that has intrigued mankind's greatest minds over thousands of years.

Let's look at what some of these sages thought about a God, through their expertise with philosophy, religion and science, particularly palaeontology, history, cosmology and quantum mechanics. Also explored is the influence of environment, human nature and human desires on the God issue.

How to address these very far-reaching subject areas? Well, broadly, this book attempts a topic based, chronological approach. Exploring the Goddish history alongside the history of humans, Earth and the cosmos seems to be a reasonable method. Humanity's ingenuity has spawned many Gods and quite a few Goddesses too. And we must not forget the spirits and other supernatural entities. We can't possibly cover them all in any reasonable depth. Our torch will therefore shine most brightly on the one God, He of Christianity; Islam and Judaism. So, let's get going. We shall start, not with a bang or anything flash; we shall simply begin with the next paragraph.

Don't hold out too high hopes though of the paragraph. Remember Winnie the Pooh's questioning of Christopher Robin: "What is a paragraph?" asked the bear, "It's a group of sentences that form a complete thought.", replied Christopher Robin. "Is there any honey in this paragraph?" queried Pooh, "Oh, sorry Pooh, no." answered Christopher," Well then, I don't find it terribly useful." concluded Pooh firmly. Sorry to disappoint you reader, but there's no honey in the next paragraph.

For ex-civil servants like me it's the norm to outline the conclusion early on in any major paper. Here goes; Dock Green's finest comes into it at the end, as does a celebrity greeting's magazine, and there's listed seven possibilities. Curious? - then read on. Dismayed, disgusted or bored already? - just throw this in the bin.

[Figure: Ink drawing of an open book falling into a wire waste-paper basket, with the words 'This book is a load of rubbish, I believe' and 'But, really, don't believe such a belief']

But, really, don't believe such a belief. For now, why not indulge your curiosity genes and read on? You can chuck it in the bin later.

Before exploring whether or not such a being as God exists we need to know more precisely what we are talking about when we refer to "God". As already indicated, the principle, but not exclusive focus will be on the why and what of the monotheistic God, that is God in the singular; the all singing and all dancing God; chiefly, the Abrahamic one.

Of course, there have been and still are many religions and cultures where more than one God, or a supreme teacher, is thought to exist, but Godly monotheism has come to pre-dominate religious belief systems in modern times. He's the one and He's the only, not for the atheists though. The agnostics are not sure. Others have other beliefs.

[Figure: Beliefs diagram showing modern world religions and philosophies]

The above is a snapshot of the most common Modern Human beliefs.

The existence, or not, of a God

Many humans would agree that the existence of a God cannot be proved by rigorous scientific method. Despite this, the one God (Abrahamic) exists today for billions of people. But there is also a large and growing disbelief, many millions either deny or ignore His existence.

Gods, in one guise or another, have been around for the greater part of the 300 millennia that Homo Sapiens has inhabited planet Earth. First, Spirits associated with the natural world were a fundamental part of life for tens of thousands of years of early human history. As human societies developed religious beliefs grew too. They became more contrived, complex and competitive. The Spirits and animism of pre-historic, hunter gatherers evolved into a changing variety of religions and a huge pantheon of Gods.

HE, the one God, arguably arrived relatively late on the scene, mainly, but not solely, from biblical times up to the modern day. Over this later period the concept of a single, omniscient, omnipotent, pre-eminent being, generally came to dominate religious doctrine, although by no means exclusively so.

Spirits, Gods and religions will be explored in more detail later, especially monotheism, but first up it will be useful to try and understand why many modern, most historic and pre-historic humans, back to 300,000 years ago, needed or wanted some sort of God.

headings.text: The existence, or not, of a God

chapters.title: Why, why, why
chapters.summary: Why have modern humans always had Gods or spirits of some sort, what are the attractions - comfort blanket, safety deposit box, Maslow, hierarchy of Needs, COUTH AV - the six attempted proofs of God's existence.

pages.text:
Chapter 2

Why, why, why?

If it is accepted that there has never been a conclusive proof of God, why is it that He has existed for so many humans? Is this something to do with our humanity?

It is difficult to imagine logic centered robots having any truck with Gods. But humans are not robots. We are not coldly logical computers, with appendages added on. Our brains allow us to compute certainly, but we also have emotions and feelings like love, hate, empathy, derision, worry, hope, despair, fear, contentment, pain and happiness. A complex mix of logical reasoning, sentiment and biological responses (mainly physical pain, hunger and sex!) guides human thinking and actions. Added to the maelstrom mixture that comprises the human psyche is our realization of a limited shelf-life. We know we will kick the bucket; croak it, pass away or pop our clogs - whatever is our favourite euphemism for the act of dying.

All this can mean that sometimes some of us are prepared to believe something to be true without clear evidence, or any indisputable line of reasoning. This is largely because humans want to believe and accept what others say, if it suits them. The result is that Gods have had not just a field day but an entire savanna epoch over the course of modern human existence.

Deities, and the attributes that humans have conveniently attached to them, have grown to fill a large, vacant niche. Exploring this niche reveals the compelling reasons why a God has so appealed to much of humanity.

[Figure: Ancient Egyptian guide to the afterlife: Anubis attends the mummy (tomb of Sennedjem)]

Anthropologists John Monoghan and Peter Just say that, "it seems apparent that one thing religion or belief helps us do is deal with problems of human life that are significant, persistent, and intolerable. One important way in which religious beliefs accomplish this is by providing a set of ideas about how and why the world is put together that allows people to accommodate anxieties and deal with misfortune."

Life Beyond The Grave

Homo Sapiens is unique in the modern animal kingdom. The "modern" distinction excludes our intelligent but extinct Hominin ancestors; including Homo Heidelbergensis, Homo Erectus, Homo Habilis, and our cousins, the Neanderthal, who died out about 18,000 years ago. We, modern man, have intelligence, emotions and a restless imagination. These attributes enable us to have a strong and usually unwelcome appreciation of our own individual mortality. Godly development may well have arisen, in part, to mitigate against our realisation of eventual death and nothingness. A form of spiritual or religious belief has helped humans over eons dismiss the thought of an inevitable void. Faith offers the prospect of continuance after death. This advantage makes religions, any religion, enticing to embrace. For archaic humans and indeed for later ones; the concept of some type of superior being - a God(s), and his promise of an afterlife was both reassuring and comforting. As Voltaire said: "If God did not exist it would be necessary to invent him." However, He is invented whether or not He exists.

Supernatural tendencies, science and evolution

This emotional yearning for continuance has been re-enforced by other fundamental human tendencies. There is scientific evidence, not conclusive, to show humans, especially children, have a predisposition towards belief in spirits and the supernatural world. In this way belief in a type of God could be inherently hard-wired into all humans (Dean Hamer - "The God Gene"), from the earliest times of pre-history. No prizes for guessing who the religiously inclined consider to have done the hard-wiring. But there is a powerful alternative to God's involvement in any innate human spirituality. Darwin puts a big oar in here. Belief in spirits or God is thought to have an evolutionary advantage. This is evolution not through competitive selection but through co-operation. The clubbiness and security offered through common spiritual beliefs would have helped cement fragile and sparse early human societies.

[Figure: The ankh, an ancient Egyptian symbol of life: a New Kingdom faience amulet (Metropolitan Museum of Art)]

At the conclusion of a major 2011 research project Dr Justin Barrett, from the University of Oxford's Centre for Anthropology and Mind, claimed that people who share an attachment to religion: "might be more likely to cooperate as societies". In a hostile world, this would be an advantage to the continued existence of the species. Curiously, there is something of a dichotomy here. A partial reason for religious growth, could be the evolutionary advantage. Yet Darwin, the great evolutionary guru, was an atheist! Did he realize that evolution itself might be a reason for religious development?

So, we have the prospect of: immortality, a tendency to believe the supernatural and evolution in the frame as three possible reasons for God's rise, over millennia, on a large balloon of faith, but these are not the only reasons for the development of Godly belief. There is more, quite a lot more.

We want it now

Human disposition and want is varied. Continuance through spiritual existence after a very final death is an attractive prospect. However, humans don't want to wait for death until they get something beneficial from their revered supernatural being. HE's got to be able to help out with life's problems too. These further wants of an incorporeal immortal are another possible answer to the "why God" question. To achieve all the things humans want from life then a God has to be endowed with a set of superior powers and abilities. These enable Him to deliver the goods. In many societies, human "want" strengthened to "need", as religious dogmas, doctrines, rituals and rites developed into a holy industry that, for thousands of years was ingrained into nearly all societal structures.

Safety Deposit Box

Let's return to the sort of pre-death bonuses that humans have looked for from their Spirits or God. A common one is a secure place to lodge that which is disturbing or unknown. Down the ages God became a safety deposit box where the mysterious, unknowable and the fearful can be securely stored. Great natural events that were not explainable were attributed to a God or spirit, like the waxing and waning of the moon, eclipses and thunder and lightning. In Viking pagan mythology, thunder and lightning was the domain of the mighty, hammer-wielding Thor. Ancient Sumerians, Egyptians and many other cultures had sun and moon Gods or Goddesses.

[Figure: Safe deposit vault: where we lock away what we cannot bear to lose]

Something unfathomable may be described as "an act of God", or the will of god. Even today the former is a recognized legal phrase, mainly in the insurance industry, also when sometimes describing adverse natural phenomena.

Attributing what we now know are natural events to a God has provided a degree of comfort throughout ages past. No need to worry further when something happens that we do not understand or are afraid of. With God around we don't have to work it out, it's all down to Him. HE knows what it is all about. HE will sort it out for us. Some major events might induce worry though, they were considered portents of nasty things to come, or as a form of punishment for backsliding individuals.

But humans needed more positive attributes of a God than just this parking place for things they didn't understand or feared. Over time, the role of superior beings, spirits and Gods, was expanded to address these new desires. Shamans, priests and other religious authorities gradually invented new, attractive and sometimes frightening abilities and dispositions attributed to their spirits and Gods.

Humans can feel remorse or guilt for something they've done. These feelings are often because the society they live in or their religion might consider some individual act or omission to be a bad thing. In these circumstances forgiveness and a clean slate is something highly desirable, particularly if without this we might suffer in both the present and the afterlife. This "mercy" facility was an attribute often credited to God. Peace of mind and sometimes even secret forgiveness - "no one need know" - is attractively on offer through belief in God. Hence, the Roman Catholic confessional box.

[Figure: La confessione, Giuseppe Molteni, 1838, Fondazione Cariplo]

Hope for the Best, now and ever after

The prospect of hope is yet another godly attraction. Hope of a better life now; with the help of a spirit or deity. Stone Age hunters probably hoped their cave bear hunt would be successful and may have appealed to natural spirits to make it so. Later, Bronze Age farmers might have danced or prayed to a rain god. (There is evidence of this sort of behavior from studies of more recent indigenous peoples). In modern times, God could be appealed to for help with a winning lottery ticket.

headings.text: Hope for the Best, now and ever after

pages.text:
We mustn't forget the personal evolutionary advantage. This could be ascribed to tier one, as a fundamental survival need. It also comes under Safety and Security in the Maslow analysis.

[Figure: Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs - A pyramid diagram showing five levels from bottom to top: 1. Basic needs for survival, 2. Safety & security, 3. Love & belonging, 4. Esteem, 5. Self-actualisation (with "Self-actualisation" at the apex highlighted in yellow)]

So, it can be argued that both Darwin and Maslow obliquely point to religious beliefs as being an evolutionary advantage. Even atheists ought to be grateful for that. If our ancient ancestors did not commonly share such beliefs, maybe none of us would be here. MHs could have died out.

We now have a longish and desirable tick list of Godly advantages. With all these, what more could be asked of a supreme being? A God who can provide so much is such an alluring prospect. Many people have desperately wanted to believe in Him because of this, regardless of the quality of evidence for His existence. "Wow, with those potential benefits, I'll sign up to that belief" they decide, often in an unconscious way. To maintain widespread belief in a God, people must be reminded of these advantages, and of the disadvantages of non-belief. This moves us on to those who are His worldly representatives.

Heed me and feed me, I'm God's representative

We must consider the power and status accorded to religious leaders; the shamans; witch doctors; medicine men; priests; vicars; bishops, rabbis, imams and their clerical ilk. It was to their advantage to strongly support and perpetuate the particular religious or spiritual brand that they avowed. They did, and still do this, through the traditional carrot and stick technique.

The "carrot" employed by these miscellaneous clerics was, and still is, the emphasis they put on all the advantages of belief in their creed. Often, conveniently, these advantages could only accrue after death.

headings.text: Heed me and feed me, I'm God's representative

pages.text:
Their own reward for succeeding in this task was frequently, with some altruistic exceptions, very earthly: money; food; housing; respect; influence and power. Not all were self-serving, power and status junkies, and money grabbers. Many had and have served their flock humbly, fairly and well, although perhaps based on a dubious premise.

[Figure: Leaders of many faiths at the World's Parliament of Religions, Chicago, 1893]

Now for the "stick". In the middle ages the Catholic Church made considerable sums from an astutely devised indulgence system. Sums of money were made by clergy promising eternal salvation and forgiveness of sins. Pay up and you can go to heaven, if you are poor and can't pay, then it's hell for you, seemed to be the message. This was a sort of combined reward and punishment scheme in one simple package. The clerics gained worldly reward from worrying people of dire after-life consequences of their actions.

Clergy and religious chiefs of all varieties warn of horrible things happening to any backsliders to keep them inline. In the not so distant past anyone of the wrong religious denomination could be tortured and killed. This continues, to an extent, even today, but it was more prevalent in times in the past. The crusades spanning the 11th to 13th centuries are a well-known example.

Even if of the right religion, sinners, after death, could expect to spend eternity in hell if they did not abide by certain rules of behavior. In some faiths, they might be re-incarnated as a cockroach. But often nasty retributions also occurred in the corporeal existence of the unfortunate sinner.

A famous example from the past is the punishment meted out by the Roman Catholic Spanish Inquisition, in the Middle Ages. In 1600CE poor Giordano Bruno was burned at the stake for his heresy in daring to state the sun was a star, and for his pantheist views. Prevailing religious dogma, unknowingly supported by Aristotle, nearly 2,000 years previously, said the Earth was the center of the universe. Later, in 1633CE Galileo was threatened with torture for supporting the Copernican theory that the Earth orbited the sun and not the other way around. There are many other examples of actual and threatened physical violence, even in the present day. In some parts of the Islamic world of today you might be stoned to death for adultery, or until recently, you could be whipped if you were a woman found driving a car. The Rabbinic law in Judaism, sets out eighteen crimes for whom the punishment is death by stoning.

Religions have set out a multiplicity of rewards for believers and punishments for lapses, of the wrong belief, or non-believers. This carrot and stick approach has been hugely successful in keeping adherents, well, adherents.

A summary of "Why", with some extra's

The benefits offered through the safety deposit box and the comfort blanket syndromes, are why many people want God(s) to exist. This desire is so strong it overrides any serious examination of evidence, especially so when combined with our cranial hard-wiring and evolutionary steer towards the supernatural. Added to this scenario is the encouragement by priests etc, in particular forms of belief. The lack of evidence does not mean that God is non-existent of course. He may actually be able to provide all those things in the box and under the blanket, because he does exist. But there is no solid proof of Godly existence, or is there? Some attempted proofs have been put forward.

Professed Proofs of God's Existence

There have been and still are many believers, billions of them, in a God or spiritual figure. It is unlikely that these believers will admit to wanting to believe solely because of the safety deposit box and comfort blanket attractions. These two are bed-rock features underpinning belief, but over hundreds of years there has been a realisation by some believers that there cannot be a God just because people find it convenient to have one. Something more substantial was needed to support the belief of thinking, questioning people. Ergo theologians and their more humbly referenced predecessors have attempted to point to stronger signs of His existence.

headings.text: A summary of "Why", with some extra's

pages.text:
Chapter 3

The six proofs for God unpacked

COTHAM - the six "proofs", what do they mean and where do they come from?

There are more attempted proofs than these 6. Anselm came up with a few more - weak, and rarely mentioned. If you want to see some brilliant spoofs try Rebecca Newberger Goldstein's book: "36 Arguments for the Existence of God". These include: "The Argument from Dappled Things", "The Argument from the Eternity of Irony" and "The Argument from Fraught Distance". You can probably get the drift from these titles. I'm going to pass on these and concentrate on the 6 proofs that are the most commonly mentioned by deeply thoughtful believers.

Cosmological Argument

An eternal God, called the unmoved mover (after Aristotle) lights the blue touch paper to kick-off the universe. HE's the prime source. This is also known as the First Cause. In essence, this is the cosmological argument for the existence of God.

[Figure: Gustave Doré's 1866 engraving 'The Creation of Light', beside the words "CREATION - In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth... Genesis 1:1"]

St Thomas Aquinas (1225-1274) is the original main champion of the cosmological argument. He was later supported by René Descartes. In more recent times, William Craig's 1979 book, The Kalām Cosmological Argument, attempted to give support to this idea.

More than a thousand years before Aquinas, those very clever Greeks, Aristotle and Plato, thought the universe had no beginning and no end, so a God is not needed they concluded. And Parmenides, who preceded them said: "nothing comes from nothing", "ergo as God is something HE cannot come from nothing." We have no evidence to suggest Aquinas view is superior to that of the ancient Greeks.

David Hume argued against the Cosmological Argument. In effect he said: 1. We can conceive of things without a cause, and 2. Explanation of the parts is sufficient. He meant we can look at and explain individual items within our universe, but we don't need to explain the whole thing.

headings.text: The six proofs for God unpacked

pages.text:
Immanuel Kant, slightly later than Hume, claimed that God is not logically necessary. In 1947 Bertrand Russell, termed his objection: "The Fallacy of Composition". What he meant was just because parts of something have a certain property it does not mean the whole does too, e.g. if a fence is made up of small panels the whole fence is not necessarily going to have the property of smallness. Ergo, because everything in the universe has a cause it does not mean the whole universe has to have a cause. Bertrand is with those ancient Greeks, saying the universe just is. In modern times, renowned quantum physicist, Stephen Hawking, sided with Bertrand Russell. He said we do not need God to light the blue touch paper, i.e. kick off the Big Bang.

The Cosmological argument should not be confused with the Cosmological Constant. This is a term Einstein used when inserting a figure into his equations to fit in with his "steady-state" theory of the universe. Steady-state was dropped when universal expansion became irrefutable, proving yet again that even the greatest minds can get it wrong.

In science, the origin of our universe begins with the Big Bang. Cosmologists cannot yet say what preceded the Big Bang, although the Multiverse concept looms larger and larger. There is certainly no hard, compelling evidence, for the Cosmological argument. It is not a proof of God's existence.

Ontological Argument

Anselm of Canterbury in 1078 put forward this idea. It requires thinking of the greatest being you can possibly conceive of. Then, Anselm says, because this thought is in the mind there must be a greater being, one who exists in reality as well as the mind.

[Figure: Speech bubble: "I can imagine a very powerful God, really I can."]

[Figure: A 12th-century miniature of Anselm presenting his Prayers to Countess Matilda (Admont, c. 1160), with the thought bubble "I can imagine a very powerful God, really I can." and the label "Proslogion, 1077–78: Anselm's ontological argument"]

Anselm's thought was certainly original and at first glance a bit weird. Maybe at second and third glance too for many people. This idea had great support from René Descartes and Gottfried Leibnitz.

The ever-pragmatic David Hume rejected it saying in effect: "where's the evidence?" David argued that we humans are capable of imagining anything, including a God.

And in respect of inanimate objects, many can be designed by humans and made from artificial material like plastic. They are only perfect if their human designer and maker is of sufficient skill and the materials worked on are also up to the job. Richard Dawkins, evolutionary biologist, puts it like this: "Paley's argument is made with passionate sincerity and is informed by the best biological scholarship of the day, but it is wrong, gloriously and utterly wrong.... All appearances to the contrary, the only watchmaker in nature is the blind force of physics ... Natural selection, the blind unconscious, automatic process which Darwin discovered, and which we now know is the explanation for the existence and apparently purposeful form of all life, has no purpose in mind. ... If it can be said to play the role of watchmaker in nature, it is the blind watchmaker." Both Fred Hoyle and Professor of Christian Religion, Richard Swinburne were proponents of intelligent design. Richard Dawkins, in his book: The Blind Watchmaker said in answer to these two: "Evolution has no long-term goal. There is no long-distance target, no final perfection to serve as a criterion for selection...... The criteria for selection are always short-term, either simply survival, or, more generally, reproductive success." Richard Dawkins followed up these ideas in his aptly titled book: "The Selfish Gene."

Hard-wired

As shown earlier belief in the supernatural could have an evolutionary advantage, particular to sparse populations in the early days of MH. This is a chicken and egg issue, which came first? Did the evolutionary imperative mean there was a tendency for a greater survival rate among people with supernatural beliefs or was there an inherent such belief that had a knock-on evolutionary benefit? Some say that the tendency to believe in the supernatural, courtesy of God, was first out of the blocks. If so, why didn't such a supposedly steady gain make it a much stronger and clearer. Many 10's of millions of unbelievers can be found in the world today.

There has been research into this question on top of the arguments put forward by Dean Hamer, referred to in Chapter 2. In 2009 Bruce Hood, Prof. of Developmental Psychology at Bristol University said: "Our research shows children have a natural, intuitive way of reasoning that leads them to all kinds of supernatural beliefs about how the world works." In a 2011 project Dr Justin Barrett, from the University of Oxford's Centre for Anthropology and Mind, said faith may be prevalent across the world because people who have a religion in common might be more likely to cooperate as societies."

Co-Director of the same project, Prof Roger Trigg said: ".....human thought seems to be rooted to religious concepts, such as the existence of supernatural agents or gods, and the possibility of an afterlife or pre-life."

Later investigation in this area has revolved around a new term: Hypersensitive Agency Detection Device, or HADD. If you are interested, look it up.

Anthropic Principle

This argument is relatively modern. It's closely connected to the teleological, design proof of God's existence. Where it differs is it is much broader in scope and more basic than the design idea. It focuses on our entire universe; looking back to its very beginning. The Anthropic Principle says that the underlying physical laws of our universe are so finely tuned that they eventually enable us humans to exist. In their 1989 book John Gribbin and Martin Rees made this argument, saying: "The conditions in our Universe really do seem to be uniquely suitable for life forms like ourselves." Very tiny differences in the laws of physics could mean that the strong nuclear force was not sufficiently strong to enable elementary particles to form atoms, and perhaps even for any form of organic complexity.

Other laws, of gravity and quantum mechanics could also have been different, causing mayhem with the structure of our universe and nullifying the possibility of any life. Ergo, with different physics, after the Big Bang 13.8 billion years ago, elementary particles would have remained just that. No atoms would have formed. That means there would be no matter as we know it. Stars, Planets and Galaxies would not have been created. We would not have any place from which we could evolve into being. Closely connected to the Anthropic Principle is the purported Goldilocks Zone. This is the zone in which planet Earth is perfectly located. The Earth is just the right distance from the sun so that it is neither too hot (like Mercury and Venus) or too cold like (Mars, the gas and ice giants). That means water can exist in liquid form on Earth.

There's Jupiter, a giant planet positioned just far enough away to be able to scoop up, with its massive gravity, enough comets and other space debris so that Earth would not be blasted into lifelessness in the early days of its 4.6-billion-year existence. But Jupiter is not so close that it attracted all such comets. Many of them were water bearing. Earth needed these to form the oceans, lakes and rivers. Water is the base of all life, as we know it.

The Theists say the Anthropic Principle demonstrates that a guiding hand, i.e. God, exists. Countering this claim are two arguments.

The first simply says it's a matter of observation. That is, we humans are bound to recognize what universe we are in and its physical laws, because we are here. The second contention says our universe may be one of countless trillions, one in a multiverse. This is a suggestion made by Martin Rees, Astronomer Royal and Emeritus Professor of Cosmology and Astrophysics at Cambridge University. Each of the universes in the countless trillions within the multiverse, so speculate some cosmologists, could have different physical laws. There is such a vast number of universes, one of them is certain to have the right laws and a Goldilocks Zone to allow our existence.

The multiverse idea is unproven but growing in popularity. It is an argument against both the Anthropic Principle and Cosmological claimed proofs.

Moralistic Theory

Religious theorists argue that since every person has awareness of some form of morality, that is what is right and what is wrong, this is a norm for all humans. The source of this moral normality, they say, can only be God. Therefore, God must exist, according to this moralistic theory.

Many philosophers, as well as theologians argue in favour of a moral or ethical lifestyle. But the philosophers do not necessarily bring God into the argument. From ancient eastern traditions Confucius was a great supporter of personal and governmental morality. He stressed the importance of sincerity and justice. Buddhism teaches ethical conduct as part of the eightfold path. Truth is an aspect of morality. Interestingly the existence in the Bible of lies, what is now termed "fake-news" has been pointed to by Pope Francis in 2018. He said that Eve was given fake-news when the snake encouraged her to give Adam an apple. French anthropologist, Pascal Boyer claims that moral sentiments exist perfectly well in societies that have to a large extent abandoned religion, such as those in Czech Republic and Scandinavia. He says: "Moral intuitions don't come out of moral codes. They develop very early in children, who understand that moral questions are about co-operation, and about constructing coalitions."

The early Socratic philosophers, Socrates, Plato and Aristotle, also pontificated on morality, mainly linking happiness to virtue. In particular Plato thought morality was knowable, a priori, through reason. Later, Hume said morality comes from human sentiment, i.e. we view other people's actions against the moral and ethical standards we ourselves have.

He said: "Take any action allow'd to be vicious: Willful murder, for instance. Examine it in all its lights, and see if you can find that matter of fact, or real existence, which you call vice... You can never find it, till you turn your reflection into your own breast, and find a sentiment of disapprobation, which arises in you, towards this action." - from Treatise on Human Nature.

Immanuel Kant disagreed and argued morality derived from human reason. He referred to it as the "categorical Imperative".

John Stuart Mill claimed that "...actions are right in the proportion as they tend to promote happiness, wrong as they tend to produce the reverse of happiness. By happiness is intended pleasure, and the absence of pain; by unhappiness, pain and the privation of pleasure." Perhaps John Stuart had in mind what some of those ancient Greeks had said. Friedrich Nietzsche said, in effect, morality is a load of baloney.

So, typical with philosophers, after the ancient Greeks, we have different approaches to the issue of human morality. Some think it's based on reason. Hume says it's down to our own emotional reaction. Mill thinks moral actions promote happiness and Nietzsche dismisses morality. However, the ideas of all have one thing in common - God is absent from their argument.

The issue of what is considered to be moral has raised an even more intriguing question, generally known as the Euthyphro Dilemma, from Plato's dialogue. In essence what this asks is whether something is moral because God wills it, or are there moral standards independent of God. If the former, can God decide something is moral that most humans would consider definitely not? Aquinas thinks we can have it both ways, that there is a set of basic moral laws that even God has to accept and cannot change, like the Biblical 10 commandments. In addition, Aquinas thinks there are some moral decisions over which God can decide, particularly when making judgements of individual human behaviour. Those philosophers that offer serious criticism say if there are moral standards outside of God's influence then He is bound by some greater force, does not have free will and is not omnipotent.

The question of God as the foundation stone of morality has been debated right up to modern times. In 2003 Agony Aunt and author Anne Atkins said it's impossible for people to hold to strong ethical standards if they are faithless. She made this comment on the BBC radio programme "Thought for the Day": "Without God, where do we find the absolutes of right and wrong? What is to stop a secular society sinking to depths of depravity that, as yet, we only dream of."

Professor Alice Roberts, President of Humanists Association, responded: "In answer to her first question, how do we know right from wrong - a humanist would perhaps reply that ethical behaviour is best guided not by recourse to religion, but by employing empathy, self-control, a moral sense, and reason..."

What else?

Apart from the COTHAM six proofs, or more accurately attempted proofs, there is one other worth noting: The Principle of Sufficient Reason (nihil est sine ratione), or PSR for short) - the +1.

This one is a real poser, as well as a POSR. It claims that nothing happens without a reason or cause. Spinoza explained his thinking for this philosophical principle: "Since existing is something positive, we cannot say that it has nothing as its cause. Therefore, we must assign some positive cause, or reason, why (a thing) exists - either an external one, i.e., one outside the thing itself, or an internal one, one comprehended in the nature and definition of the existing thing itself." Leibnitz also dabbled in the same water. He made the point we cannot always know the reason or cause: "…...most of the time these reasons cannot be known to us." There is much debate over PSR, but it has been used as an argument for God. HE being the reason or cause of all that exists, it is claimed. How can we know this? We cannot, there might be other reasons, aka Leibnitz.

FIFU is not a blue rinsed aunt's favourite poodle

Finally, we have FIFU the answers of last resort for a God. When faced with difficult arguments that challenge both religious texts and COTHAM+ proofs, FIFU is often used by believers to claim that God exists. There are four contentions, any or all may be quoted as a final defense of religious beliefs that are under serious challenge.

[Figure: A poodle, painted by George Stubbs c.1780]

[Figure: Diagram showing four oval shapes labeled: "God is Unknown", "Faith - the big one", "Free Will", "God's Inside Me" with text "Fallback position if God's existence is seriously challenged"]

headings.text: FIFU is not a blue rinsed aunt's favourite poodle

pages.text:
Don't listen to the Devil. He will want you to criticize FIFU, the Bible and the Church. He will ask your cries such as "..but I'm praying to God, where is He?" and "God, when calm, "You must have faith!" Theologian Alister McGrath says: "Faith is not something that goes against the evidence, it goes beyond mere reason." This is something similar to the 13th century German philosopher and Bishop, Albertus Magnus. He said that there were some mysteries that had to be accepted by faith alone beyond reason. There are plenty of things we don't understand, but that is not the same as being beyond reason. Every day we know more and more about our universe and ourselves. Why is God constantly posted at the frontiers of science? HE always has to move because the frontier is continually shifting forward, as Richard Feynman said. And, why is faith beyond reason, according to Alister?

The question is, why do we need faith? Why does God require people to have faith? HE is a being of immense power. HE could easily erase all doubt and make His existence crystal clear to us if he wished and if He exists.

God is Inside me: In fact, some claim, God is inside everyone, no need to search for Him externally. For most people, if God is inside them, He is a very silent, that is, a totally silent partner. HE is also a partner that freely allows some of those hosting Him to engage in what could be called evil and ungodly practices. Why is this? And why does He not make His presence clearly known? What is the point of being inside people if many do not recognize this?

Free Will: When queried as to why God allows people to do bad things, religious supporters will say we have been given free will. But, is this possible for an all-powerful, all-knowing God. HE knows exactly what we will do long before we are born, according to the abilities attributed to Him. Not only that, but if He has indeed set up the entire universe and if, as is claimed, He is incapable of a mistake, surely all outcomes are His planned result? That would mean whatever we do is as God intends.

He set up something like a vast computer program that churns out predictable and intentional outcomes. There is much debate over this issue of free will. Theologians have wrestled valiantly in trying to prove its existence. This is understandable because unless it can be clearly demonstrated that humans have free will then there is a problem arguing the case for a God. For a supremely powerful God to be about in a no-freewill universe, pre-destination then reigns. All human efforts are rendered pointless. He's already set out every condition that leads us only in His planned direction and outcome, no matter what we do.

2,300 years ago, the Greek philosopher Zeno of Citium, explained his concept of freewill. He likened it to a puppy who is tied to the back of a moving cart. The puppy can move a little side to side but it can never go back or move forward beyond the cart. It also cannot stop, without having its neck broken. Ergo, we all have to move in the direction and at the speed dictated by the cart. If there is a God He's the cart and we are the puppies.

400 hundred years ago philosopher Thomas Hobbes said: "A free agent is he that can do as he will, and forbear as he will, and, that liberty is the absence of external impediments." The key phrase is "absence of external impediments." That can include a God.

[Figure: Image: Book cover or illustration showing "Zeno of Citium"]

Unknown: Religious clerics have a common response when they are pinned down with difficult questions such as: "Why doesn't God stop children dying?". This question might be asked by greatly distressed parents of a terminally ill child. Another more general query is "Why does God allow evil? (more on the question of evil very soon)." The clerics' regular answer is that we cannot know the detailed will of God. HIS purposes are unknown and beyond our capabilities to understand. This idea is partly supported by Plato's cave and Einstein's child in the library illustrative stories. These two may be reckoned as some of the cleverest humans there have been, but they did make mistakes. Plato thought light came from the eye and echoed off an object, combining with sunlight. Einstein, at first, did not believe discoveries in quantum mechanics, or of an expanding universe, but later accepted that he had been wrong.

The concept of an unknowable God is a difficult topic. John Steinbeck, Nobel Prize winning author, found it so. He took 5 years to write his 1933 novel: "To a God Unknown." This book explores some of the issues arising from adverse circumstances that challenge an individual's faith. Farmer Joseph Wayne attempts to understand the ways of God.

The FIFU contention that God is unknown is highly challengeable. Surely an Abrahamic God wants us to know? According to Biblical and other religious texts HE is very much a hands-on God, interceding most readily in the Old Testament, showing His powers with quite a number of miracles and responding to his followers' prayers - in one way or another. In more modern times He has been much more behind the scenes, so far behind as to be undetectable and unknowable to most people. HE does not need to be unknown. There is no need for such a mighty being to engage in highly disputable or easily dismissible hints. HE could make it abundantly clear that he exists and what He is about. Alternatively, HE could give us irrefutable clues so all of us can clearly work it out for ourselves. After all, if there is a God, it's Him that gave us our brains and reasoning abilities. Does He not want us to use them to unearth, hard, indisputable evidence?

What about evil?

A common argument against the existence of God is to say how can He, an all knowing and all powerful and all loving entity allow evil to exist? The main counter argument used by theists is that God has a morally sufficient reason for allowing evil.

Timothy Keller in his book, 'The Reason for God', says that just because people don't see a reason why God allows evil it does not mean there isn't one. In answer to this point two questions can be asked:

Is the traditional God omnipotent, i.e. all powerful? If so, He can make everything conform to his will. The answer all Christians and other Abrahamic religions give is an unqualified "YES", God is super-super capable.

Question 2, does this God want evil to exist? Answer, "NO", otherwise there would not be all the Biblical incitements to be 'good", also we would not have the constant threat of hell for those falling into evil ways.

So, because evil exists, either God is not all powerful and cannot do anything about evil, because evil is a more powerful force than God, or He is capable of doing something about evil and suffering - often the two go hand-in-hand - but chooses not to do so. If the latter is the answer, this puts a hole in the purported kind and loving God - a few examples of this, mostly New Testament, version of God: the Jesus, who cured a leper, the Jesus who raised Lazarus from the dead, the Jesus who fed the 5,000 because they were a bit peckish and the Jesus who kept the party going by turning water into wine. The God of the Old Testament is a different kettle of fish, starting with turfing Adam and Eve out of Eden because of that apple. But the broad theological consensus is that it is a kind and loving God.

Timothy Keller suggests that, evil and suffering can be good for you, and that's why God allows it. He illustrates this through the Biblical story of Joseph who was sold as a slave by his jealous brothers, enduring years of misery. Apparently though, this experience strengthened his character and he made good in the end, becoming a leader of Egypt, sort of. God knew what he was doing, seemingly in making Joseph suffer. It was all for the best. This argument does not hold water. There are numerous examples of people making the grade without having to endure great suffering. God, if he exists, could allow this to be the case for all. However, there are probably hundreds of millions of human beings, throughout history, who have endured suffering, of one type or another, maybe through chronic disease, injury, starvation, deprivation, unfair treatment, and perhaps seeing their children or other loved ones suffer because of horrible circumstances. They have not gained any advantage from this suffering. These people will not join Timothy in saying these heinous occurrences are obviously for the best in the long run.

Augustine saw the problem of having both evil alongside a benevolent and omnipotent God. He said that evil was just a deficiency of good. About 600 years after Augustine Alvin Plantinga cleverly associates the reason for God allowing humans to have freewill (Libertarianism), is so they are then free to decide whether to be good or bad. To allow either of these states, evil must exist. There are strong counter arguments against the free will idea. How is it that an all-knowing God, cannot know what is happening and will happen? Someone with those super-extreme capabilities He is claimed to have tells us He is outside of time. Time cannot be something that impacts on Him. HE is in charge of time and everything that happens. For God, everything past, present and future is 'now', just as Parmenides said in "The Way of Truth", 2,400 years ago. In these circumstances how can He fail to know what humans will get up to. Can He turn a blind eye, somehow? That would require a lot of turning, or perhaps a lack of eyes would do the trick.

[Figure: Small illustration: Cartoon/sketch of a figure with a magnifying glass]

The Oxford Companion to Philosophy says: "The problem of evil has always been the most powerful objection to traditional theism." Yes, evil and the traditional Abrahamic God do not go together, nor does freewill.

Acceptance - Top of The Pile

Many, probably most religious believers, are so because of where they live. Location, location, location is the key. People don't necessarily make an in-depth study of various competing religions, or of atheism and humanism before deciding what it is they believe or don't believe.

They mostly hold a particular belief because of where they live, or in a few cases, who they marry. For example, someone in Rome is likely to be a Roman Catholic, while a Tel Aviv resident will most probably be a Jew and if you live in Mumbai the odds are that you are a Hindu and so on. People tend to accept the religion and beliefs that they are born with and which surround them. Life is much easier this way. They accept their religious situation. Just imagine telling your Islamic parents in Teheran that, after careful consideration, you have decided to give up on Islam and become a Christian. Even worse, a son of strict, orthodox Jews in Tel Aviv would have a very hard time with his parents were he to tell them he was marrying a Muslim girl and was going to convert to Islam. These scenarios are barely conceivable, and highly unlikely. Those areas, cities, or countries, which are predominantly of a particular faith throw up, over time, very clever, or just dogmatic individuals. These seek to draw up a justification for the faith they have been born to. This process helps make every follower toe the line.

The Pew Research Centre's (PRC) 2012 findings, following a global survey, confirm that generally, peoples religious beliefs are those of the country they live in: "Nearly three-quarters (73%) of the world's people live in countries in which their religious group makes up a majority of the population." They also found that adults under age 40 were much less likely than older adults to say religion was important in their lives. Older and younger adults tend to be members of the religion that is most prominent in their locality, a natural acceptance of the status quo. So, location-based ACCEPTANCE is the greatest reason why people have a particular religious belief.

[Figure: Diagram showing silhouettes of people with arrows pointing down to text]

Acceptance

The powerful influence of local environment.

"I don't want to be the odd one out. I accept without question the religion of my family and neighbours."

Oxford Dictionary definition of acceptance:
"Agreement with or belief in an idea or explanation."

How the religious mountain was built

It started 300k ago, with very little, and built up to something high and wide.

![Diagram: An inverted pyramid/triangle showing layers from bottom to top:

Bottom (widest): "Acceptance"
"Religious texts"
"Ultimate comfort blanket"
"Safety deposit box"
"Evolutionary advantage"
"The six proofs + 1: COTHAM + PSR"
Top (point at bottom labeled): "FIFU"]

Beliefs began with various forms of spiritualism in mankind's early, pre-historic days. Since then it has built up into a mighty edifice, supported by carrots, sticks and unthinking acceptance. This mountain, because it's pointedly standing on its head, defies logic and science. Some atheists may see this as highly appropriate to religion.

Consider this from Chaucer:

Persuasive clerics:

How, more specifically, do shamans, priests, vicars, monks, imams and miscellaneous clerics of all creeds underpin the religious mountain? They certainly ensure that it does not collapse.

To achieve this, they commonly insist on adherence to many rules concerning: behaviour - particularly sexual; rites and rituals; clothing and eating habits; and other requirements indicated by their interpretation of holy text, or what's best to support their own purposes, or those of national/local leaders. They cajole, justify, encourage, promise, threaten, punish and attempt to bury inconvenient truths - sometimes with the truthsayers.

[Figure: Two historical images showing religious figures/clergy from medieval or renaissance periods]

headings.text: How the religious mountain was built

pages.text:
Consider this medieval example of religious rules and priestly chastisement from Chaucer's Canterbury Tales (1475 CE):

THE FRIAR'S TALE

Once on a time there dwelt in my country
An archdeacon, a man of high degree,
Who boldly executed the Church's frown
In punishment of fornication known,
And of witchcraft and of all known bawdry,
And defamation and adultery
Of church-wardens, and of fake testaments
And contracts, and the lack of sacraments,
And still of many another kind of crime.
Which need not be recounted at this time,
And usury and simony also,
But unto lechers gave he greatest woe,
They should lament if they were apprehended.
And payers of short tithes to shame descended...

Clerics of the same religion, but of different sects, also argued in favour of the particular version of their religion. They were sometimes helped by brilliant authors like Anne Bronte. Here's part of her warning to Calvinists.

That none deserve eternal bliss I know;
Unmerited the grace in mercy given,
But none shall sink to everlasting woe.
That have not well deserved the wrath of heaven.

Anne Bronte (A Word to Calvinists 1843)

Calvinism was a reformed version of Protestantism. It arose in the 16th century via John Calvin, theologian.

Rather than making a threat, like Anne, religious persuasion can also take the form of acknowledgement of a common pleasure. Renowned for starting up an anti-Catholic Christianity, fierce, dogmatic Martin Luther said: "Whoever drinks beer, he is quick to sleep; whoever sleeps long, does not sin; whoever does not sin, enters Heaven! Thus, let us drink beer!" Brilliant logic Martin, you should be made the patron saint of all brewers.

[Figure: Image: Portrait of Martin Luther with caption "Martin Luther 1483 to 1546CE"]

Was Martin trying to drum up support for his new Lutheran, Protestantism from those who enjoyed a pint or two, or did he have interests in a brewery company?

Aside from past writers like Anne and Martin, there are modern authors who also try to argue the case for religion, sometimes while acknowledging there are problems in treating holy books as providing literal guidance. Karen Armstrong in her book "The Case For God" put it like this: "Religion was never supposed to provide answers that lay within the reach of human reason. That was the role of logos. Religion's task, closely allied to that of art, was to help us live creatively, peacefully and even joyously with realities for which there are no easy explanations and problems that we could not solve: mortality, pain, grief, despair, and outrage at the injustice and cruelty of life."

If it is indeed religion's task to encourage people to live creatively, peacefully and joyously the evidence of history shows it has failed spectacularly. For thousands of years there have been wars, either in religion's name, or because of religion. These have resulted in much death and destruction, throughout the whole of history. This inducement, though not yet succeeding at institutional level, is demonstrated by individual people of all and no religion, these are the community minded TDF crowd explained in Chapter 22. The last part of Karen's quote suggests accepting the worst life may offer - pain, grief, despair cruelty and injustice. This is similar to Timothy Keller. Many would say this has the wrong emphasis. These things should not just be too readily accepted. Attempts should be made to prevent or correct them, by individuals, groups and government, even if solutions are not immediately available. If the Abrahamic God exists, these bads should not be there at all.

A rather cynical analysis of the devout was made by Nobel Prize winning French poet, Anatole France: "Devout believers are safeguarded in a high degree against the risk of certain neurotic illnesses; their acceptance of the universal neurosis spares them the task of constructing a personal one."

Along similar lines to Anatole a psychological term could also be applied to some of this Godly thinking: "The Argument from Ignorance". This simply says it is a fallacy to say something is true because it has not yet been proven false.

[Figure: Image: Portrait with caption "John Locke, perhaps originator of The Argument from Ignorance?"]

In essence, there are holes in all of the claimed proofs and in the FIFU defence. Additionally, the problems of evil and freewill remain just that - a problem.

chapters.title: Why to What
chapters.summary: What are the monotheistic Godly attributes? Richard Feynman and Baron D'Holbach criticisms, Einstein's God supporting illustration of a child in a library.

pages.text:
Chapter 4

Why to What

We are still concentrating on the monotheistic, Abrahamic God, mainly because He has the most supporters, not only nowadays but also much of the historic past. HE's the one worshipped currently, and for the past two thousand years, by more religious people on Earth than any other God(s). Billions have knelt or bowed before him.

What are the Godly Abilities and Attributes?

The "why" of God line of reasoning points to the litany of needs Modern Humans, from ancient times, had for a God, these were so strong it caused them to search for and eventually invent/discover the one God. From this we can infer God's attributes and capabilities to warrant all the roles vested in Him through the "why" quizology. Theologians and religious authorities are renowned for their desire to help us with this understanding of God. Through them we know that these Godly abilities and attributes are broad and deep - right up to kick starting the universe and living forever. HE has also to be a kind, loving and merciful entity. Most importantly, HE must provide His faithful with an eternally blissful after-life, called Heaven by Christians. These are desired and persuasive attributes - the carrot referred to in earlier chapters.

In addition, for many people, He must be tagged as a being to be feared; a judgmental God capable of having people, who do not toe the Godly line, condemned to eternal damnation - the stick. In fact, He has a multitude of hoops to jump through. To achieve all that's wanted of Him God has to be a being with the most extreme capabilities. HE must have a full set of "alls":

all knowing;
all powerful;
all where;
always.

Uniformly overall in fact - everything covered top to bottom. These core abilities are what God has to have to enable Him to guide, explain, understand and deliver. The needs of the faithful determine the "what" of God.

[Figure: Richard Feynman, 1918-1988, at Los Alamos, c.1943]

It's worth looking at what a great scientist said about the human need for God. Richard Feynman (Nobel prize winning American physicist and communicator of science) said: "God was invented to explain mystery. God is always invented to explain those things that you do not understand.

headings.text: What are the Godly Abilities and Attributes?

pages.text:
Now, when you finally discover how something works, you get some laws which you're taking away from God; you don't need Him anymore. But you need him for the other mysteries. So therefore, you leave Him to create the universe because we haven't figured that out yet; you need him for understanding those things which you don't believe the laws will explain, such as consciousness, or why you only live to a certain length of time - life and death - stuff like that. God is always associated with those things that you do not understand. Therefore, I don't think that the laws can be considered to be like God because they have been figured out."

Two hundred years before Richard Feynman a French/German philosopher, Baron d'Holbach, said something similar, but in a more brutally, blunt way:

[Figure: Baron Paul-Henri d'Holbach, 1723-1789, by Alexander Roslin]

"If we look back at the beginning we shall find that ignorance and fear created the Gods; that fancy, enthusiasm, or deceit adorned or disfigured them; that weakness worships them; that credulity preserves them; and that custom, respect and tyranny support them, in order to make the blindness of man serve their own interest. If the ignorance of nature gave birth to Gods, the knowledge of nature is calculated to destroy them. All religions are ancient monuments to superstitions, ignorance, ferocity; and modern religions are only ancient follies rejuvenated." A bit strong that Paul-Henri.

The Baron published his ideas anonymously, for fear of imprisonment or worse. In his time, the Catholic church had a lot of clout.

[Figure: Albert Einstein, 1921]

On the other hand, we have Albert Einstein, one of the greatest scientists of all time saying this: "I am not an atheist and I don't think I can call myself a pantheist [the belief that God and the material world are one and the same and that God is present in everything]. We are in the position of a little child entering a huge library filled with books in many languages. The child knows someone must have written those books. It does not know how. He does not understand the languages in which they are written. The child dimly suspects a mysterious order in the arrangement of the books but doesn't know what it is. That, it seems to me, is the attitude of even the most intelligent human being towards God. We see the universe marvelously arranged and obeying certain laws but only dimly understand these laws. Our limited minds cannot grasp the mysterious force that moves the constellations."

Einstein held a type of religious attitude based on admiration and wonder of our world and the wider universe.

This was well short of belief in a personal God. He expressed it like this: "A knowledge of the existence of something we cannot penetrate, of the manifestations of the profoundest reason and the most radiant beauty - it is this knowledge and this emotion that constitute the truly religious attitude; in this sense, and in this alone, I am a deeply religious man." and, "I do not believe in a personal God and I have never denied this but have expressed it clearly. If something is in me which can be called religious then it is the unbounded admiration for the structure of the world so far as our science can reveal it." (Albert Einstein, 1954)

Einstein's earlier point, that even the greatest human minds cannot conceive of what a God, or "mysterious force" is about, is an intriguing one. The force or God is way beyond our understanding, so argues Einstein. This could be said of Einstein too for most of us. Not many can do the maths behind the famous E=MC². God and His purpose will always remain something of a mystery, according to Einstein. This is a FIFU contention, but FIFU has flaws, as we have seen. Einstein also expanded his Anthropic argument, pointing, perhaps, to a deist view, by saying: "I see a pattern, but my imagination cannot picture the maker of that pattern. I see a clock, but I cannot envision the clockmaker."

[Figure: Circular diagram showing "Relativity" in the center with "The ordered cosmos" text, and "Quantum indeterminacy" with "Splat!" text below, illustrating the contrast between Einstein's ordered universe and quantum randomness]

The universal cosmic order that was at the heart of Einstein's belief was mostly, after his death, thrown into disorder by the proven randomness and incongruity found within the atom. This was discovered through developments in quantum mechanics, especially by the work of Pauli, Heisenberg and others. Would Einstein say the same things about God and atheism today? Maybe not, but we cannot know.

So, in determining the "what" of God. Some religious people point to a list of supreme abilities and attributes. For others, as suggested by Richard Feynman and Baron D'Holbach, God is given the ability to fill in the gaps not yet answered by science, but the gaps are progressively narrowing. No matter how small the gaps, Einstein thinks we are not capable of knowing the answer to the "what" question.

chapters.title: When Coming up and Noth's Story
chapters.summary: When did a God, or spirits first become important to modern humans? A brief look at the stone-age. Genius stone-ager Noth, his fictional story leading to Sun and Moon Gods, and move to the Palaeolithic Transition.

pages.text:
Chapter 5

When Coming up Now and Noth's Story

So far, the why and what of God has been explained. This, is partly conjectural, although based on a strong thread of reasoning. We move on to consider the issue of when God first became important to men. In this chapter concrete, pre-historic data will be presented showing man's interest in a form of spirituality. We will see what solid evidence - literally solid - has been uncovered to demonstrate spiritual aspects from the dawn, or early morning of mankind - the Stone Age.

[Figure: Neanderthal hunters and flint-workers at Le Moustier, with their stone-tipped weapons and tools (Charles R. Knight, 1920) - a spear-carrier stands beside people knapping flint]

When was it that mankind became interested in some kind of God? If He's been around always it follows that there ought to be some record of Him throughout every age of mankind. Modern Humans, that is Homo Sapiens, have existed for about 300,000 years, with a nod to those impatient Creationists. I'm going to try and ignore them from now on. They can really cramp one's style for ages.

For a good chunk of this time (the 300k years) there were no recording and communications mechanisms like computers or mobile phones. One could be excused in calling this the pre-text age, but this period is more correctly known as the age of pre-history, or more commonly, the Stone Age. The implements and tips of hunting weapons were made of stone; hence the name Stone Age. There is yet another name for it. The Palaeolithic era is its scientific name, in a European context.

headings.text: When Coming up Now and Noth's Story

pages.text:
Stone Age man couldn't write, let alone send Text messages. This wasn't because he was high on drugs. This was the stone, not the stoned, age. He couldn't write because there were no biros or paper, and he had not invented a written language. However, eventually he could shape objects and paint, he could imagine and wonder and he could develop a view of the world and his place in it.
Mankind was short on numbers back then in pre-historic times. There were an estimated 20 million people on Earth at 30,000 BCE, one for about every 240 who exist today. This meant Stone Age hunter gatherers were very interested in fertility. The promise of new life was vital. It ensured continuance of the sparse family, clan or tribe.

Once people became too old or incapable of hunting they could not fall back on the state for help through meals-on-wheels and other social services. The only recourse they had was to look to kith and kin for aid. The old, who could no longer hunt or gather food, ("old" is a relative term with the average lifespan around 27), would either be looked after by the young, or they would wither and die. An adequate food supply was essential to survival and continuance, but food resources were often precarious, especially in winter. Stone Age mums could not just pop down to the supermarket when they ran out of muesli. This might explain why, once Stone Agers got into painting and sculpture they generally chose prey animals and fertility figures as their subjects; more on these later.

[Figure: Bryn Celli Ddu, a Neolithic passage tomb on Anglesey]

Because of the lack of written evidence from these pre-historic times, much remains a mystery to us of mans' pagan beliefs. But we have indicators that strongly suggest Palaeolithic man was likely to have had some form of belief in the supernatural or spirit world. This has been reasonably conjectured from the many "earth mother", fertility Goddess, carved figurines that have been excavated and from other evidence. Archaeologists have discovered that the bones of certain of the dead were laid out in a seemingly ritualistic way and the bodies buried with earthly objects.

The objects could be intended to be of help to the dead person's spirit in the spirit world. Then there are the skulls, not only human but also those of cave bears. The way these were placed indicates they might have been associated with some form of religious ceremony. This is the hard evidence we have, together with a number of cave drawings.

We will look at all this in more detail after Noth's story. Who or what is Noth you might ask? Well, wait a bit, all will be revealed in less than a young male attendant at a royal court (i.e. in a page)

We also know something of the environment within which Palaeolithic man lived. It was a harsh, hand to mouth existence. Death was never far away. Infant mortality was high and life expectancy short.

Unlike other animals, humans had high intelligence and an ability to conjecture. This would have led them to wonder about the world around them. At every age of mankind wonder and speculation has been core human attributes. These always lead to the desire and search for certainty or an acceptable truth. Stone Age man would not have been any different. But much more of the world was a mystery to him than it is to us now. Where did animals, trees and plants, come from? Why were some hunts successful and some not? Why was the weather on occasion amenable and at other times furiously unreasonable? How and why did people get sick and sometimes die? What happened to people when they died? The mighty sun, the moon and the stars, what roles did these play, in the material and spirit world?

Such thoughts must have crossed the mind of some Stone Age people. These early humans did not have the advantages of the knowledge we enjoy today. There was no weight of scientific study in zoology; botany, geology, climatology, astronomy and other sciences. They could not log on to the Internet to find the answer. Palaeolithic man had to arrive at some simpler understanding of all the mysteries and unknowns of the world he inhabited. It is a natural human tendency to seek out some form of answer. In the lack of any other explanation spirits or Gods could have been invented to help fill in Stone-agers gaps in knowledge and understanding of the natural world, the "safety deposit box" syndrome, referred to in the previous chapter. So, pre-historic religious beliefs would have acted as a spiritual polyfilla. They conveniently filled in holes in the comprehension that ancient humans had of their world. This embryonic religiosity established the first hillock of a religious mountain that was to grow and grow over subsequent millennia.
Let's borrow Dr Who's time machine, the Tardis, and travel back 35,000 years and take a brief look at what's going on in one Stone Age family. We arrive during a time sometimes referred to as the Transition. Modern man is still the hunter gatherer he's been for millennia. His tools are of flint and stone, as they have been for the preceding 265,000 years. Now though, they have become more sophisticated and varied. Great changes are afoot, truly a major shift from what has gone before.

In this period of transformation modern man is not only developing his hunting weapons and creative abilities, more importantly, he's improving his language skills. In addition, he also pushes out, or kills and replaces, his primitive cousin and predecessor, the Neanderthals. These intelligent hominids lived in Europe and elsewhere before Homo Sapiens arrival. The Tardis, our time machine, takes us back 35 millennia to a place in what is now southern France, close to the Spanish border, and within a few miles of the Mediterranean Sea:

The flickering fire chased shadows across the rock face of the cave. Noth absent mindedly added another log to the glowing embers. It was late at night. He'd been up for hours after his family had gone to their bed furs. Cassea, his wife, had fallen asleep last. Looking across the fire, to the back of the cave, Noth can see the five of them huddled in their furs. Cassea was nearest to him, her black hair shrouding a round face; still beautiful even though she was now over 23 years old. Noth smiled tenderly. His eyes shifted from Cassea to his three children. They were all a man could wish for. Huddled close on Cassea's left was Lurco; the youngest at seven years old, Lurco was inquisitive and alert. His interest extended to everything. He asked questions non-stop. On the other side of her mother slept Semith, his daughter. Her sharp features and fair hair were in keeping with her nature. She was like a little jewel. She sparkled and darted everywhere, full of laughter. Every clan hearth brightened up when Semith paid a visit. Tam, a little away from his two siblings, was the eldest. He was tall and strong for a young boy. In temperament, he was calm and wise beyond his 10 years. He helped Cassea with the younger two, as did Cassea's mother, Letia. She was at the back of the cave, sleeping in the heaviest furs. Her grey hair and lined face were a testament to her 36 years. Noth turned back to look again at his son Tam. Today, had been a milestone for Tam. For the first time, he had gone on the hunt, with Noth and three other clan adults. Tam was instructed before they started out. He was told to move quietly and keep still when signalled.

He had always to remain at the back of the group, with his father. Tam found it hard to keep up with the adults, but Noth was proud that his son never complained of the pace and had not fallen behind.

The hunters made for a river that danced and tumbled through a valley in the mountain foothills. It was just a morning's fast walk from the clan's camp and a favourite place for the clan to hunt. Animals often came down to the stream bank to drink. A good hunter was sure to make a kill. The hunters skirted the river, remaining alert and quiet. They picked their way between dense shrubs and trees before halting at the edge of a small clearing. Here the river bank sloped shallowly down to the swift stream. And there was their prey, standing in the shallow water. Tam was not allowed to take a direct role in the kill of the slowly limping great stag. A spear was deeply embedded in its left flank. This had clearly weakened the deer, so the kill was easy and quick for the experienced hunters. They gave humble thanks to the spirit of the deer in a brief ceremony. This concluded with Tam, having to drink blood of the kill; signifying a new hunter's rite of passage.

Noth pulled out the strange spear and examined it closely. Its point had been crudely struck from a flint and was roughly bound to a heavy wooden shaft. It lacked the sophistication and good balance of a human spear. He knew at once that it was a weapon of the low-brows. There were still some around. Humans and low-brows tried to avoid each other. There had been many more low-brows when Noth's clan came to the area some 8 years ago, but most of them had gone since then. The four adult hunters staggered slowly home each dragging two poles hitched over their shoulders with a hide stretched between.
