Tam was pleased that he was allowed to carry the low-brows' spear back to the clan dwelling caves. Children excitedly crowded around the hunters when they returned, Semith skipping between Noth and Tam. Lurco wanted to know why Tam was carrying a strange spear. Cassea was relieved that Tam and Noth were back safely from the hunt. Letia knew Tam would be thirsty and had a drink ready for him. After gulping cool water from the drinking horn, Tam was ready to tell his tale to a big audience. These were mostly children but some adults too wanted to hear from the clan's newest hunter and find out more about the strange spear. Noth recalled the serious and unassuming way that Tam told his story of the hunt. Tam praised his fellow hunters and did not try and claim any of the credit, nor did he dwell on the arduousness of the return journey. Noth knew that Tam had shown by his conduct that he would be a clan leader one day.

He had told of the day's hunt accurately and without embellishment, to the slight disappointment of some of the children. They wanted to hear a wilder, even more exciting tale. Noth was enjoying his reminiscence of the past day, but knew he must stop and plan for something that would cause a great upheaval in his clan and probably in other clans too. The children were going to get their excitement soon, although not in any way that they could anticipate.

Noth got up from the fire side and walked to the cave entrance. The cave was low down on a rocky hill side. But it was still some way above the valley floor. He could make out the shape of trees in the gloom. The sounds of the night-time drifted up to him from the woods below. He recognized all of them. There was the hoot of an owl, the barking of a fox nearby, and very faintly, in the distance, he could identify the sound of a wolf-pack. He raised his head to study the night sky. Dominating the sky was a pock marked white ball; the full moon. It was haloed with a host of twinkling lights. He felt a thrill of excitement. He had worked it all out clearly in his mind. At last he understood, after months of thinking. He now knew how the moon, the stars and the mighty sun fitted into the world of spirits, especially those elemental entities; the Earth mother and the spirit of the hunt, symbolized by the clan rock paintings and the mighty cave bear. The spirits occupied a mystical realm, beyond the material world around him; one that only the clan shamans had regular access to. The shamans though were conservative and repetitive. They repeated the traditional mantras at every clan event that honoured the spirits. Noth had become increasingly dissatisfied at the shamans limited view of the spirit world. For some time he had thought that the mighty sun; moon and countless stars must have a role too, although the shamans never mentioned them.

Noth did not know it, but he was a genius. He was able to conceptualise and use his high intelligence in ways that no one else in his clan, or in most other clans, could. He was capable of exploring areas of thought outside the demands of day-to-day living in a harsh environment. Analysis, interpretation and origination came relatively easily to him, even though he was wholly unaware of this terminology. As he studied the face of the moon Noth felt a light touch on his arm. Cassea was at his side. She smiled and leant her head on his shoulder. "Why are you up so late Noth? You need your rest after the hunt today." "I've been thinking, mostly about Tam and the hunt." said Noth. "I know you, my husband." responded Cassea, "that's not all you've been pondering. For months now you've had that faraway look on your face whenever you get more than a few minutes free."
Noth was the youngest elder of the clan. Cassea appreciated that he was highly respected for his knowledge of animals, their habits and the best way to track and catch them. When cave bears and other larger prey were scarce last winter the clan hunters attempted to spear river fish, but the fish often slid back into the water off the spear point. It was Noth who had the idea of making a shallow notch in the spear point, to hook on to the fish. The clan was amazed at the effectiveness of this innovation. Soon boys were spearing fish as well as adult hunters. Cassea speculated that Noth was about to come out with another important new idea. She did not know what it was though and was determined to get Noth to tell her, so she went on: "You've been planning something haven't you?" Noth looked sideways at her; did Cassea know what he had been thinking? It wouldn't surprise him. She was so astute. He sometimes wondered whether she could read his mind. He decided it was time she knew: "I wanted to tell you Cassea, but not before I was sure. Look up, what do you see?" Cassea did as Noth asked and craned her neck: "I see a black, black night sky studded with little lights. Of course, I can also see the round face of our moon. It's shining on us so brightly tonight." Noth nodded: "I'm sure I know what those lights are Cassea." and he went on: "The shamans say that when we die, our spirits move into the spirit world above. But they have never been able to explain exactly where this world is that the spirits inhabit. I think the shamans "world above" is as we see it now. Each one of those flickering lights, stars, is an ancestor. They are our departed kith and kin looking down on us."

Cassea studied the lights more closely: "There are so many." "Yes, there has to be." said Noth. "Think how many generations have died and passed into the spirit world." This was a new concept to Cassea, but she realized the spirits must go somewhere above. "Yes, I can understand what you say husband. Perhaps that is why the lights twinkle, our ancestors are trying to keep in touch with us, their Earthly brethren." Noth was slightly taken aback at Cassea's perception. "There is more." he said, "The ancestor-stars are many but small. They sit above us at night with the moon. The moon is much bigger than any star, even when it hides part of itself. On cloudless nights, it gives us gentle light. It must be an important spirit." "Is that its only role, to sometimes give us light in the darkness?" said Cassea, Noth put his arm around Cassea's waist. Then replied: "No, there's the sun too. The moon has a role linked to the sun I think. How essential the sun is for us. It lights our day much more brightly than the moon, so we can hunt. The cave bear spirit is only captured when the sun lights the way of our hunters. The sun warms us and at winter's end it melts the frost and snow. Great Mother Earth waits for the sun to awaken her from her winter's slumber. Earth life is renewed every spring through the gentle caress of the sun's golden rays.
New plants begin to grow and leaves uncurl on the bare branches of trees. The sun must be the mightiest spirit to achieve all this, yet we do not recognize this or honour it, as we should." Cassea: "Yes, perhaps this is why no one can look on the face of such a powerful spirit when it shines in a bright blue sky. But, if the sun is the greatest of spirits, what is the moon?" Noth was pleased that Cassea had so readily accepted his ideas. He eagerly responded: "The moon gives a softer light than the sun. It's much smaller and usually gives way to the sun, although they are sometimes together in the sky above us. I think the moon is like a woman. I believe it is the wife of the sun. We must honour her too."

Six weeks later, at the mid-summer gathering of all the local clans, Noth stood and spoke powerfully about his beliefs. He had intelligently paved the way beforehand. His own clan shaman and chief knew that Noth would make an important revelation about the spirit world. The shaman was uneasy over the prospect of anyone meddling in his territory, but he respected Noth. It also helped that Noth had told him that his shaman status would be enhanced after he had spoken.

Nearly a hundred and fifty people listened entranced to Noth as he wove his tale with eloquence and conviction. Many glanced up at the sky as he spoke. They hoped to catch a clearer sign of the sky spirits that Noth told of. By co-incidence as the camp fires blazed in the darkening early night, a shooting star wove a fiery trail across the heavens. Then another followed and finally a third.

People shouted in awe at the sight. Noth seized on this chance to prove his case. He pointed dramatically skywards and said: "Look, the sun, moon and ancestral spirits have been listening to me. They tell us that I am right. They want our respect and honour."

Noth did not know it but he had started a revolution in Palaeolithic man's concept of the spirit world. A decade later, after Noth had died, Tam had first taken over the chieftainship of the clan. An enraged cave bear killed Tam in the first year of his leadership. Lurco was the natural successor to Tam. His sharp wit, perception and boundless energy helped him, in time, to become a great clan chief. Semith became known and respected by everyone. She always wanted to help, especially when death marked a transition to the spirit world. She easily took up the role of a revered female shaman. Together with Lurco, she promoted and spread her father, Noth's, revolutionary ideas among many clans.

The concept of a sun and moon God took thousands of years to spread among the Homo Sapiens communities. This was because people were few on the planet and distances great when walking is the main means of transport. Communication between far flung communities was slow and infrequent. But Noth's ideas endured for thousands of years. They were taken up and developed by the Mesolithic people who eventually built the first Mesopotamian town - Eridu and the first city of Sumer - Uruk.

Of course, this is just a story made up by me, the author of this book. Noth, Cassea, Tam and the rest did not exist. Noth was but a figment of imagination. He was, in effect nothing. Hence his name, "Noth". But "Nothing" can sometimes give rise to something. Our Universe started from nothing - if this is what preceded the point of singularity 13.8 billion years ago. Look at what's become of that particular "nothing". From it a great deal of "something" has arisen with the multitude of galaxies, stars and planets that now populate the cosmos. Noth's story may also lead us to something, not remotely on the scale of the expanding singularity of course. There must have been very clever people like Noth in the transitional period from Middle to Upper Palaeolithic. Incidentally, this period was also known as the Late Stone Age, especially in reference to Africa. Another name for it is the Reindeer Age, for more obvious reasons, i.e. there were a lot of reindeer about.

[Figure: A herd of reindeer in the snow (c.1900)]

Some palaeontologists refer to this time as the Upper Palaeolithic Revolution. Whatever the terminology used - Transition; Late Stone Age, Reindeer Age; or the Upper Palaeolithic Revolution - it lasted between 45,000 and 20,000 years ago. Because it's a time of change, Transition probably best describes this new period.

chapters.title: Why Transition, and what is it exactly?
chapters.summary: Big improvement in language, tools, art. Cave paintings at Sulawesi, Lascaux, Chauvet and their significance. Cult of the cave bear, voluptuous Venus.

pages.text:
Chapter 6

Why Transition, and what is it exactly?

No one seems to know why the Transition, or Upper Palaeolithic Revolution, occurred when it did. After a more or less static period for Modern Humans, in technical, linguistic and artistic development lasting about 260,000 years major changes occur. These were briefly referred to earlier. But it's important to know more precisely what the new developments were during this time. For a start, Noth type individuals (see previous chapter) would have led the development in religious understanding and belief, despite this was largely restricted to a spirit world and shamanistic practices.

Apart from Noth and religious change, new developments took place in three areas:

Tools - both hunting and other tools;
language;
art.

Perhaps, through the necessity of adapting to climate change and prey availability, Stone Age man invents more sophisticated and delicate stone tools. These are differentiated and made for specific purposes: for example, burins for working antler bone or for drawing. Harpoons and darts were made along with other piercing points for hunting weapons and for more delicate needles, these were used for sewing clothes. There are also the very first signs of fishing. We know this from finds at the Blombos caves in South Africa. Upper Palaeolithic man's language develops allowing him to communicate more clearly, although some palaeontologists debate this. What is indisputable is that he also engages in activities like rock painting and more elaborate ritual burial.

It is a little misleading to suggest these changes "suddenly" happened. This is only correct if measured against a geological timescale. If we compare the rate of change in the Palaeolithic Transition to other major technical and culture transformatory periods, it's like comparing a tortoise to a race horse or cheetah. The Industrial Revolution lasted at most a couple of hundred years from Victorian times. The more recent Space Age and Computer Age have been around for much shorter timescales still. The Transition period took place over a more leisurely period; a few tens of thousands of years in fact.

Cave Paintings

headings.text: Why Transition, and what is it exactly?

pages.text:
Of all the products of the Transition, archaeologists have pondered most over the mysteries of Palaeolithic rock paintings. This Stone Age art has intrigued palaeontologists for ages past. Particularly enthralling is the Upper Palaeolithic period when Homo Sapiens artists were daubing and scratching on cave walls. What was their purpose? Were the images simply a form of artistic expression without any significant underlying meaning? Did they relate in some way to the lives that people led at the time? Was there any spiritual or religious meaning? What was the reason for the chosen subject matter?

Favourite, but unintended models, were the animals Stone Age hunters pursued. The depiction of prey animals and hunting scenes was a general feature of ancient cave galleries. This may be associated with a form of spiritual belief. There is a commonality but not absolute uniformity between the various cave galleries. The paintings do show some variations, not surprising when considering they are found in different, widely separated locations and are sometimes thousands of years apart. However, what they definitely all have in common is a complete lack of depiction of a white, bearded old man, thundering down edicts from a fleecy cloud. If God had been involved in influencing the thoughts of Stone Age artists, then one might expect to see some clearer evidence of His remotely controlled brush-work.

It is possible that Godly influence, if there was any, was subtler in nature and because of this open to some misinterpretation by the painter. Of course, the issue then becomes why a supremely powerful God allows any form of misinterpretation.

Cave paintings have been found all over the habitable world. Some of the most ancient are at East Kalimantan in Borneo. Thousands of paintings have been found here. A hand stencil dates back 52,000 years and paintings of aurochs are 40,000 years old.

[Figure: Cro-Magnon artists painting woolly mammoths by lamplight in the cave of Font-de-Gaume, France, as painted by Charles R. Knight in 1920]

In India, there are Bhimbetka rock shelters with paintings dating from 30,000 years ago. Indonesia though, has the current prize for the oldest figurative artwork at Sulawesi. Here, rock paintings have been discovered which are nearly 40,000 years old. They show dwarf buffaloes and mammals being hunted by figures part-human and part-animal. It may be the scene was painted over a number of years. Adam Brumm, archaeologist at the Research Centre for Human Evolution at Griffith University, Australia said:
"We were stunned by the implications of this image," and "It suggested to us that this extraordinary scene suggests a story or some kind of myth." This seems clear evidence that some rock paintings, or perhaps all of them, are associated with stories of a world beyond man.

[Figure: Cave painting at Leang Karampuang, Sulawesi, Indonesia, about 51,000 years old]

But the best-known and most prolific region for these paintings is Europe, particularly in France and Spain. Nearly 350 sites have been discovered in these two countries. The artistic endeavors of our ancestors in gloomy rock shelters cover a span of more than 20,000 years; dating from the Upper Palaeolithic to the Neolithic age. Some of the earliest, i.e. Upper Palaeolithic were found at the Chauvet-Pont-d'Arc cave, in the Ardeche region of southern France. This cave is huge and contains a series of chambers. It would have made fine living accommodation for a Stone Age clan. The animals depicted on the walls were drawn by skilled artists approximately 32,000 years ago. An unusual feature is the subject matter of the paintings. Normally these would be hunting scenes, depicting prey animals, but many of the animals on the rock walls of Chauvet are dangerous. They include lions; bears and rhinoceros. Perhaps the Chauvet clansmen were particularly macho, and liked to court with danger when hunting!

The most famous cave paintings are those found at Lascaux, in the Dordogne region of France. Some 600 images have been discovered here, dating back 17,000 years. Lascaux is the Stone Age equivalent of the National Portrait Gallery. Except that most images are of horses, stags and bison. These animal animals were of more interest and importance to Stone Agers than the human animal of latter-day portraitists.

[Figure: Lascaux, Dordogne, France: painted aurochs and horses (replica)]

There are some human images too but not many. One is of a man who has a bird's head. It's suggested he could be a shaman, who carried out rituals in the cave. Other theories say some of the paintings are linked with the constellations of the Pleiades and Taurus. These might be associated with ritual dancing. In some cases, this can induce trances and cause visions. What is for sure is at Lascaux there was no Palaeolithic equivalent of Constable, or Turner either, because landscapes are notable by their absence.

The archaeologist, Lewis-Williams, has drawn an interesting parallel between Palaeolithic rock art, typified by Chauvet and Lascaux, with that of the modern San bushmen of the Kalahari. He suggests that by studying the San we can get a clue as to why Stone Age artists depicted mainly prey animals. The San used their drawings as a link to the spirit world. Perhaps Stone Age man had this intention too. Curiously, this has some vague similarity with Plato's idea of "perfect forms" as the essence of animals.

Cult of The Bear

It was not only through cave paintings that Stone Agers depicted their spiritual attachment to prey animals (assuming Lewis-Williams is correct). Palaeolithic people had some affinity with cave bears; massive creatures, up to 800 kilograms in weight. We know this from the thousands of cave bear skulls found. Some of these were seemingly placed in specific positions which could indicate a type of spiritual ritual. We also know, from ancient cultures that still survive into fairly modern times, that the cult of the bear is not uncommon. Bear cultism survived mostly in Northern Polar Regions.

The Aino people (in their language their name means people, who number about 150,000 in Japan still have a bear God named Kamui which is also a general name for Gods. They eat bears believing the meat and fur was a gift from their God.

[Figure: Chauvet, France: horses and other animals painted about 30,000 years ago (replica)]

Other Northern ethnic groups to engage in bear worship include the Sami (or Laplanders); pre-Christian Finns and the Nivkh. The latter are now just a few thousands occupying land in the vicinity of the Amur River in Russia. They still practice shamanism and hold a winter Bear Festival. They think the bear is an earthly materialisation of both ancestors and Gods.

Voluptuous Venus

So, we have some archaeological evidence of cave paintings with a possible spiritual dimension; ritual burial and cave bear cultism. What else is there that indicates shamanistic, primal religion abounded in the Stone Age and after?

Well, there have also been finds of voluptuous female figurines symbolizing not only fertility but the important status of women in Stone Age societies. Of the figurines, one of the best known is the Venus of Willendorf. This carved figure was discovered in 1908 near Willendorf in Austria. It dates from about 23,000 to 25,000 years ago. An even older Venus figurine was found in 2008 at Schelklingen, Germany - the Venus of Hohle Fels. It dates from at least 35,000 years ago. That suggests pre-historic Venus sculptors were at it for at least 10,000 years; not quite as long as their cave painting brethren, but still an impressive period of time.

[Figure: Venus of Willendorf, Austria, about 25,000 years old]

Most Venus figurines were found in Europe but discoveries stretch to Eurasia, with the furthest find, so far, at Lake Baikal in western Russia.

These small sculptures are thought to represent either an Earth mother Goddess or fertility charm, perhaps both. Either way they were a symbolic object to which Palaeolithic man, or woman, attached some form of supernatural or spiritual power.

Much of the Stone Age focus so far has been on Europe. That's because we have more evidence from here of the Palaeolithic Transition than anywhere else. But Homo Sapiens populated nearly all of the rest of the planet before they were found in Europe. How and when did this happen? Well, let's have a look at the story of mankind's, i.e. Homo Sapiens, origin and associated dispersal theories. As Prof. Alice Roberts said in 2008: "We're all members of a young species... Wherever we've ended up, all over the world, we're Africans under the skin. And uncovering that story, retracing the steps of our ancestors, has given me a profound sense of our common humanity: our shared past, and our shared future"

Uncovering the human story reveals much about why many humans hold belief in supernatural entities.

chapters.title: Out of Africa
chapters.summary: Homo Sapiens evolution from Homo Heidelbergensis or Homo Erectus. Mankind's origin, Ethiopia or Morocco? Single origin theory. The Red Sea crossing at Bab el Mandeb to populate Earth. Eve, Earth mother. Mighty volcano Toba almost wipes out modern humans.

pages.text:
Chapter 7

Out of Africa

Where did we all come from? Yes, I know you know, but aside from the womb, or even maternalistic storks, where did Homo Sapiens, sometimes called Modern Humans (MH) originate? The hot money, and even the slightly warm dosh, is on Africa. This is known as the single origin, out of Africa theory. It says that all Modern Humans originate from Africa. This is backed up by impressive analysis of mitochondrial DNA. The genetic evidence strongly suggests we all, apart from some Africans, have the same ancestral lineage, with an Africa origin.

A much less supported alternate theory of MH origin is the multi-regional model, which has a few variants. This model proposes that Homo Sapiens arose from evolutionary ancestors, possibly Homo Heidelbergensis or Homo Erectus, in several locations across the globe at about the same time. The multi-regional theory is now very much on the wane. Africa and the single origin is almost unassailed but not yet absolutely so.

If mankind's story started in Africa what evidence is there of very early human existence in that continent?

It follows that archaeological discoveries in Africa of MH ought to be the oldest found on planet Earth. Holding the prize for nearly 40 years, as the location with the oldest finds of MH, was at Omo, Ethiopia. Here, in 1967, Richard Leakey uncovered evidence of Modern Humans. His find revealed MH existence of about 200,000 years ago. But in 2004 fresh discoveries at Jebel Irhoud, Morocco were made by Jean-Jacques Hublin.

[Figure: The Jebel Irhoud skull, Morocco, about 300,000 years old, among the oldest known Homo sapiens fossils]

Originally, the Jebel Irhoud remains were thought to be Neanderthal but since it's been suggested they are in fact MH bones, 300,000 years old. If confirmed, these will be the oldest remains of MH yet discovered (as at 2020). If we do originate from Morocco, that means we arrived after 99.8% of the cosmos' existence. We are new kids on the block.
Similar types of bones, now also thought likely to be of MH, have been found in Florisbad, South Africa. The Florisbad bones are dated to 260,000 years old. Archaeologists have not found traces of MH existence on any other continent dating this far back. It's all about Africa for many millennia.

Before going on further, a little bit of translation might be useful for those of us who are not Latin scholars. Modern Humans (MH) are technically known as Homo Sapiens. From the Latin, Homo means man and Sapiens wise. Despite we can all quote historical and personal evidence to the contrary, for the entirety of their existence on planet Earth, all MH are wise men.

What do we know about these wise men, the ancient Moroccan and other Africans. They were the earliest of our modern human ancestors. Not much to say about them, because they were few of them, so there has not been a great deal to find. There were about 10,000 MH in Africa, before the gradual dispersal to the rest of the world, possibly through a main migration 60,000 to 70,000 years ago. So, in the millennia before the dispersal to other continents there would have been far fewer than 10,000. Climate and geography were also not conducive to preserving archaeological clues of these very early MH. Finally, they lived in a pre-historic period which means we have no written evidence to help us.

One of the few ancient African artifacts that we know of are the pierced bead shells that were discovered at the Grotte des Pigeons, Taforalt in Morocco. The shells are dated 82,000 years ago. The Aterian, North African, culture they represent is now thought to be from at least 110,000 years past. Previous to the Taforalt find, the Blombos caves, in South Africa were in the lead as the earliest evidence of Modern Human behaviour. Here similar shell beads were dated to 72,000 years ago. Blombos also shows evidence of the use of ochre, a red colouring agent. This has no useful purpose and can only be used for ornamentation. Also discovered was some abstract art.

[Figure: Abstract engraving on stone ochre, made by Modern Humans 70,000+BCE Blombos Cave, South Africa]

The Blombos ochre was found in layers dated from 70,000 to 100,000 years ago. Apart from a centre of art, we know that Blombos was also a fishing base. As might be expected, with such a thin veneer of early Africans there is even less knowledge of any spiritual or religious activity.
One lead though is the possible traces of python worship 70,000 years ago in the Ngamiland region of Botswana. The San people in this area of the Kalahari traditionally believe that mankind originated from the python. Twisting ancient, dry stream beds that ring the hills are said to have been made by the snake as it circled, forever looking for water.

Heading for pastures new

It appears that MH began to populate most of the rest of the world; from Africa about 70,000 years ago. 90% of modern-day non-Africans inherit DNA from this small group. But in 2018 finds in India, if confirmed, suggest a much earlier dispersal, at least 250,000 years ago, however it is not certain these were modern humans. They may be MH precursors.

There is growing possibility of several breakouts from Africa. The Bab el Mandeb one, 70,000 years back, may just be the most successful. New findings are always likely to alter the planetary dispersal date. In January 2018, scientists at Wales, Aberystwyth University published a paper on climatic conditions in Ethiopia going back 150,000 years. This suggested that conditions were favourable to allow humans to move out to the rest of the world much earlier, up to 130,000 years ago, then there's the Indian possibility mentioned in the previous paragraph.

There may have been some movement out of Africa by both Northern, via Levant (Sinai, Israel and Syria) and Southern routes. But to date, the best evidence of a planetary-wide, permanent move is that a small tribe crossed over from that Southern route, via the southern end of the Red sea, 70,000 years ago. The crossing point is known as the Bab el Mandeb straits. They landed on the Arabian side probably somewhere near what is now Yemen or Aden. How they achieved the crossing is not known. Perhaps they used coracle type small boats, or rafts.

We know that both modern humans and Neanderthals used rafts. There is evidence in the Mediterranean at Cova de sa Multa of Neanderthal rafts back to 300,000 BP. Rafts may even have been used by Homo Sapiens ancestor, Homo Erectus, as long as 800,000 years ago.

The pioneering breakout from Africa would not have been as arduous seventy thousand years ago as it would be now. During that time sea levels in the region were much lower than they are today. The distance across the Red Sea that our Stone Age ancestors had to travel would have been much shorter than the same journey today.

Even so, this must have been a huge undertaking for our ancestors. Why did they attempt it? We can only speculate. It's unlikely that the continental shift of home ground was for a tribal holiday. This dangerous journey into the unknown probably stemmed from the pressure simply to survive and continue to exist. Maybe the pioneering tribe was running short of food on the African side. Expanding human population may have resulted in competition for limited food resources. The coast line facing them across the narrow straits would be clearly visible and it would be tempting to go over. It is a common Human trait to believe, or want to believe, that "the grass is greener on the other side." A mixture of hunger; the threat from strangers; and simple hope of a better life are most likely to be what drove them to attempt the perilous crossing. But they did attempt it and achieve it. We can be pretty sure of that.

[Figure: Map showing migration from Africa through the Arabian Peninsula to India - showing the Nile, Es Skhul/Qafzeh, the Neanderthal range across the north, the Bab al-Mandab Strait, Jebel Faya, the Strait of Hormuz, and migration routes from Africa to the Arabian Peninsula and India]

From that Aden crossing Modern Humans went on to colonise the whole landed world, give or take the odd desert, icy waste and mountain extremity.

Eve, the Earth mother

Interestingly, all non-sub-Saharan Modern Humans have a common ancestor. Modern DNA research tell us that we are all related to just one woman who came out of Africa with the first tribe to shift continents. She is known as Mitochondrial Eve. Technically she is the most recent common matrilineal ancestor. This does not do Eve any justice. She should be given the title of Earth mother.

Only sub-Saharan Africans and 10% of everyone else may not have Eve's DNA. If it were not for Eve, most of us might not exist.

It's astonishing to think that the billions of people alive today, of all colours and sizes are related. We all go back to Eve, the Earth Mother. This includes people as diverse and generally small, narrow eyed Japanese to tall blond-haired Scandinavians, from dark skinned and dark eyed Aborigines to red haired and green-eyed Scots. All have this common, ancient ancestor. She was a woman whose gene line had the good fortune to survive through four thousand generations. Good on you Eve, we all owe our lives to you. You deserve a statue, a Nobel prize, commemorative coinage and a city named after you.

The voyage across the southern end of the Red Sea was the Stone-agers second attempt to move out of Africa. The first try was several hundred miles to the north of the successful Aden traverse. Favourable climatic conditions, which resulted in a green Sahara, led to this earlier settlement in the Near East at caves in Skhul and Qafzeh, Israel. These caves show signs of modern human occupation between 90,000 and 120,000 years ago. Unlike the later attempt at Bab el Mandeb this was not the sling-shot that launched modern humans on their path to world domination, although a small group might have got to India. The barrier imposed by the terrain of that time probably largely restricted further movement eastwards. It was mainly desert, Arabian and Sinai, and mountain ranges. This would have posed huge problems. The lack of ambulatory success by these ancient ancestors is given credence by the dating of the earliest known MHs in Europe, from a site in Bulgaria, the Bacho Kiro Cave, to around 45,000 years ago. It does not take 55,000 or so years to walk from Israel to Bulgaria, even if the roads were very bad (more accurately, non-existent).

The Aden arrivals, crossed the water around 20,000 years after the Skhul lot. Their onward migration probably followed coastal paths. The ocean is always a potential source of food, and, for the most part, travelling might be more easily conducted at sea level, near to the sea.

Fair dinkum walkabout

Curiously, evidence suggests MHs reached Australia seemingly before setting foot in continental Europe. We know from finds in Kakadu, 150 kilometres from Darwin, Australia, that the first Aussies were enjoying a barbie on the beach about 65,000 years ago. This is when a small group of MH landed in northern Australia, maybe using a raft to cross 90 kilometres of sea.

From Africa to Australia, without any form of mechanical transport, wow what a trek, no wonder it took those ancient people around 5,000 years. But modern Europeans were not in evidence until about 40,000 years ago, a minimum of 26,000 years after Aussies were chasing Wallabies. Perhaps the tendency to follow coastlines accounts for this dichotomy. It looks like the ground-breaking route to Europe was via India.

Those original Europeans were known as Cro-Magnon people, named after the big cave near Les Eyzies-de-Tayac-Sireuil in southwest France. Here, remains of these ancient people were discovered.

Today terminology has moved on, instead of Cro-Magnon, the earliest Europeans are known, rather unoriginally, as European Early Modern Humans (or EEMH).

Humans took with them their hunting skills, spirituality and art on their travels. These skills and beliefs developed along similar but slightly different paths due to isolation; lack of communication between groups; and time periods (thousands of years). Australian aborigines inherited a spiritual culture handed down verbally generation to generation right up to the present day. Aborigines are renowned for their unique belief in Dreaming, where every person is thought to exist for ever in Dream Time. Ancient aborigines also used an original hunting weapon, the boomerang. They did a bit of art work too. The oldest authenticated Aboriginal paintings have been discovered at Ubirr, in Arnhem Land, Northern Australia. These date from 30,000 BCE.

The last parts of the world to be colonized were North and South America. Human big game hunters reached North America from what is now Russia across the Bering Plain to Alaska. Sea levels were lower then.

Not surprisingly, artistic evidence from the Americas is of more recent origin than elsewhere in the world.

[Figure: Some of the many petroglyphs of the Volcanic Tablelands near Bishop, California, USA]

Californian petroglyphs (rock etchings) at Bishop speculatively might be 20,000 years old, but Mexico holds the oldest evidence of human occupation in N and S America. The Chiquihuite Cave, in Mexico, shows humans were there about 30,000 years ago.

Seemingly, much later, modern humans reached Argentina. Hand stencils at the Cuevas de las Manos near Rio de las Pinturas date about 9,500 BCE. In South America, a new form of weapon was developed; the bola

Toba coughs up

Peopling of the planet and expansion of population numbers did not go unhindered. A major natural catastrophe occurred about 74,000 years ago. The super volcano that was Toba, in what is now Sumatra, let rip in a very big way. The blast was so big it affected the whole planet. The better-known Krakatoa eruption of 1883 was the equivalent of a largish firework going off compared to mighty Toba's sizeable bomb.

[Figure: Diagram comparing Toba (74,000 years ago) shown as large circle with Krakatoa (1883) shown as much smaller circle, the circle areas drawn to scale by the volume of magma erupted]

The ancient eruption spewed many tens of millions of tons of dust and gas high into the atmosphere. This was carried by weather systems around the globe. The sun was partially blocked for 6 to 8 years by all the debris from Toba, resulting in a volcanic winter with temperatures worldwide falling between 3 to 5 degrees. Global cooling lasted for 1,000 years. Not surprisingly there was a huge detrimental impact on the animals and plants that humans hunted and gathered. The result of all this was a dramatic fall in Modern Human population numbers, they dropped from an estimated 100,000 to below 15,000.

Ever since Toba MH population numbers have generally been on an upward trend, despite the mitigating effect of Malthusian war, famine and pestilence.

[Figure: Graph showing Population and Food over Time with Control point and Malthusian catastrophes (War, Famine, Pestilence) limiting population growth]

We are now over 8 billion and still rising, at least until another major extinction event like Toba, or the comet that did for the dinosaurs. Maybe Climate Change will be a major brake on population numbers too.

Some gloomy pundits say Climate Change will result in massive population movements because of rising sea levels. It will also cause water and food shortages, perhaps starvation, particularly in poorer countries. Other than a big volcano or comet; Climate Change, wars, pandemics, like COVID 19, may act as a severe brake on population size in mankind's future. One or more of these will possibly result in a Malthusian catastrophe.

pages.text:
Chapter 8

Ice ages, the five major extinctions and terminology explained

Now for a short break from consideration of our early MH ancestors. You can skip the next 5 or 6 pages if you are familiar with the terminology used to describe the ancient world, or if you are not interested. Instead of explaining some technical wording in an appendix it's coming up now, in the main body of the text. A few bits of necessary terminology have crept into this chapter, and the previous. Anyone reading around the topics covered may come across other relevant terminology too. It's useful to set out some explanation of these and expand them. The reader can then form a clearer picture of the context. Since that reader is likely to me, I would find this of benefit as my ageing memory becomes less reliable.

Paleontology, Archaeology and Anthropology?

What's a paleontologist, or with an extra 'a' palaeontologist, and how does this differ from an archaeologist? Well, the palaeontologist studies prehistoric fossils. These include animals, which could be humans, and plants. Generally, palaeontology is associated with fossils that are hundreds of thousands or more likely millions of years old. Palaeontologists are interested in all life; from bacteria to dinosaurs and beyond.

[Figure: Logo of the Paleontological Society showing "PALEONTOLOGICAL SOCIETY" text]

[Figure: Logo of the Paleontological Association showing "THE PALEONTOLOGICAL ASSOCIATION" text]

Archaeology, on the other hand, has a much narrower focus. It concentrates on the study of past humans; particularly their artifacts, such as tools and weapons, but they are also interested in human fossils. Since their focus is on humans, who haven't been around that long, archaeologists are generally looking at shorter time periods, normally hundreds of thousands of years, that is if the subject is a modern human or a Neanderthal. To slightly confuse matters further, there are also specialists called anthropologists. These are focused on both past and present human behaviour, language and culture. The three specialists have different primary interests but they do overlap a little. All three disciplines study clues from the past, to gain a fuller picture of life on this planet.

[Figure: Logo showing "ARCHAEOLOGY - CLUES FROM THE PAST" with a globe icon and text "Bernardino de Sahagún 1499 to 1590CE, Founder of Anthropology"]

headings.text: Ice ages, the five major extinctions and terminology explained

pages.text:
[Figure: Bernardino de Sahagun, 1499-1590, founder of anthropology]

Geological Epochs and Periods

Apart from the fossil related sciences of palaeontology, archaeology and anthropology there are definitions for various geological timescales to consider. The most commonly used geological time definitions are: Eras; Periods and Epochs.

Eras embrace a timescale of 100 million years or more;
Periods tens of million years;
Epochs just a few million, or shorter.

The various classifications define important events that have occurred over the course of Earth's history, like mass extinctions. There are estimated to have been at least five mass extinction events over the last 540 million years. Our present world emerges from the change engendered by these cataclysmic events of the past.

The best-known example is the asteroid that struck in the Gulf of Mexico 65 MYA. This ended the 165 million years reign of dinosaurs (excluding birds) and accounted for 83% of reptiles. Three-quarters of all plants and animals died in a relatively short time. This is known as the Cretaceous-Tertiary period mass extinction.

And what Era, Period and Epoch do we humans live in? Modern Humans, i.e. Homo Sapiens, have been around for 200,000 years. We have existed in an Era of which most of us are ignorant, the Cenozoic. This stretches back 65 million years and marks the boundary with the last of the terrestrial dinosaurs. The Cenozoic Era is split into three periods. MH and their hominid ancestors fall mainly within the last one, the Quaternary period. These periods are further reduced into Epochs. The Quaternary is composed of into two Epochs: Pleistocene and Holocene.

As of now we MH live in the:

Cenozoic Era (the last 65 million years);
Quaternary Period (the last 2.6 million years);
Holocene Epoch (11.7 thousand years, up to today)

Some experts claim that the arrival of industrial age humans has resulted in such a massive impact on the planet that we are now in the Anthropocene Epoch. However, this designation had not yet been approved by the International Union of Geological Sciences as at May 2020 but there is growing pressure to formally recognize the Anthropocene, as commencing from the mid twentieth century. The Pleistocene Epoch, which preceded the current Holocene Epoch, covered a period of 2.6 million to about 12,000

years ago. This spanned the period of Earth's most recent glaciations and marked the end of the Paleolithic age.

The first 2.4 million years of the Pleistocene saw the continued rise of our evolutionary predecessors, the bipedal ape derivatives. In fact, the earliest hominids, like Australopithecus and Ardipithecus Ramidus, walked upright for the first time in an even early epoch than the Pleistocene. The two A's were on their feet about 4.4 million years ago, during the Pliocene epoch. And Ardi R's ancestor, Ardi Kamada, was around even earlier, 5.6 MYA. So, hominids covered three Epochs. But Modern Humans occupy just two, discounting for the moment the Anthropocene.

Holocene: from ancient Greek
holos = entire and kainos = new,
the whole term means entirely recent.
It pre-dates Egyptian, written - hieroglyphic - history.

[Figure: Egyptian hieroglyphs carved in limestone relief, from a chapel of Ramesses I (Metropolitan Museum of Art)]

MH were hunter-gatherers during the time of ice (mostly), that is the Pleistocene Epoch. They survived into the current epoch, the Holocene, when written history began, with Sumerian cuneiform writing on stone, using wedge shapes. Later the Egyptians used a pictorial, hieroglyphic language.

Shamans

There is one specific human profession that has spanned both the Pleistocene and Holocene Epochs. No, not the female one commonly thought of as the "oldest profession on earth". The job I refer to was seen, in many human communities, as a top drawer rather than a drop drawers' occupation - the shaman.

[Figure: Rock drawing of dancing figures, Almaty region, Kazakhstan, about 6,000 years old]

Shamanism still exists today in some indigenous communities, as it has since MH were first about, 300,000 years ago. It is the oldest spiritual or religious practice in the world.

What are shamans? They are expert, and sometimes unique, human intermediaries with spirits. Shamans believe they are a conduit to the spirit world.

Commonly, they follow specific rituals, chant certain mantras and dress in a distinctive fashion. Sometimes, with aid of repetitive movement, chanting and music the shaman enters a trance state in his quest to enter the spirit world. They seek to heal sick people by driving out evil spirits and can perform rituals to help with hunting game animals. Shamans are strongly associated with the natural world. Not only ritual but also music often formed a part of the professional shaman's modus operandi. Depending on the culture, this can involve drums; rattles or gongs. Feathers, smoking pipes or swords can play an important role in shamanistic ceremony. Significantly in shamanism there is no sign of the one God.

Ice Ages, Glacial Periods, Stadials and Inter-stadials

Sometimes when ice ages are mentioned it's not at all clear when they happened and what areas of our planet were affected. Then expressions like stadials and inter-stadials can creep in.

Let's start with ice ages. These are lengthy cool periods which can last millions of years. Why does an ice age occur? There are four reasons:

The greatest likely influence is the change in Earth's orbit around the sun and even the sun's orbit around the galaxy. The earth's position relative to the sun changes over time, causing a variation in the amount of sunlight we receive. These Earth orbital changes are known as the Milankovitch cycles.

Changes in CO₂ (carbon dioxide or greenhouse gas) concentration has occurred over time. In the past this may have come about by the impact of large meteorites or wide scale volcanic activity. Carbon dioxide can also result from plants and animals. Carbon dioxide can act like a blanket, with too much of it we get global warming, as at present. The growing impact humans have had is human-caused, but it has a huge impact on the environment. If there is much less carbon dioxide, this leads to cooling and ice formation. Significantly decreased levels of CO₂ can trigger an ice age.

Continental drift, which affects the location of continents and oceans and can impact on the total heat absorbed from the sun;

The rise of large mountain ranges, like the Andes and Himalayas, can impact on air circulation and cause warming or cooling.

The Earth has experienced 5 ice ages. Here they are:

[Figure: Chart showing Earth's five ice ages across geological time. Columns show millions of years ago, the geological periods (Quaternary, Neogene, Paleogene, Cretaceous, Jurassic, Triassic, Permian, Carboniferous, Devonian, Silurian, Ordovician, Cambrian and the Precambrian), a curve of global average temperature, and the ice ages: Ice Age 1, Huronian (2,400 to 2,100 million years ago); Ice Age 2, Cryogenian "Snowball Earth" (720 to 635 million years ago); Ice Age 3, Andean-Saharan (460 to 420 million years ago); Ice Age 4, Karoo (360 to 260 million years ago); and Ice Age 5, Late Cenozoic (34 million years ago to now).]

headings.text: The Earth has experienced 5 ice ages. Here they are:

pages.text:
[Figure: Image of the above table]

The average planetary surface temperature falls sufficiently during an ice age to allow vast sheets of ice and enormous glaciers to form. These covered much of the Earth's surface. The last ice age started about 2.5 million years ago. At its peak, known as a glacial maximum, much of what are now temperate regions were iced up. This included much of Germany, Poland, Russia and northern Britain. 20,000 years ago, the glacial ice sheet of North America covered land below the great lakes. It's generally known that most of human pre-history happened during an ice age.

We know about woolly mammoths roaming the frozen tundra. They have been depicted by many artists and they've been dug up out of Siberian permafrost often in a well-preserved state. These giant, shaggy beasts were a favourite prey of our early human ancestors.

[Figure: Woolly mammoths in a snowy Ice Age valley, with a herd behind - Charles R. Knight's 1915 painting, as an ink plate]

Woolly Mammoths, creatures of the old ice (Pleistocene)
They survived for 400,000 years, up to about 4,000 years ago.

From within an Ice Age there can be a period called a Glacial. Glacials are colder, shorter periods during an existing ice age. They are thought to last about 12,000 years but there is some evidence showing they could last up to 28,000 years. Conversely an Interglacial is a short period of warming during the millions of years of an ice age. There are two others, less common terms to get to grips with in the climate context: stadials and inter-stadials. A stadial is an even shorter cooler period during an interglacial. Yes, you've guessed it, an interstadial is a short warmer period during a glacial.

Let's put these geological climatic periods into some perspective. Taking length measurement as an example, ice-ages are equivalent to measurement in kilometers; glacial and inter-glacial equivalent measure is in meters and stadial or inter-stadial measures in centimeters.

The five ice ages in the Earth's history are sometimes called ice houses. These represent about 15% of Earth's history with 85% in green house stages. The worst known ice age was so severe the Earth may have looked like a complete snowball. The ice reached the tropics and even oceans froze over. Fortunately, this did not bother any ancient MH or their immediate ancestors. There were none about.

[Figure: Two ink-drawn globes side by side: "Snowball Earth, long ago" - a globe covered in ice with pressure ridges and cracks and no continents, and "Earth today, our blue planet" - with today's continents and oceans]

Snowball Earth occurred between about 717 to 635 million years ago (the Sturtian and Marinoan glaciations), in pre-Cambrian times. This was a period before the dinosaurs and even before any vertebrate animals existed. Well, if they had existed they would have become extinct, unless they could thrive on a snow and ice diet. MH at this time were still a very long way off, way down the evolutionary production line.

Although, as mentioned earlier, currently the Earth is in an interglacial period called the Holocene some think differently. Ecologist, Eugene Stormer and chemist Paul J. Crutzen argue that we are now in a new era, the Anthropocene. This is an era when MHs are now so numerous and industrialised their activities are impacting on Earth's climate and ecosystems. Hence the continuing concern over human induced climate change and extinction of living organisms. If we humans do become partly responsible for a mass extinction this will be the sixth time in Earth's history. We can confidently say we're not responsible for the other five.

That's enough on geographical and climatic terminology except to remember that when there is a cold year during a period we suppose it will be warm this is because climate is what we expect, while weather is what we get (i.e. The former is long term, the latter short term, which can be an interstadial.).

Moving on from cold and climate, what are the extinction events that have shaped the history of life on planet Earth?

Earth's five mass extinctions of flora and fauna

Period When (Million years ago) Extinction Event and Life on Earth
Cambrian 541 to 485 Most life was of trilobites, in the sea
Ordovician-Silurian 443 1. Massive glaciation and sea level changes wiped out 85% of sea life (most life was in the sea). There were two peak dying times hundreds of thousands of years apart.
Devonian 359 2. Asteroid strikes and oxygen starvation in the seas may be the cause of 75% of all species becoming extinct over several million years.
Carboniferous 359 to 259 A time of huge forests, high oxygen levels, amphibians. No mass extinction.
Permian 252 3. The Great Dying. 96% of marine life went extinct, volcanoes and pyroclastic lava flows are thought the culprits together with an explosion of methane producing bacteria. It got very hot.
Triassic 200 4. Plants were OK but 50% of other species died off over several million years.
Jurassic
Cretaceous-Paleogene 65 5. The famous one. A huge asteroid, 7.5 miles across, struck the Gulf of Mexico, resulting in the demise of all dinosaurs, and 76% of all life. Global cooling and volcanoes contributed.
Holocene/Anthropocene Current? The sixth mass extinction may be occurring in the current Holocene/Anthropocene period. Human expansion and activity are likely main culprits, aided by, and aiding, "natural" Climate Change.

headings.text: Earth's five mass extinctions of flora and fauna

pages.text:
Did He (God) cause these catastrophic events? Were they a part of a carefully constructed holy plan? No doubt there are devout, religious people who think this is so. Others will take the view from science that these extinction events are all explainable without the need for divine intervention. Some forms of life survived each extinction event, fortunately for us. Are we now leading into a 6th mass extinction event, as at 2021? Climate Change scientists say this is a possibility, partly caused by the huge contribution MH have made to greenhouse gases, like CO₂ and methane.

There's been a meteoric rise in these since the industrial revolution, contributing to global warming, but as we see from Earth's history other periods of global warming occurred, unaided by humans. Humans were completely unaffected by these earlier periods of global warming, that's because they had not yet evolved during these sweaty times, a minimum of 65 million years ago.

[Figure: Diagram showing the greenhouse effect and human contributions to climate change. The illustration shows Earth with arrows indicating radiation absorbed, reflected, and escaping at the edge of atmosphere. Various sources of greenhouse gases are depicted including: deforestation, oil and petrol engines, CFCs, fossil fuels, and radiation absorbed by greenhouse gases and the atmosphere/Earth. Text labels point to different processes: "escaping radiation," "reflected," "absorbed," "absorbed by atmosphere and Earth," "absorbed by greenhouse gases," and "deforestation."]

After early planetary history, the biggest temperature rise was across the Permian - Triassic boundary, about 250 million years ago. At this time the average global temperature exceeded 22°c, with sea surface temperatures at the equator in excess of 40°c. 95% of all planetary species were killed off. Hopefully, Earth, through human assisted Anthropocene Climate Change, is not on the way to breaking this record. If it does succeed, there may not be many humans left to log the feat.

chapters.title: Now back to our Ancestors
chapters.summary: Australopithecines, Homo Habilis, Danuvius and more. The Neanderthals in some detail, the rise of the intelligent biped, maybe Homo Superior or Homo Extinctus?

pages.text:
Chapter 9

Now back to our Ancestors

To date we've focused on Modern Humans (MH). These are people like you and me. If you transported the first MHs from 300,000 years ago to modern times, they would not stand out in a crowd. Of course, first you would have to give them a bath, haircut and then put them in jeans and a shirt. If they spoke, that would be a giveaway and they might swiftly come to a sticky end if plonked down in a busy city street. Cars are more dangerous than mammoths and cave bears. But the human family lineage goes back much further in time than the 300k period occupied by Modern Humans (MH), i.e. Homo Sapiens.

Our MH ancestors include: Homo Heidelbergensis; Homo Ergaster; Homo Erectus; Homo Habilis and the Australopithecines. The latter are oldest. They can be traced back more than 4 million years. Our bipedal ancestors are thought to have split from the ape line about 6 million years ago. But we know little or nothing about the very first non-ape creatures, who could have broken away from apes about 12 to 6 million years ago. We will talk about the ones we do know something about later. What these ancestors all had in common with MH, their evolutionary descendants, is a bipedal, upright posture. They also had comparatively large brains, although smaller than ours. All of them used tools, mostly stone of varying sophistication, although usage of tools by one of our earliest ancestors, Australopithecines, is debated. The very first of these bipeds, Danuvius, could be over 12 million years old. This baboon sized ape's bones were discovered in a clay pit at Hammerschmiede, Bavaria, Germany in 2019. Danuvius was still very much at home in trees, like other apes, using his long arms to swing on branches and climb trees. He had not moved on to open savannah to spend life mostly by walking upright. Interestingly, Bavaria is some distance from Africa where us Modern Humans are thought first to have evolved from bipedal ancestors. Is Germany really in the frame as a long-distance ancestor of us Modern Humans? The jury is still out on this one. Perhaps Danuvius died out without leaving a successor. Later, brainier and walkier MH predecessors were definitely African.

Neanderthal (Homo Neanderthalis)

But if we are considering MH predecessors the premier focus has to be on Neanderthals. These fierce browed individuals are more often portrayed in the media than other MH predecessors. They've made regular appearances in newspapers and scientific journals (Science, Scientific American, New Scientist and National Geographic). They've also captured our imagination through books (Jean Auel's engrossing

Earth's Children series) and in films (Quest for Fire, 1981). They even appear on TV (Neanderthal, Channel 4; Neanderthal Code, ABC documentary 2010, among others). Through all this Neanderthals have become a small part of popular culture, although sometimes cruelly misrepresented as brutal, ugly, shambling beasts.

The name Neanderthal stems from the first discovery of a partial skeleton in 1856. This was unearthed in a cave located in the Neander Valley, near Dusseldorf, Germany. 50 odd years later (1908) a French paleontologist called Marcellin Boule wrote about the Neanderthal remains found at La Chapelle-aux-Saints in France. Boule's description of a hairy, bent-kneed creature, who was very slow witted, was characterised by his illustration.

[Figure: Two early depictions of Neanderthals side by side - Hermann Schaaffhausen's 1888 profile head, and the 'Ideal Restoration of the Neanderthal Man' bust from J. P. MacLean's A Manual of the Antiquity of Man (1875)]

In 1888 Herman Schaaffhausen, Professor of Anatomy at the University of Bonn, drew an illustration of a brutish Neanderthal man which may have influenced Boule. This, we now know, was an even worse travesty than the later re-construction made by Boule. To be kind to these two, they did not have the wealth of fossils since discovered. Nor did they have the investigative techniques available today.

[Figure: A hairy, stooping, bent-kneed Neanderthal with a club, as imagined in 1912 - Alice B. Woodward's drawing 'Homo mousteriensis', made after Boule's description]

Together, the Boule and Schaaffhausen drawings set an indelible image of our cousin for about 100 years. But today, we know that our cousin was much more like us. An increased number of skeletal findings, nearly 500, and the application of scientific techniques completely unknown in Boule's time, especially DNA analysis, has helped raise the stature (literally and metaphorically) of the Neanderthal.

In 2020, Rebecca Wragg Sykes well received book, "Kindred", explained the life and culture of Neanderthals was more complex than originally thought.

They extended across most of Europe; the Ukraine; parts of Russia and the Levant (roughly Syria, Lebanon and Jordan). No remains have been found in Africa.

Both MH and Neanderthals shared a common ancestor. There seems to be debate about timing. Our common ancestor could have lived about 600,000 years ago, possibly Homo Heidelbergensis, or perhaps Homo Rhodesiensis - discovered in Rhodesia (now Zambia) by Arthur Woodward in 1921.

Neanderthals hunted big game, just as did humans, but their weapons were cruder and more limited. They had to get close to use short, stabbing spears. As a result, many Neanderthal skeletons show signs of bone fractures, perhaps from having to get closer to their prey than human hunters. This may also be evidence that although Neanderthal brains were at least as large as MH, it did not mean they were as intelligent. They were artists too as evidenced by cave drawings at El Castillo, Spain which date back nearly 41,000 years.

[Figure: Red dots and hand stencils on the cave wall at El Castillo, Cantabria, Spain]

If you query their part in popular culture, referred to earlier, what is indisputable is the role they play in us, i.e. in our bodies. Research into DNA has revealed that in present day Eurasians up to 4% of human DNA is from Neanderthals. So, we are partly Neanderthal, sort of. "They are not totally extinct. In some of us they live on, a little bit," said Professor Svante Paabo, from the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig, Germany.

Whether or not Neanderthals and Palaeolithic MH were kissing cousins is in dispute. Some research suggests that although some European MH and

Neanderthals share a limited amount of DNA the origin of this may be from an earlier time. It could come from the common ancestor, probably Heidelbergensis, of both MH and Neanderthals. The diversity offered to MH through Neanderthal DNA is beneficial. It helped strengthen the MH immune system and so increased survival rates. They were an evolutionary advantage.

Neanderthals are known to have engaged in intentional burial which indicated the possibility of religious or spiritual beliefs. The earliest such burial, so far discovered, dates back 50,000 years ago. In a 70,000-year-old site the Shanidar Cave, Iraq, Neanderthal skeletons appeared to have been buried with flowers. The site in Sima de las Paloma in Spain found three Neanderthals buried with their hands close to their heads. There is the possibility of an even earlier burial site at Krapina in Croatia, dating to 130,000 years old. In February 2020 Dr Emma Pomeroy of Cambridge University said: "In recent years there has been increasing evidence that Neanderthals were more sophisticated than previously thought...." Rebecca Wragg Sykes explained these discoveries in her book 'Kindred'.

Evidence of intentional burial is not surprising given how close they were to MH in intelligence, habitat, hunting weapons and prey. Neanderthals are also thought to have used the feathers of birds for decorative purposes. This usage is common to many older MH societies. But they were a very long way back from the more sophisticated religious practices of later Mesolithic, Modern Humans, and even further away from the first biblical written works.

So, if there is God, how does he deal with our cousin the Neanderthal? Here was a creature very similar to Modern Humans. He had a brain the same size, at least, as ours. The Neanderthals art and spiritual beliefs seem similar to ancient MH. It appears God, if he exists, decided to remove our close cousins completely from the scene. They have been extinct for about 40,000 years. Not surprisingly, modern, major MH religions ignore the question of Neanderthals and offer no cogent explanation of their relationship to a God.

Our evolutionary predecessors

We, Modern Humans (MH) or Homo Sapiens, follow behind a long line of long legged and increasingly intelligent bipeds. This lineage is known as Hominins. Apart from a few Ardi creatures our ancestral Hominins were all other varieties of Homo. Homo is the Latin for "human" and is the genus name designated by the great Swedish taxonomist Carl Linnaeus in his ground-breaking classification system.

[Figure: Carl Linnaeus, father of taxonomy, 1707-1778 (portrait by Alexander Roslin, 1775)]

Our emergence is from a long line of Hominin lineage. Bipedalism, better brains and opposing thumbs were the main forte of this line. The evolutionary process concluded that these anatomical features were definite winners. So, each succeeding bipedal Hominin was better equipped physically and mentally than their predecessor.

Our Hominin line meanders and has a few dead-end offshoots. It also is unclear in places. We are not entirely certain who exactly were our earliest or latest bipedal ancestors. It's likely that some very ancient bipeds were neighbours and cousins rather than parents or grandparents. But as more fossil discoveries emerge we are viewing a clearer picture of who was great (x times) granny or granddad. They would have been several thousand generations back.

About 6 million years ago some tree living apes in Africa decided life was a bit easier if they came down from the trees. These were go-ahead types who learned to stand on their own two feet and walk tall. Why did this ground-based habitat start to become favoured? Probably because of changing climate, maybe several to-and-fro changes within a relatively short geological period. These climatic fluctuations would have put pressure on food resources. Smarter bipeds could scavenge for food further and faster when on the ground than when swinging through trees. Climate change may have eventually resulted in fewer trees and more open country, with the need to adapt to different foods. Our direct ancestors were the ones able to evolve and adapt to the changing environment. Other hominids died out because they were too stuck in the mud, or in the trees, and were specialized eaters who ran out of food. But, the Pliocene epoch tree dwellers did not all die out. Some went on to become present day chimpanzees, bonobos, orangutans and gorillas.

Who exactly were our bipedal ancestors?

Hard to pronounce as well as hard to define, Sahelanthropus Tchadensis (named Toumai, "hope of life") who padded around Chad 6/7 million years ago may have been the original ancestor of us MH. Toumai had his feet more firmly on the ground than his mainly tree living predecessors. It is disputed though whether he really differs from the earliest Ardipithecus (Ardi for short). Ardi is generally thought to be the first intelligent biped in direct line to us. The more pronounceable and later Orrorin (original man) from Kenya is another front-runner vying for the title of first in line. Orrorin seems to have more going for him/her anatomically, but the jury is still out. Ardi holds on to the gold medal for now.

headings.text: Who exactly were our bipedal ancestors?

pages.text:
This is probably the current best presumption of Modern Humans main evolutionary chain origin but does not encompass all the intelligent bipeds. Apart from Toumai and Orrorin some others were offshoots from the main line. Most of these died out without gifting an evolutionary successor. This included a much more recent biped, discovered in 2013, Homo Naledi, who lived in South Africa between 2 and 3 million years ago and may have ritually buried their dead. Ancient burials of Naledi have been found in the Rising Star cave in South Africa.

The other dead-enders include: Australopithecus Sediba and Australopithecus Africanus. There are several others but two much more recent species are particularly interesting because they were definitely contemporaries of MH. First we have Denisovans. In March 2010, a finger bone was discovered in the Denisova cave, located in the Altai Mountains in Siberia.

[Figure: Denisova Cave, Altai Mountains, Siberia]

The bone was dated to 41,000 years ago and genetically distinct from Neanderthals and Modern Humans. Denisovans are thought to have had the same ancestor, Heidelbergensis as both Modern Humans and Neanderthals. Their descendance began about 350,000 years ago.

These stone-agers were a separate species of human but crossbred with some of our ancestors. DNA analysis shows that up to 6% of their DNA is in present day Melanesian (South Sea Islanders) and Aboriginal people. It is thought that Tibetans successful adaptation to high altitude is due to inheritance of a Denisovan gene.

Second up, in the list of dead-enders, we have the aptly named hobbit species, Homo Floresiensis (Flores Man). This 3ft high hobbit-sized had long arms and a skull about as big as a large grapefruit. Flo lived about 95,000 until as recently as 12,000 years ago on the island of Flores in Indonesia.

[Figure: What Flo (Homo floresiensis) may have looked like: a computer facial approximation by Cicero Moraes and colleagues]

For a while they co-existed with Modern Humans on the same island. It is disputed whether Flo was a separate species or just a smaller than usual Homo Sapiens. It can be very difficult for anthropologists to determine whether ancient MH ancestors were slight variations of the same species or a completely separate species. Imagine an alien landing on planet Earth today and meeting a short, yellowish skinned and narrow eyed Japanese then a beefy, black curly haired Nigerian and finally a tall blond blue-eyed Swede. He might think these were all different species, but we know better. These are all part of the great modern human family.

Anthropologists can fall within one of two camps. There are the lumpers - those who think that the many possibly different intelligent bipeds are in fact slight variations of the same species. And then the splitters, not a hard one to guess what they think - that there are many different species.

Our immediate ancestor in the Hominin line is believed to either be Homo Heidelbergensis or Homo Erectus. Both have been found through Europe, Asia and especially Africa. H. Erectus were uniquely long-lasting among all Hominins. They were about for at least 1.9 million years and spread around the planet from their original African home at least 1 million years before MH made their move.

Five Homo Erectus skulls, dated from 1.8 million years ago, were found in a cave at Dmanisi, Georgia in 2013. These have been analysed and show a wide variation in brain case size. This has led some palaeontologists to believe that some of the claimed different species thought to be discovered in Africa and elsewhere, like Homo Habilis, are of the same lineage as Erectus. Other experts still disagree, saying the brain size is just one aspect of differences. The debate continues, we still have the two camps, lumpers and splitters, vying for the supremacy of their hypothesis.

[Figure: A skull of the early Homo from Dmanisi, Georgia, about 1.8 million years old]

Prof. Alice Roberts tells more about the evolution and planetary dispersal of us humans in her BBC TV series and book, "The Incredible Human Journey", followed with:

[Figure: Book covers showing "EVOLUTION: THE HUMAN STORY"]

The rise of the Intelligent Biped - our immediate ancestors
