4.4 million Ardipithecus Ramidus Known as Ardi Illustration of Australopithecus Ramidus head Ardi was preceded by the more tree loving, debatable, Orrorin 6 MYA, Sahelanthropus 7 MYA and Danuvius 12 MYA. Ardi though was one of the very first to spend much more time on the ground than in the trees. Small, 4ft tall, an early Hominin with a brain 325 cm³, about the same as a chimpanzee. Lived in Ethiopian forests. Was omnivorous but probably relying mostly on fruit and softer foods.
3.9 million Australopithecus Afarensis Illustration of early hominin figure Named after the Afar region of Ethiopia where Lucy was found Bipedal and possibly partly arboreal. Brain 405 cm³, almost 25% larger than Ramidus. Was hunted by sabre toothed tigers. The famous Lucy fossil was discovered in Ethiopia by Donald Johnson in 1974 and later immortalised by the Beatles in their song: "Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds". Lucy means born at dawn, from the Latin.
3 to 1.4 million Australopithecus Africanus Photo of fossil remains There were other australopithecines up to the large jawed Paranthropus Boisei Africanus had a 20% larger brain than Lucy, about 485 cm³, with a slender build. He was more human like but with ape-like long arms and fingers. Possibly inhabited open woodlands.
2.5 million Homo Habilis "handy man" because it used tools The original DIY bloke? Illustration of Homo Habilis face First remains were found in 1964 by Louis and Mary Leakey, parents of Richard Leakey - of Lake Omo, early Homo Sapiens fame. Habilis was the first of the Homo species and had a larger brain, around 600 cm³, than any of the Australopithecines whom it overlapped with. Had long legs and waist, such adaptations were for running down prey on open savannahs. May have been a version of Homo Erectus.
1.9 million to 143,000 Homo Erectus "upright man" Sometimes referred to as Homo Ergaster "working man". Various sub-species including Floresiensis (very small) and Georgicus Illustration of Homo Erectus face At about 900 cm³ Erectus had an even larger brain than Habilis, possibly because of cooked food, and less time spent eating helped evolution. Erectus was first to use fire, 1 million years ago, and engaged in ritual burial. A very successful species, lasting at least 1.5 million years. Overlapped with Habilis and Ergaster. All three may be Erectus types but some experts consider these separate species. Erectus spread out of Africa 1 million years ago to Asia and possibly Europe. Suggested to have evolved into H. Heidelbergensis, or directly to Modern Humans (MH)
600,000 to 20,000 Homo Neanderthalis the Neanderthal Photo of Neanderthal reconstruction showing realistic human-like face Shorter and stockier than MH but with brains slightly larger than ours, but maybe not wired up so well. It's likely there was a common ancestor of both species 500,000+ years ago (Heidelbergensis?). Neanderthals overlapped with MH in Europe and spread into Russia and parts of Asia. They interbred with MH too. Up to 4% of most humans is Neanderthal. They used stone tools, wore clothes and buried their dead and may have engaged in animal worship. They even painted cave walls near Malaga, Spain 42,000 years ago.
600,000 to 200,000 Homo Heidelbergensis Photo of a reconstruction of Homo Heidelbergensis First fossil discovered in 1907. Named after the University of Heidelberg, Germany by Professor Otto Schoetensack. Homo Antecessor is possibly the same species. Average brain size only slightly less than MH. Possibly descended from African Homo Erectus or Ergaster. Heidelbergensis had a larger brain than these two. It's suggested HH were forbearers of both MH and Neanderthals. HH buried their dead and probably had primitive speech. They were the first human species to live in colder climates. A tibia bone of a HH specimen named Boxgrove man was found in West Sussex along with many flint tools. He lived 500,000 years ago and is Britain's oldest Hominin so far discovered.
300,000 to Now Homo Sapiens "wise man" Illustration of an ancient human painting on a cave Photo of two people in the mountainsKnown as Modern Human (MH) Following a period of dramatic climate change, we, i.e. MH (Modern Humans) evolved. We had bigger brains than our ancestors, were less hairy, of lighter build and taller. MH have spread out from Africa to colonise all of Earth, except for extreme regions like Antarctica, deserts, mountain tops and the sea. Even in these places, some humans can be found. MH now number over 8 billion and have a major impact on planetary resources, especially flora and fauna. Who will be the next, after MH, in the future evolutionary line, if any?
The future Homo Superior? or Homo Extinctus? ?

chapters.title: What of God and the pre-history Hominins?
chapters.summary: Evidence of stone age spirituality. From Palaeolithic to Neolithic. The beginning of agriculture, Sitari's story. First towns/cities Jericho, Catal Höyük and Pot Belly Hill.

pages.text:
Chapter 10

What of God and the pre-history Hominins?

There's evidence indicating that some form of spiritual belief goes back 300,000 years. This comes from a cave site at Atapuerca in Spain, which was probably occupied by Hominins, Homo Sapiens and predecessors, for 800,000 years. Here were found signs of intentional burial, although not all experts agree. Skulls and complete skeletons have been discovered, either of Neanderthals or Homo Heidelbergensis. The earliest undisputed MH (modern human) ritual burial was at Qafzeh, in Israel, where a mother and child had been buried with their bones stained with red ochre. The find dates back 100,000 years. Red ochre is thought to have been an important part of burial for many thousands of years.

Some later signs of stone age spirituality arose in the upper Palaeolithic era. Earth mother statuettes began to appear. The famous Venus of Willendorf and Venus of Hohle Fels have already been mentioned. These were only a few of many such statuettes. They were sculpted over a period of at least 24,000 years, from 35,000 to at least 11,000 years ago (the Venus of Monruz). Then there are the cave paintings, also produced over several thousand years by stone-agers. They too are thought to have some spiritual significance.

If God exists and is interested in Homo Sapiens, then what evidence, if any, do we have of His contact with Palaeolithic man? Why did He allow these ancient people to go down the relatively blind alley of animism or shamanism type spiritualism? After all, Stone Age people had the same intelligence and desires that Modern Humans have. Surely God does not start his serious involvement with humanity from say a mere 3,000 years ago, which is about the time the first books of the bible were written?

How did God give guidance to all those humans that lived before the biblical period? Did God trigger the Palaeolithic Transition? Did He encourage agriculture, because this would give humans greater thinking time? They might even think of Him.

You don't need to be good at arithmetic to work out that the pre-history Palaeolithic Transition took place many, many generations before the first glimmerings of the bible story, before the Qur'an, Torah, sacred Vedas and other holy texts. These all emerged many tens of thousands of years later.

headings.text: What of God and the pre-history Hominins?

pages.text:
Out of the Palaeolithic and into the Neolithic

We are going to move on from the Palaeolithic to the Neolithic. This means by-passing the Mesolithic. This latter is a slightly controversial, variable length, middle era between the Palaeolithic, old stone age, and the Neolithic, new stone age. Some palaeontologists think it is an unnecessary distinction.

Sitari's story.

The seeds she had dropped accidentally on the muddy soil some months before were now tall grass plants. The clan had returned from their wanderings to the area. Between two mighty rivers this flat plain was a favourite hunting ground. Imago, the clan chieftain, decided they should spend increasingly longer periods in this one location, because the hunting was good and the climate mild.

Sitari wondered about the plants waving greenly in front of her. When her tribe returned again in the autumn, would the plants bear seeds that she could harvest? If so why not press a few more seeds into the ground from her store. Fortunately, the men had had a succession of successful hunts. There was plenty of meat, river fish too. The store of seeds Sitari held were not needed immediately as food. She could spare a few so took out a small handful of from the storage horn. After clearing a small area of damp soil, she pressed the seeds into the red earth. Sitari marked her seeds with a small branch from a nearby bush. She tended them over the summer months, watering and pulling up other competing plants. In the autumn she was rewarded with a tall, ripe crop. This gave her many more seeds than she had originally planted.

[Figure: Stone Age farmers break the ground and sow seed: a man hoes a furrow with a horn pick while a woman sows seed into it, and another woman carries produce and leads a goat, with cattle, sheep and a dog nearby. Émile Bayard's engraving 'The Cultivation of Gardens' (1870).]

Neolithic people co-operate to break the ground and sow seed

[Figure: Stone Age bread-making: a woman grinds grain on a stone quern while two youths bake flat cakes on stones heated in the fire, with a herder driving cattle, sheep and goats behind. Émile Bayard's engraving 'The Art of Bread-making in the Stone Age' (1870).]

headings.text: Out of the Palaeolithic and into the Neolithic

pages.text:
Sitari knew she must tell chieftain Imago of her success and persuade him to have a much larger area of ground cleared for more seed sowing. Fortunately for Sitari her clan leader was willing to accept new ideas. He was impressed with this assured source of food and decided that the clan should stay put and build more permanent shelters. He ordered that, under Sitari's guidance, the clan should clear a large area of land for cultivation.

About 10,000 years ago an unknown woman, or women, like Sitari, started the Neolithic (late Stone Age) revolution. This probably happened somewhere in the middle east. The best evidence is that plant cultivation began at Abu Hureyra, which is located in the Euphrates valley in present day Syria. The site was originally occupied by a culture known as Natufian hunter-gatherers.

Sitari, the imaginary first agriculturist, had made a crucial step forward from being a hunter/gatherer. She was trying to exercise more control over her food supply by growing her own food near her dwelling place. This was a big break with the more uncertain world of hunting and searching far and wide for animals, fruit, berries and roots of wild plants. She was the originator of farming on planet Earth. This is an assumption. We don't know of any specific woman, or man, who first planted seeds and tended the soil.

But someone must have started agriculture. It's more likely to have been a woman than a man because generally, women were the gatherers of seeds, nuts and berries while men hunted - although South American women appeared to share the hunting with men.

Agriculture is likely to have grown up independently in different areas of the world. Around 10,000 years ago the development of agriculture, and domestication of animals, which ran alongside, marked a sea-change for people. A food supply on the doorstep meant there was no need to continue the nomadic way of life of the hunter gatherer. This switch to a sedentary lifestyle was by no means all for the best. Those producing the food, the Neolithic farmers, had to work longer hours on average than their hunter-gatherer forefathers. Diet was more restricted and generally poorer. In consequence, average height fell from about 5ft 10in to 5ft 5in for men with a similar reduction for women. Denser populations also meant diseases were rifer, sometimes transferred to humans from domesticated animals, but over time humans developed some resistance to diseases.

There were advantages too. Agriculture allowed food supply to become more reliable, especially in winter. People no longer needed to move on when the local supply of prey animals, fruit, nuts and berries had run short. They could stay put, plant, harvest and store food. This meant building permanent instead of temporary shelter. They could now live together in larger groups. Surplus food meant some people could turn their skills to activities other than farming. These new artisans, producing necessary tools at least first bartered and then later sold goods and services to the Neolithic farmers.

There emerged more pros than cons for MH with the emergence of agriculture. The new way of life was more demanding for most, but it meant more food was available for any given area of land. On balance, agriculture was more favourable to the development of MH than his previous hunter-gathering lifestyle. A crucial fact supporting this contention is that world population expanded under agriculture rather than contracted. Studies in France suggest that in the upper Palaeolithic there was 1 person per 3 km² but by the middle Neolithic this had changed to at least 1 per km².

Increasing populations and the need for focal points to meet, exchange goods and services led to the building of first hamlets, then villages and then towns. Finally, some social organisation was achieved resulting in the appearance of

Jericho and Catal Höyük

These two were probably the first such town-states but were initially too small to be named a city. Jericho, originally known as Tel es-Sultan, holds a further distinction. It has been continuously occupied for a longer period than any other town or city on the planet. Located in the West Bank, Jericho's first dwellings go back to about 9,000 BCE, that is 11,000 years ago. Then the town consisted of about 70 dwellings, occupied by 200 or so people. Jericho is made famous, or infamous, through its story in the Bible. Probably all Christians and Jews know the deadly tale of Joshua and the battle of Jericho.

[Figure: Reconstruction of Çatalhöyük seen from the air: flat-roofed mud-brick houses built against each other with no streets between them, ladders leaning against the walls and down through roof hatches, and people working on the rooftops.]

Çatalhöyük as it may have looked, about 7,100 BCE: houses built against each other, entered by ladders through the roofs

Catal Höyük, in Turkey, is not quite so old, at about 7,100 BCE. It eventually became home to about 5,000 people. At its height, the surrounding farm land was probably rich and productive. There is some evidence that the townsfolk engaged in trade with roving merchants. The town was curiously constructed of linked buildings with access through ladders and roof entrances. There were no doors.

Catal Höyük had no written language, and unusually there were no priests or social hierarchy. It is thought, without absolutely clear evidence, that religious beliefs would be simple, based on previous hunter-gatherers. Religion may have been practiced in household shrines and the dead buried beneath floors of houses. From evidence of female figurines recovered the stone-age reverence for an earth mother figure may have persisted in Catal Höyük, but this is not certain.

[Figure: Mother goddess figure from Çatalhöyük, c. 6000 BCE, Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, Ankara]

Mother Goddess figure 6,000 BCE Catal Höyük From Ankara Museum

Catal Höyük did not last anything like as long as Jericho. It existed for about 1,400 years, being finally abandoned in 5,700 BCE, maybe as a result of climate change, or because of pressure from other peoples. Then again, perhaps the inhabitants got fed up with having no streets and having to use the rooftops and ladders. Anyway, whatever the reason this iconic early human town was eventually abandoned.

Another very ancient archaeological site is also from Turkey, Göbekli Tepe, (Turkish for "Potbelly Hill"). This one is not quite so unusual, building wise, as Catal Höyük, but its origins are even older, 9,000 BCE. It had more than 200 stone pillars, but their purpose is unknown, perhaps a temple.

[Figure: Göbekli Tepe, Turkey, c. 9500 BCE: stone enclosure and T-shaped pillar under the excavation roof]

Göbekli Tepe is on a par with Jericho in terms of age, but Jericho remains ahead as the oldest continuously occupied city.

[Figure: Tell es-Sultan, ancient Jericho, West Bank, today: occupied for some 11,000 years]

chapters.title: Moving from City-states to Civilisation
chapters.summary: Briefly, Harappan of the Indus valley, Mohenjo-Daro, Xia and Shang Chinese dynasties. Before all these, here comes Sumer, Earth's first civilisation (nothing to do with Jerry Keller's song), Ashtar's story, Marduk and Tiamat, King Ashurbanipal, Assyrians, Babylonians, the Hittites.

pages.text:
Chapter 11

Moving from City-states to Civilisation

City-states, like Jericho and Catal Höyük, were individual, a law unto themselves. Next on the ever upward ladder of human development was the banding together of several cities into a distinct, homogeneous group with common governance and laws. Trade was more easily developed in a safer setting provided by the power of the bigger state. The sense of group belonging was re-enforced by increasingly developed religious beliefs. Countries and what we would call civilisations were born.

And what was the first civilisation that we know of? There are a few early cultures in the frame. The Harappan folk of the Indus valley in north west India and parts of Pakistan are one. Here cities were built, including the mud-brick houses of Mohenjo-Daro, this was from around 2,600 BCE. Some claim it was much earlier.

[Figure: Map of the Indus Valley (Harappan) civilisation across modern Pakistan and north-west India, with Harappa, Mohenjo-Daro and Lothal marked along the Indus, and Mehrgarh, an earlier farming village]

Mohenjo-Daro and other Harappan cities of the Indus Valley Civilisation, about 2,600 BCE

These towns or cities joined up and developed into a regional culture which lasted in the early period for around 700 years. Then there are various claims that an ancient Chinese civilisation was the first of all. The Xia then Shang Chinese dynasties are thought to have existed about 2,000 and 1600 BCE respectively, but not much is known about what these consisted of. More on these later.

Despite that early modern humans took a long time to reach South America, Peru can claim to be the home of an ancient civilisation at Caral. This was a large settlement of more than 3,000 people and dates back over 4,000 years. It was around at the same time the great pyramids of Egypt were constructed. Caral had a temple and amphitheatre as well as houses. It was one of about thirty population centres, comprising the Norte Chico civilisation.

Here comes Sumer, Earth's first Civilisation (probably!)

However, in the debate over what is Earth's first civilisation most experts say that the accolade can be given to Sumer. Located in the middle east, all the trappings of a civilisation were established here 6,000 years ago.

The title is not about the great Jerry Keller song of 1959. That was about summer, with two m's, this Sumer only has one and was around a long time before Jerry's.

[Figure: Map of the Fertile Crescent, arching from the Levant across northern Syria and down the Tigris and Euphrates to the Persian Gulf, with Sumer, 6,000 years ago, on the southern plain. Cities marked include Nineveh, Ashur, Mari, Kish, Nippur, Uruk, Lagash, Ur and Eridu]

Sumer, Mesopotamia, now largely Iraq

Sumer was the name for a group of cities located in the fertile crescent, Mesopotamia, this was the land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers in the Middle East. These are all references to the same geographic area of what we know today as mostly Iraq, with parts of Kuwait and Iran.

Sumer was the earliest grouping of cities over a wide geographical area. It existed as early as 4,500 BCE. The land was named Sumer but it might be more appropriate to call this, the first flowering of civilisation, Spring rather than Sumer. The Sumerians did not know they were the first. They may have been aware though that theirs was a different, bigger, wider culture, because Sumer has a distinct and appropriate meaning: "the land of the civilised lords". Why was Sumer the first civilisation on planet Earth? We cannot know for sure but there are positive indicators.

headings.text: Here comes Sumer, Earth's first Civilisation (probably!)

pages.text:
Firstly, the area of Sumer is on the route to Asia and Europe for MH, after their breakout from their original home in Africa. By following the coast line, from the Red Sea crossing from Ethiopia into Yemen, MH eventually reach the Persian Gulf and Mesopotamia. Here, settlers would find a rich land for hunting and gathering, with a good climate and plenty of fresh water. At a later stage the two rivers, Euphrates and Tigris, would help with transport and trade. It took thousands of years for MH to reach Europe, Asia and other areas. MH living in Mesopotamia could use this time to develop first agriculture then settled communities and later on individual city-states. Let's imagine how Sumer began to expand from its earliest city-state base of Eridu.

Ashtar stopped. He knew that with ten steps still to climb he was out of sight from anyone on the altar platform above. No one could see, him, in the faint, glowing light that preceded the dawn. He could not appear to be weak. To maintain his prestige, as High Priest, he must always give the impression of indomitable strength and reliability. That was why he was now pausing, to gather his breath, to stop wheezing and gasping. The climb up the 120 steep steps of the Ziggurat was exhausting for anyone. But Ashtar had been making this climb twice a day for the last 5 years, ever since this first mighty temple to the god Enki had been constructed. And Ashtar was now 54 years old, well past the average life span of most Sumerians.

He began to breathe evenly and slowly. After pausing to adjust his tunic he calmly climbed the last few steps. As he stepped out on to the wide stone platform a young figure hurried towards him. Ashtar maintained his rigid posture and stern demeanour. He knew that his young acolyte would be waiting for him, despite it was still not quite dawn. Imoun smiled briefly but with his head slightly bowed so Ashtar could not see his expression. He had known for many months the procedure that Ashtar followed when climbing the Ziggurat. But Imoun was devoted to Ashtar and did not want his master to lose face, so he pretended to be unaware of the rest that Ashtar took when near to the temple platform.

The caged chicken which Imoun held did not know it was fated to be sacrificed. Ashtar said: "Imoun, we will pause before making the dawn sacrifice. I want to look to the south in the light of the rising sun." Ashtar and Imoun walked to the southern edge of the platform and stared southward. In the sun's red morning glow, they could just make out in the very far distance wisps of dark smoke. Imoun asked: "What are you looking for master?" "Your eyes are sharper than mine Imoun, what do you see." said Ashtar, pointing dramatically.

"I see smoke faintly rising. The fire must be a long way away." "That is the future you look at Imoun. The smoke signals the mighty work our great King Meskiagkasher has commissioned. Uruk will be a city the like of which no one has seen before. The smoke is from the cooking fires of 2,000 workers."

Ashtar and Imoun are imaginary people. They must have had extremely good eyesight because they could see smoke in Uruk about 45 kilometres from their temple in Eridu, but the atmosphere was much clearer back then. Eridu is considered the first town/city of a region later to be called Sumer. It had expanded from a village, at the centre of a small agriculture community about 5,400 BCE. A number of autonomous city-states grew up alongside Eridu and Uruk in this region - the fertile crescent between the rivers Tigris and Euphrates. This area became the cradle of civilisation on planet Earth.

The very early culture in Eridu and immediate region was not Sumerian but known as the Ubaid culture, named after a village, Al-Ubaid, where remains were first uncovered. Ubaid society had a hierarchical structure but with elements of democratic decision making. They had a chieftain-priest as top man who was advised by a council, although this structure may have changed over the 2,700 years of the Ubaid period (about 6,500 to 3,800 BCE), especially because Semitic immigrants brought and integrated their own cultures. The Ubaids also had painted pottery; made tools like hoes, sickles, knives and adzes. Importantly, they made bricks, an essential component for building. They were expert in irrigation, draining marshes and used this skill to keep their drier southern settlements going. The climate became increasingly arid and eventually forced the abandonment of villages. This was the prelude for the end of the Ubaid period. Their culture represented an embryonic civilisation, and they gifted important elements to Sumer, especially their governance and religious worship.

People called Sumerians came to the Ubaid region, possibly from Anatolia (modern Turkey) and probably mixed with local populations. By 5,000 years ago there were several Sumerian cities like Eridu, Uruk, Ur, Kish, Nippur, Lagash, Bab-Tibira and Larsa. Each of these was characterised by certain common features. They comprised a walled city, with surrounding villages and agricultural land. Each city had its own deity whose temple was the main, central building. Early on, the citizens held political power but gradually kingship became the form of governance. These were features of the Sumerian, Uruk period, which succeeded Ubaid. Uruk, for its time, grew to become a big city and the most important in Sumer.

The Sumerians referred to themselves as the "black-headed people" and to Sumer simply as "the land". Much of what is known of Sumer comes from both the archaeological record and the Sumerian King-Lists, although the latter is clearly a heroic record. Several versions of the lists have been discovered by archaeologists. The oldest, from about 2,000 to 2,500 BCE, come from Larsa and Nippur. They were written in the Sumerian, cuneiform language on clay tablets. The lists attempt to show continuity of governance, by listing all the kings of the region in order. They claim that Etana of Kish was the first King to bring a common order to the land. Before him the city-states were probably broadly independent.

The Sumerian King List tells of eight kings before the great flood. In the flood myth Ziusudra, who was the last king of Sumer before the mighty flood, heard of the Gods decision to drown humanity, apparently humans were becoming a serious nuisance. Ziu built a very large ship to save himself from the flood.

[Figure: Woodcut of Noah's Ark, lettered 'ARCHA NOE', with Noah at the window, his family in the doorway and animals on deck]

Noah's Ark: the Bible's version of the flood story told earlier of Ziusudra and Utnapishtim. Woodcut, Koberger Bible, 1483 (University of Edinburgh, CC BY 2.0)

This myth is repeated later in the 1800 BCE poem, the Epic of Gilgamesh, where Utnapishtim builds a huge vessel to save himself, his family and animals. Floods were thought to be the Gods punishment for human wrong-doings. The same flood story appears in other ancient cultures and in the Bible, but for biblical readers it is Yahweh who is the instigator, not the Sumerian or Mesopotamian Gods.

One feature of the pre-deluge kings of Sumer was their unbelievably long-life spans (shades of biblical Methuselah). The 4,000-year-old Weld-Blundell cuneiform stone tablet, which is in the Ashmolean Museum explains: "After the kingship descended from heaven, the kingship was in Eridug. In Eridug, Alulim became king; he ruled for 28,800 years." Eridug was Eridu.

[Figure: Proto-cuneiform tablet recording barley and emmer, Mesopotamia, c. 3100 BCE, Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York]

Sumer became a powerful region of cities holding allegiance to one King, although the cities continued to vie with each other. This was the first such arrangement, as far as is known, on planet Earth. Sumer had all the trappings of a discrete civilisation with the first written word, government, laws, trade, taxes, customs and a social hierarchy. They certainly had a sense of humour, some Sumerian sayings: "For his pleasure, marriage. On his thinking it over, divorce." And "You may have a lord, you may have a king, but the man to fear is the tax collector." But the key cohesive element of Sumer's civilisation was religion.

Governance and religion

Sumerians believed their civilisation was the result of the Gods triumph over chaos. Each of the cities of Sumer had a priest-King. These Kings ruled originally with advice from a General Assembly made up elected men - evidence that democracy, of some sort, pre-dated the ancient Greeks! This system eroded over time and Kings, known as lugals, became more or less the sole power. Kings claimed their authority came from the city God and that they were able to act as the mediator between citizens and their God. This is the earliest example we have of the use made of religion to support the ruling body.

Religion was integral to all aspects of life. Citizens often had specific duties to perform related to the temple and its maintenance. They thought that civilisation came about through the Gods victory of order over chaos. The Sumerian creation myth claimed the God An, and Heaven and Earth, came from the primeval sea, called Abzu or Nammu. At a later stage in Mesopotamian history, Abzu was renamed Tiamat, a dragon like monster and Goddess of the watery deep. Tiamat was part of another creation myth. She battled the Gods champion, Marduk, who eventually slayed her. Marduk, according to Babylonian texts, founded Eridu, the earliest city of Sumer.

Sumerians worshipped four creator Gods:

Enki (God of water),
Ki (God of earth),
Enlil (God of air and storms),
An (God of heaven).

An was counted as the most important. His wife was Ki. Sumerians believed that these Gods ruled the universe, which they thought was heaven and earth. There were hundreds of other Sumerian Gods, all brought into being by the four original creators.

The individual city Gods, all anthropomorphic, were varied. Citizens of the famous city of Ur patronised the moon God Nanna, Eridu's God was Enki and Kish worshipped Zababa, the warrior God. Regular worship, which included animal sacrifice, took place in the most dominant, mud-brick city building, the temple. This later developed in the shape of a ziggurat - a pyramidal construction with a platform at the top.

[Figure: Photograph of the Ziggurat of Ur in Iraq: the massive lowest stage of the stepped temple tower, with its great triple stairway]

The Ziggurat of Ur, built about 2100 BCE for the moon God Nanna. Only the lowest stage survives (partly rebuilt); a temple once stood on top

They thought that civilisation came about through the Gods victory of order over chaos. The Sumerian creation myth claimed the God An, and Heaven and Earth, came from the primeval sea, called Abzu or Nammu. At a later stage in Mesopotamian history, Abzu was renamed Tiamat, a dragon like monster and Goddess of the watery deep. Tiamat was part of another creation myth. She battled the Gods champion, Marduk, who eventually slayed her. Marduk, according to Babylonian texts, founded Eridu, the earliest city of Sumer.

Religion was integral to all aspects of life. Citizens often had specific duties to perform related to the temple and its maintenance.

Beyond the early days of Sumer

Sumerians believed in an afterlife, although it was a dismal, dark one where people sat around eating dust and clay. This was an early version of hell. It may possibly have influenced later Jewish, Christian and Islamic ideas. They hyped up hell to be a fiery, much more frightening place, than the dull, boring one of Sumer. The Sumerian Heaven was reserved for the Gods.

Sumer existed for 1,000 years before invaders from the North, Akkadians, defeated them. Their leader was Sargon I. Several stories are told of Sargon. In one he was claimed to have once been a lowly cup-bearer to the King of Kish. In another the baby Sargon was found floating on a river in a basket made of reeds - shades of the later Biblical story of Moses, more plagiarism perhaps?

[Figure: Map of Mesopotamia within modern Iraq: Assyria in the north around Nineveh, Nimrud, Ashur and Arbela, and Babylonia in the south along the Tigris and Euphrates, divided into Akkad (with Babylon) and Sumer (with Nippur and Ur)]

Akkadians lasted about 200 years, up to 2154 BCE, before morphing eventually into Assyria in the North and Babylonia in the South. These later people, the Assyrians and Babylonians continued with heavy-duty religious beliefs, with the polytheistic, huge pantheon of Gods that had been pioneered by the land of Sumer. Their names and/or functions differed though. In ancient Assyria, Assur was King of the Gods.

headings.text: Beyond the early days of Sumer

pages.text:
There was a god of wisdom, Enki, Nisaba was first a Goddess of agriculture then became in charge of writing, perhaps she got too old to be out in the field all day. Biblical Nimrod, (Genesis 10:8-9) apparent builder of the city of Nineveh and possibly a King, was also accorded divine status.

One famous Assyrian warrior King was Ashurbanipal. He expanded Assyrian territory and control to such an extent this was the first empire on Earth. Ashurbanipal was an unusual warrior King, he was interested in books, or their equivalent. These were written on papyrus and sometimes chiselled on stone. At his palace in Nineveh he assembled a huge library and was proud to be a literate king, unlike his predecessors. His pride did not end there, he said: "I am Ashurbanipal: King of the World, King of Assyria." His reign lasted over 40 years, from 668 to 627 BCE.

[Figure: Ashurbanipal hunting lions from horseback, relief from Nineveh, c. 645-635 BCE, British Museum]

Ashurbanipal hunting on horseback 645-635 BCE (British Museum)

The Babylonians, vassals to the west of Assyria, captured Nineveh and conquered Assyria in 605 BCE, after many civil wars. This was perhaps the height of Babylonian power, but the city itself and its rulers had held sway in the region some 1,000 years before. At this time Hammurabi was king of Babylon, in 1810 to 1750 BCE. Ancient Babylon had lots of Gods and religious rules. Clearly though, the rules were insufficient so thought Hammurabi.

[Figure: The Code of Hammurabi, c. 1754 BCE, Louvre, Paris]

In 1754 BCE the Code of Hammurabi appeared with 282 laws chiselled on to a 2.25 metre stone. Almost half the laws concern contractual matters, like the wages to be paid to an ox driver. They do not say how much should be paid to a lawyer.

The length list of laws is a sign of the increasing complexity of society and the attempt to establish some commonality of behaviour, with penalties for infringements. This is a core feature of any civilisation. Hammurabi should be revered by all lawyers because his Code of Hammurabi was the first major listing of laws.

Abraham, the first prophet of Judaism, Christianity and Islam, was thought to have been born in Ur just before the reign of Hammurabi. Ur, was a Sumerian city originally. There is no absolutely clear evidence of Abraham's existence.

The fertile crescent, bounded by the two rivers, Euphrates and Tigris, was also known as Mesopotamia. This was an attractive piece of real estate and so was squabbled over by various peoples. Sumerians, Akkadians and Babylonians have already been mentioned. There were also Elamites, Ammorites and Hittites. All of them had a wide range of Gods and Goddesses.

The Hittites had an unusual claim to fame. They introduced iron. Before this bronze had been the main metal for use in weaponry. Their realm, at its height, covered the northern part of what was Sumer and a large chunk of modern-day Turkey. Assyria was to the south and ancient Egypt to the west.

Hittites Religion

Hittites tended to adopt the deities of the Hattic people that they partly displaced. They were also influenced by Sumerian and Akkadian religion. As a result, in common with other early middle-eastern culture, they had a large number of Gods and Goddesses. The total number of Gods named on various stone tablets exceed 600.

For the Hittites, Gods were highly knowledgeable but not omnipotent, or omniscient. Theirs were Gods to ask favours of, through prayer. It seemed though that the Gods reserved the Hittite afterlife only for Kings and high

[Figure: The Lion Gate, Hittite capital of Hattusa, Turkey (c. 1400-1200 BCE)]

Lions Gate, Hittite capital of Hattusa, Turkey

Just like the Sumerian Marduk and Tiamat myth, the Hittites told of a weather God battling with the monster Illuyankase. This time the monster was an enormous serpent, rather than a dragon. And again, like some Sumerian rulers, Hittite Kings had divine status, although this did not save them from assassination.

[Figure: Neo-Hittite relief of an armed figure, c. 9th-8th century BCE]

Hittites are mentioned several times in the Bible under the name Heth in Genesis. In the Book of Judges 1:26, the Israelites allowed one man to escape to: "the land of Hittites". These references, together with Abraham, who lived in Ur make clear Biblical authors were fully aware of the various Mesopotamian powers. This knowledge may have extended to the flood, creation, and afterlife myths which they then could have adopted and embellished.

The Hittites were about for some four hundred years, from 1600 to 1178 BCE. Eventually, they were fatally weakened by battles with Assyria and Egypt, and the disruptive, murderous mayhem within the Hittite royal family.

chapters.title: Now for The Pharaohs and Ancient Egypt
chapters.summary: Akhenaten and his move to monotheism - Aten, Nefertiti, Tutankhamun, Ramesses 2, Nefertari and Abu Simbel, Cleopatra, Gods - Ra, Amun, Isis, Osiris, Anubis, Horus, Hathor of the Milky Way, cat Goddess Bastet. The great female Pharaoh Hatshepsut.

pages.text:
Chapter 12

Now for The Pharaohs and Ancient Egypt

To the west of Mesopotamia and the Hittite empire was another fertile area. This also had an inviting climate, and a major river, for transport and irrigation, the Nile. The region was relatively easily accessible from MH original home in Africa. It's not surprising then that another early, major civilisation grew up here, in ancient Egypt.

According to some the first Pharaoh (Egyptian King) was Narmer also known as Menes. He started to unify Upper and Lower Egypt about 3,000 BCE. At this time, Egypt was contemporary with Sumer, some claim Egyptian civilisation is even older than Sumer. Egypt began as a narrow strip of land, about 20 Km wide, bordering the fertile flood plain of the River Nile. It stretched 500 Km from the Mediterranean. Eventually the Egyptian Empire expanded to control an area hundreds of kilometres long north to south bordering the Red Sea and west to east along the Mediterranean coast. To the west ancient Egypt, later under Ramesses II, went into part of what is now Libya and to the east through modern day Sinai and Syria. Much was sparsely populated desert or semi-desert. In terms of size, this Empire was probably larger than any preceding or contemporary empire between the Persian Gulf and Mediterranean or Black Sea.

[Figure: Map of the Egyptian Empire at its peak under Thutmose III, 15th century BCE: direct rule along the Nile from the Delta to Kurgus, with Sinai and the western desert oases, tribute-paying city-states in the Levant, and northern Syria to the Euphrates reached on campaign but not held]

Ancient Egypt was a dominant power in the region for more than 2,000 years until the Assyrian Ashurbanipal's army arrived in 667 BCE. Apart from his fame as a conqueror, Ashurbanipal also gains kudos for establishing the oldest library in the world at Nineveh, his capital.

headings.text: Now for The Pharaohs and Ancient Egypt

pages.text:
Egyptian Pharaohs had a long run before Ashurbanipal upset the apple cart. They even continued after him, for another 600 or so years, until Cleopatra VII had the distinction of being the last of the Pharaohs. But they never again wielded the same influence and power. So, what can be said about the great line of pharaohs who ruled Egypt for such a huge length of time, nearly 3,000 years? Well, apart from being rulers of the longest lasting empire, Pharaohs had the biggest, most luxurious, burial tombs on planet Earth. They are the pyramids of Egypt.

[Figure: Nineveh imagined: Assyrian palaces and ziggurat as restored for Layard's Monuments of Nineveh (1853)]

See below the pyramids in the Giza complex:

There are over 100 pyramids built by various Egyptian royalty. The first was completed by 2611 BCE, for Pharaoh Djoser and the last by Pharaoh Ahmose, more than 1,000 years later, in 1525 BCE. These colossal constructions were amazing feats of architecture and building. They required enormous resources to complete and were a testament to the mighty power of the reigning Pharaoh.

Like Mesopotamian rulers and Hittites, the Pharaoh was considered divine while retaining his humanity. He was most closely identified as Horus, son of the God Osiris. Ancient Egypt's rulers therefore followed the established trend of claiming Godly authority over their subjects.

[Figure: The Giza pyramids: Khufu (Cheops) 2575 to 2566 BCE, 147 m tall (originally) and 230 m wide, built of some 2,300,000 limestone blocks]

When passing on from their earthly life the Pharaohs joined the Gods, so they hoped, and achieved some form of existence after death. The mummified bodies of some have been dis-entombed from their original resting places, 2,000 or so years later, by eager archaeologists. In some cases, the prospect of unearthing gold and valuable objects, was the main driver. Much of what western Egyptologists and explorers unearthed in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries now reside in various European museums. Their findings gave fresh insight into long dead Egyptian Pharaohs.

Among those Pharaohs who now enjoy a new remembrance, either through being de-mummified or other reasons are:

Akhenaten, originally Amenhotep IV

1353 to 1336 BCE

This chap might have been fourth but clearly he wanted to be noted as first at something. The Greek form of his name meant "satisfied". He was far from this, starting with his discontent with Thebes as Egypt's capital. Akhenaten was prepared to ignore Thebes long history as Egypt's governing city. He set up his own capital city. Moving downstream to Amarna he established his new capital. But Akhenaten wanted more than just a new location with new scenery. To emphasise who it was that founded Egypt's new capital he had it named Akhenaten, this was followed by much building of palaces and temples. For speed, they were constructed with small and easily removable mud bricks - a fatal error in terms of ensuring longevity. Then he had a close look at Egyptian traditional religion, with its many, many Gods. This polytheism is not good enough he thought. Someone has to be the sole, supreme Godly authority. The mighty shining sun, Aten, was Akhenaten's choice of a pre-eminent, universal God. He also promoted himself to God status as the son of Aten.

[Figure: Colossal statue of Akhenaten from Karnak, Egyptian Museum, Cairo]

It's possible that Akhenaten suffered from an inherited form of epilepsy. This can cause religious visions on sunny days. If so, hence his monotheistic sun God Aten. Pharaoh Amenhotep IV became Pharaoh Akhenaten.

So, with a new capital and new religion, this was a good start in making sure posterity would remember him. He made a little mistake though in the choice of one of his five consorts, Nefertiti (meaning: "The beautiful one has come forth."). She assumed the status a female God.

Nefertiti's name is better remembered than Akhenaten, mainly the result of her lovely gold bust, that is a statue type not bra type. Of course, she may also have had a gold bust of the other sort as well, given Egypt's sunny climate.

Nefertiti's bust is kept at the Berlin Museum. Here she is.

[Figure: Bust of Queen Nefertiti, c. 1345 BCE, Neues Museum, Berlin]

Nefertiti tried hard to keep things going once her husband had died. She approached the Hittite King and asked him to send one of his sons so she could marry him. Had she succeeded in joining the two main powers of the region, she might have established a new, huge and powerful empire. However, the priests of the old God Amun were not happy at the prospect of a continuation of Akhenaten's form of monotheism. They had the Hittite prince murdered on his way to Egypt.

Akhenaten's capital, its temples and palaces, were pulled down and plundered - the small bricks were relatively easy to remove. The God Amun disappeared from the main scene, the old Egyptian religion was re-established and Nefertiti faded into the background. But Akhenaten still had one last card to play in ensuring his name lived on, although he could not know that this was a top trump. His progeny included the legendary Tutankhamun.

[Figure: Photo of Ludwig Borchardt, German Egyptologist with Nefertiti bust, 1912]

Tutankhamun

1336 to 1327 BCE

[Figure: Funerary mask of Tutankhamun, c. 1323 BCE, Egyptian Museum, Cairo]

Poor boy, he became chief aged 9 and, a sickly youth, died at 19. Tut was not much of a Pharaoh, no serious smiting of enemies, no new territories added to the Egyptian empire, no new God, no interesting consort or new capital city. He was quite boring really. But Tut was smart enough to change his name from Tutankhaten to Tutankhamun. The winds of change were clear to him, or more likely to his advisers. His father's new Godly supremo, Aten, was on the way out. God Amun and the multiplicity of Egyptian Gods were back in the ascendency.

He was fortunate to have a well-hidden tomb, unlike the more demonstrative constructions of other Pharaohs. Tut's tomb in the Valley of The Kings remained undiscovered and unrobbed for 3,000 years, until Howard Carter arrived in 1922. Then Tut became the most talked about Pharaoh in the world. This is because of the stunning finds of jewelled chairs, gold death mask, golden coffins, three of them, and chariots among thousands of other items.

[Figure: Howard Carter, English Egyptologist, who uncovered Tutankhamun's tomb in 1922 (photographed 1924)]

All this, together with his mummified body was contained in one of the smallest Egyptian tombs. One intriguing find was of a golden fan. This originally had 42 ostrich feathers. The tale of the fan, etched on its handle, says these feathers were from birds the Pharaoh himself had hunted. Some Egyptologists speculate this could suggest the Pharaoh died on an ostrich hunt. Hunting ostriches though must have been safer than hunting lions.

Ramesses II

1279 to 1213 BCE

[Figure: Colossal statue of Ramesses II at Abu Simbel, photographed by Maxime Du Camp in 1850]

This Pharaoh was known as Ramesses the great for good reason. He reigned for 66 years and made his mark on Egypt and beyond. Under him Egypt took back control of two territories, the Levant in the east and Nubia in the south. He had a massive battle at Kadesh (Syria) with the Hittites. Up to 6,000 chariots and 50,000 infantry were involved. Employing an early form of fake news Ramesses claimed victory. Historians think it more likely to have been a draw. The Hittites won the first half but Ramesses warriors came back to take the second half.

As a result, Ramesses showed what wise statesman he was. He signed a peace treaty with King Hattusilis of the Hittites. Ramesses gained a historical accolade for the first recorded peace treaty between two states. As part of the deal two Hittite princesses joined Ramesses collection of wives. These two were just add-ons. His Great Royal Wife and favourite was Nefertari. Her name meant beautiful companion. Rameses built a great temple for his favourite wife at Abu Simbel and had a greater one constructed for himself.

[Figure: The Small Temple of Abu Simbel, built for Nefertari, photographed by Antonio Beato c. 1870]

Abu Simbel, the Small Temple, built by Ramesses II for Nefertari

Nefertari has appeared in novels and in these films: Exodus: Gods and Kings 2014; The Ten Commandments 1956 and The Mummy Returns 2001. She did not make any money though from these artistic depictions of her, having been dead for 3,200 years by the time they appeared.

[Figure: Queen Nefertari, wall painting in her tomb, Valley of the Queens, c. 1255 BCE]

Like Akhenaten before him, Rameses also wanted to establish his own capital. He chose Piramesse, on the eastern side of the Nile delta. Pi - Ramesse meant the domain of Ramesses. Centuries later, due to the shifting of the Nile's deltaic course, this city silted up and was abandoned. French Egyptologist, Pierre Montet re-discovered it in 1929. Pierre was quite a thorough Egyptian tomb raider. He discovered or disentombed Egyptian pharaohs at Tanis (an ancient capital in lower Egypt): Psusennes I, Amenemope, and Shoshenq II and Takelot I.

Pierre found gold belonging to Osorkon II here including the representation of a Godly triad, Osiris, with his son Horus on the left and wife Isis on the right.

[Figure: Osiris flanked by Horus and Isis, gold and lapis lazuli, Tanis, 22nd Dynasty (Louvre)]

When it came to tomb raiding those films of Indiana Jones and Lara Croft had nothing on Pierre.

Cleopatra

69 to 30 BC

We've now heard of Nefertiti and Nefertari, but the most famous Egyptian woman of all is Cleopatra, or Cleopatra VII Philopator to give her full name. Well, you would think that she was Egyptian, but no, Cleo was a Greek. Some 250 years before Cleo Alexander the Great had taken control of Egypt. He even adopted the Egyptian God Amun. The Greek dynasty Ptolemy followed and Cleo was a descendant of this family. The Rosetta Stone, key to the translation of Egyptian hieroglyphs, was inscribed in the time of one of the Ptolemy's, number V.

Cleo at first ruled jointly, with her father, later with her two brothers. But she was the real power. A clever woman, she spoke several languages. Cleo claimed to be the reincarnation of the Goddess Isis, no doubt expecting this to give her greater authority. She tried to re-establish Egyptian prominence by cementing close ties with the burgeoning power of Rome. So close were these ties that she bore a son, Caesarion, to Julius Caesar.

[Figure: Statue attributed to Cleopatra VII, holding a cornucopia, Hermitage Museum, St Petersburg]

Cleopatra, holding a cornucopia and going for a bath?

After Caesar's assassination Cleo attached herself to Mark Antony, bearing him three children. He was a contender for head of the Roman Empire. She backed the wrong man though; Antony and Cleo's forces were defeated by Octavian at the Battle of Actium. Shortly after that Antony and Cleo committed suicide. Her departure was via an asp, a poisonous snake, although this is disputed. Young Caesarion, was killed by Octavian, who became Emperor Augustus, and Egypt was demoted to become a Roman province. Cleo obviously tried to cultivate powerful friends but ended up putting all her eggs in the wrong basket. 1,600 years after her demise, Cleo became a Shakespearean star and later still appeared in films.

Ancient Egyptian Religion, Science and Women of Power

When it came to Gods, ancient Egyptians did not do things by halves, but by thousands. It is estimated there were well over 2,000 Egyptian Gods and Goddesses, all were anthropomorphic types. Some Gods had the head of an animal on the body of a man. Egypt at this time was the epitome of polytheism.

headings.text: Ancient Egyptian Religion, Science and Women of Power

pages.text:
There was something of a changing hierarchy. Those Gods at the top of the tree varied over time, not surprising since the religion lasted over 3,000 years. At one stage Ra, the sun God was top dog, later it was the turn of the creator God Amun and then Isis, a mother Goddess. For a short while Aten, on his own, was elevated by Pharaoh Akhenaten.

The Egyptians had three sun Gods, the rising sun was Horus (more on him later), the hot, strong mid-day sun was Ra and the evening sun was creator God Amun. How far did Horus rise before he had to give way to Ra? Exactly what time did Amun take over from Ra? Egyptians did not have super-accurate atomic clocks to help them so there must have been a bit of uncertainty, at change-over time, about which God was now in the sky. The Gods themselves might have engaged in a few punch-ups because of the inexact junctures. Other well-known Gods included Osiris, Anubis and Horus.

[Figure: Osiris, Anubis and Horus: wall painting in the tomb of Horemheb (KV 57), Valley of the Kings]

Gods Osiris, Anubis and Horus

Osiris (god of the afterlife, rebirth, fertility and agriculture), Anubis, God of the dead, and Horus, at first a sky God then God of royalty. Horus beat up Seth, for killing Osiris and then used his gouged-out eye to resuscitate him. So, the "eye of Horus" is associated with sacrifice and healing.

Another God associated with Horus is his mother, Isis. She was also the wife of Osiris. Isis was one of the greatest Egyptian Goddesses; revered as a mother figure and thought to have magical powers.

[Figure: Isis nursing the child Horus, bronze statuette, Metropolitan Museum of Art]

Isis - A 'goodie' Egyptian Goddess, she protected women and children and healed the sick

Yet another Goddess was Hathor, originally a cow Goddess, associated with the Milky Way. The Milky Way was thought to be the milk of a heavenly cow. Hathor challenged Isis, eventually, for the title of the most renowned Goddess. She was worshipped in several countries outside of Egypt; seen as the Goddess of women, childbirth, beauty and the stars among other things. Like Hathor, Egyptian Gods and Goddess, changed their attributes and sometimes their names over time.

Religion permeated every aspect of Egyptian life. There were Gods or Goddesses for every occasion and for every natural aspect - sun, moon, motherhood etc. Egyptians always had one or other specialist God they could pray or appeal to. Fortunately for them, their religion did not require them to pray regular to all 2,000+.

There were lots of temples and rituals. Some annual festivals included a procession, such as Opet Festival celebrated in Thebes. This was where the God's image in a model ship was trundled around temples. Opet was the mother of Osiris. The Pharaoh was seen as the intermediary between people and the Gods. Egyptians believed in an afterlife and thought the souls of the dead could be preserved after death by proper provision of grave goods. They believed in an original creation too. There were slight variations of a basic creation myth which said the dry earth emerged from an ocean of chaos.

Egyptian's may have been the original cat lovers. Egyptian cats did not just have staff, they had followers. The reverence and love of cats was such that Egyptians had a domestic cat Goddess, Bastet. She was thought to protect against evil and had a festival in the northern city of Bubastis.

[Figure: Goddess Bastet as a cat, bronze, Late Period, Louvre, Paris]

Goddess Bastet

Religion in ancient Egypt was a huge industry. It supported those in power, particularly the divine Pharaoh. Resources invested were large but Egypt could afford it, benefitting from its wealth as a country astride the mighty and life-giving River Nile. Wealth gave them time to think as well as revere their Gods. They were expert mathematicians and astronomers. The first known measure of weight was the Egyptian beqa. They invented the 24 hour day, a base 10 numbering system and perhaps the first sun-dials. They used the stars as their calendar. Their year was 365 days but with 12 months of 30 days plus 5 feast days. The summer solstice marked day one.

Egyptian women? Women rights were not perfect, but certainly ahead of their time in ancient Egypt. They were legally equal to men in court and could own property. Some women were allowed to become powerful figures too. There were women Pharaohs, sometimes disguised in the form of a regency, such notables were: Nitocris; Sobekneferu; Hatshepsut; Neferneferuaten, Twosret and several Cleopatras.

[Figure: Hatshepsut, fifth pharaoh of the 18th Dynasty: seated statue, Metropolitan Museum of Art]

Hatshepsut - 5th Pharaoh of the 18th Dynasty
Hatshepsut was the most successful of these women, and had the longest reign, possibly 21 years. Unlike most male Pharaohs, Hatshepsut avoided regular military conflict with surrounding states. Nubia was an exception. Nubia was sorted out militarily with Hatshepsut firmly at the fore of the conflict. Nubia aside, trade and diplomacy were Hatshepsut's weapons of choice. Her clever diplomacy helped Egypt become wealthier by establishing new trade routes and good relations with surrounding states. She also had hundreds of new buildings constructed, including the colonnaded Temple of Karnak with its statue of Rameses II.

[Figure: Hatshepsut in the White Crown: kneeling statue from Deir el-Bahri, Metropolitan Museum of Art]

Other than Hatshepsut there were the powerful consorts Nefertiti and Nefertari. About 350 AD Hypatia, a philosopher and teacher, was a major figure in Egypt's Alexandria. After the Islamic conquest of 642 AD women were not allowed to achieve nationally powerful positions. Egypt has not seen any women of similar prominence to those of old Egypt in the 1,400 hundred years since the arrival of Islam.

Ancient Egypt's Decline

It may be that Ashurbanipal, in 667 BCE brought about the demise of the Egyptian hegemony, as mentioned earlier. However, the decline and the final and complete disappearance of Egyptian Gods, hieroglyphics and power may have been a more gradual process, over 1,200 years or so, from the time Ashurbanipal. Other major players in ancient Egypt's downfall include the Greek, Alexander the Great in 332 BCE; the Roman Emperor Augustus (Octavian) in 30 BCE; Roman Christian Emperor, 306 to 337 CE and finally the Rashidun caliphate who oversaw the Muslim conquest of Egypt during 639 to 646 CE.

[Figure: Augustus of Prima Porta, Roman marble statue, Vatican Museums (representing the Roman empire)]

chapters.summary: China, more on Xia and Shang Dynasties, and early Gods, Taoism, Confucianism, Buddhism the state religion, India and Hinduism, the Vedic period, Bahai, Cao Dai, Jainism, Shinto, Sikhism, Sinism, Zoroastrianism. African, South American and other religions.

pages.text:
Chapter 13

The ancient world of the Far East and elsewhere

While the likes of Sumer, Akkad, Assyria, the Hittite empire, Babylon and Egypt were developing all the trappings of civilisation, things were moving in the Far East too.

China

The first Emperor of China was Qin Shi Huang. He, by force of arms, unified the whole of China in about 225 BCE. His legacy is still to be seen, in thousands of terracotta warriors, the Great Wall of China, and in establishing the first controlling bureaucracy. But Qin's empire was not the first Chinese civilisation. It was the first to cover the whole of China, mostly as now known. A much earlier dynasty, the Xia, ruled a large Chinese territory, but not the whole of China. They were probably the first civilisation in China. The Xia dynasty was around in 2000 or 2200 BCE, according to different calculations. That's one claim, but because of lack of permanent written records, it's not certain Xia was the first. The Shang Dynasty, about 1600 BCE, might have that honour. The ancient Chinese sensibly used the materials to hand to both build and to some extent write on, i.e. mainly bamboo. This does not last as long as the stone work of Mesopotamian and Egyptian civilisations, so old records and structures for ancient China are sparse, or non-existent. Anyway, whatever, Xia or Shang, both were located around the Yellow River. Unlike the Nile farmers, Xia clans did not appreciate the major flooding that regularly occurred with the Yellow River. Chinese myths talk of the efforts of Gun followed by his son Yu to stop flooding. The latter succeeded by building a series of canals, that took water to the sea. This story suggests a large, organized society, capable of major constructions.

[Figure: Map of eastern China showing the Shang heartland on the Yellow River plain, around Anyang and Zhengzhou, c. 1600-1046 BCE, and a wider Shang sphere of outposts reaching the Yangtze and its copper mines]

People of the Shang Dynasty worshipped a lot of different Gods, just as did ancient Middle Eastern civilisations. Many of these early Chinese Gods were associated with the natural world: they had a weather God and a sky God. Their chief deity, was named Shangdi. Shangdi had a lot of roles to perform: responsible for success in battle; the harvest; weather and the capital city. Later in the Zhou dynasty, Shangdi was supplanted by Tian, a supreme deity meaning heaven.

headings.text: The ancient world of the Far East and elsewhere

pages.text:
Gods and ancestors were thought important because they could impact on crops, childbirth, weather and warfare. Therefore, attention, had to be paid to them.

The religion of the Shang probably developed from a much older, maybe 3,000 years older, form of ancestor worship and shamanism. This can be inferred from burial practices of the Neolithic Chinese including orientation of the dead. These were buried with offerings liquids and animal skulls.

Eventually, some philosophies emerged between 600 and 450 BCE, which can be likened to a religion. These were Taoism or Daoism, Buddhism and Confucianism.

[Figure: Venn diagram of three overlapping circles: Buddhism (the Noble Eightfold Path; founder Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha), Taoism (live in harmony with the Tao, the force or way; yin and yang, dark and light; founder Laozi) and Confucianism (right way of life: ren, li, yi and zhong; founder Confucius)]

All three have some commonality in their teachings. They are known as generally peaceful, non-threatening religions or philosophies. Their focus is on personal ethics and they tell people how best to live life in harmony with themselves and others. None involve a personal God of the sort favoured by Abrahamic religions. Buddhism, eventually, had widest support.

[Figure: Portrait of Empress Wu Zetian from the British Library]

Buddhism was made the state religion by China's only woman Emperor, Wu Zetian, in about 683 CE. This was partly because of the ideological support she received from the Buddhist community. A similar pattern was found in Mesopotamia and ancient Egypt where the state religion was used to prop up the power of the chiefs. Nowadays, Buddhism is the most prevalent of the three religions or philosophies in China with about 250 million followers and 13,000 temples. (see Philosophy, Chapter 23 for more on Buddhism, Taoism and Confucianism.)

Apart from the religious form of Buddhism, China has had many indigenous and traditional religions. Together, these represent about 10% of the world's religious population. They have in common certain features: an oral tradition with no holy literature; a belief in spirits; veneration for the dead; encouragement of traditional medicine and attempt to use magic. Some take on elements of Christian beliefs, i.e. they are syncretic.

India

It's not clear what religious beliefs were held, if any, by inhabitants of India's ancient Indus Valley, the Harappan culture. No evidence has emerged. There are no temples, or written clues and burial practices were varied. It has been suggested, arguably, that some female figurines from around 2,000 BCE may represent a fertility Goddess.

After the end of the Indus Valley civilisation period came the Vedic age in India, leading directly to Hinduism.

Hinduism arose in India and Nepal and is the oldest major religion in the world. It still has many followers in this part of the world, about 900 million. Hindu is Greek for the land beyond the Indus River. The religion has no single source or founder. It's thought to be an amalgam of various ancient beliefs and cultures, which go back to 2500 BCE, i.e. 4,500 years ago.

Hinduism

There is no clarity about the timing and beginning of Hinduism. Early Hinduism may stem from religious rituals of the Indus Valley civilization, centered on the defunct, ancient cities Harappa and Mohenjo-Daro. It's thought these had a religion that involved temple rituals, mass ritual bathing, animal sacrifice and possibly Goddess worship. Such practices feature in later Hinduism.

[Figure: Shiva as a wandering ascetic (Indian painting, c.1780)]

Hinduism further developed in the Vedic period, 1500 to 500 BCE. The religious guidance described in the four Vedas, (sort of scriptures) was written in Vedic Sanskrit during this time. They are the oldest writings in Hinduism and thought to originate from revelations made to ancient sages after a period of heavy meditation.

The four Vedas are: the Rigveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda, and Atharvaveda. These describe various mantras, rituals and sacrifices. It's not clear whether this also involved use of mind-bending substances. Other ancient literature, containing some of the central ideas of Hinduism, is found in the Upanishads texts that encourage meditation and acquirement of spiritual knowledge. The modern practice of Yoga, which has become popular in the west, originates from the Rigveda, perhaps before, even beyond, Hinduism. Yoga is both a physical and mental - meditative - exercise, aiming to promote well-being. The Hindu God Shiva is thought by some to have been the first yogi. Others may thing a man had a hand in it. One well known, common mantra used in yoga is the word, or hum, ohm, ohmmmmmmmmmmmm. So repetitive, this does not just go on and on but ohm and ohm. Yoga is proven to be good for humans for its gentle exercise which improves flexibility and strength, and because it is mentally calming. It is sometimes used in association with 'mindfulness' - self-awareness conditioning.

Some cross-fertilization of religious ideas occurred around the time of Buddha's death, including the idea of the problems caused by human desires - hence yoga. The next major contribution to the development of Hinduism was the arrival of the Bhagavad-Gita ("Song of God", 100 CE). This text explains three ways to salvation: duties; knowledge and yoga.

All this ancient textual advice is intended to guide believers in order to achieve a sort of divine goodness. Such moral improvement might take many lifetimes. Re-incarnation, called Samsara, is an essential belief of Hinduism. The religion claims that in an endless cycle of re-birth Hindus need to pursue knowledge of truth and reality. In the process Hindus must seek a moral order and a peaceful tolerance towards others. The right karma, that is the way a person acts or re-acts, which can be either good or bad, is how this is achieved. They believe there is one ultimate reality called Brahman. Confusingly there is also an important God, named Brahma. Brahma is one of a triumvirate of Gods, he is the creator, second up is Vishnu who keeps things going and finally we have Shiva the destroyer. She is the sort of necessary destroyer to allow things to start up again. Hindus think Brahman pervades the whole universe and is inside humans in the form of atman, the soul. The eventual aim of samsara is to move close to Brahman.

There is a wide variety of Hindu Gods and Goddesses. These are thought to be aspects of the Supreme Brahman. Hinduism easily outstrips every other religion in terms of number of Gods. They hold the gold medal for Multitudinous Deities without a worthy challenger in sight.

This proliferation of divinities arises because every village, group, caste and even family can have their own set of Gods, resulting in many thousands of Gods.

As with other major religions Hinduism has different sects. The main sects are: Vaishnavites, for them Lord Vishnu is top God; Saivites, whose chief God is Siva; Shaktas, where Goddess Shakti reigns supreme lastly there are Smartas (an unfortunate name. It has quite a different meaning in colloquial English), these are the liberals, not necessarily smugly clever as the English word would indicate.

For the Indian Hindu associated with the Smarta sect the choice of Deity is left to the believer but usually they claim loyalty to all the Hindu Gods. Smartas' are members of the upper classes - Brahman, Kshatriya or Vaishya.

Other Eastern Religions

Hinduism, with 1.1 billion followers is by far the biggest Eastern religion, closely followed by Buddhism, if this is considered a religion rather than a philosophy. Most other religions of the area bear some association with features of Hinduism but are not as popular. They include:

Bahai Began in Persia, now Iran. It is a relatively new religion starting up in 1863. Bahaullah, the founder, claimed he was a new prophet of God, like Jesus or Mohammed. It has about 6 million followers in more than 100 countries. The central message is twofold: 1. The whole of mankind is one unified spiritual whole. Under Bahai, there is no racism or nationalism. All people are equal. The world is a unified oneness, or should be, according to Bahai.; 2. God is unknown but is gradually revealing himself. In this process all major messengers of monotheistic religions, and others, are a part of this unfolding knowledge of God. These include Buddha, Abraham, Moses, Zoroaster, Jesus and Mohammed.

Cao Dai This is a one-size-fits-all religion with about 2 million followers. Meaning "High Tower" or supreme God Cao Dai is a newish, 1920, Vietnamese religion. It's an amalgam of many beliefs: Confucianism; Taoism; Buddhism and Roman Catholicism. Cao Dai's list of saints is unusual, embracing both famous religious and non-religious figures, include Brahma, Jesus Christ, Mohammed; Confucius; Pericles; Julius Caesar; Sun Yat-sen, Joan of Arc and Napoleon I. In structure Cao Dai copies Roman Catholicism with a Pope, Cardinals and Archbishops. It has lots of rituals and

Jainism This religion began and is largely based in India with about 4.2 million adherents. Like Hindus Jains believe in leading an ethical, non-violent life and in an endless number of re-births. They are also vegetarians and try not to harm any living creature. Their first teacher, they claim, was Rishabhanatha. He is meant to have lived millions of years ago. Given that we Modern Humans are about 300,000 years old this seems unlikely. Mahavira, who was around in about 540 BCE, is more likely to have influenced modern Jainism through texts called Agamas. The oldest Jain religious text is the Acaranga Sutra, 5th to 4th century BCE. Jainism is mainly confined to India, but pockets exist in a few other countries. There are about 4 million Jains.

Shinto Just over half of modern day Japanese practice Shinto, which means "Way of the Spirits." It has no founder nor does it have just a main, single sacred writing. In essence it encourages devotion to spiritual beings known as kami. These kami are not Gods but have the power to help with happiness, health, exam results and prosperity. They need proper respect. Japanese Shinto followers may have a small shrine-altar in their homes to appeal to the kami. There are also public shrines and public festivals. The spirits are considered as one with our world. There is not a transcendental, other world. Shinto is specific to Japan.

Sikhism This is yet another Indian founded religion with 20 million followers. It originated in the Punjab province in the 16th century by Guru Nanak. It differs from Hinduism in its monotheism. But some other teachings show a similarity. Sikhs think everyone should be treated equally. People should conduct themselves honestly, be generous, work hard, and keep God in mind. The key Sikh scripture is the Guru Granth Sahib.

Sinism, or Mism, or in China Wuism This is an ancient, Korean folk religion based on Shamanism. Its title means "religion of the spirits". Gods, ancestors and nature spirits are a feature. Spirits and Gods abound. In modern times it does not feature much, if at all. Koreans are now much more likely to be mainly non-religious, second up are Christians then Buddhists.

Zoroastrianism It vies with Hinduism as the world's oldest religion, arising in Persia about 3,500 years ago. It was the main religion of the great Persian Empire of Darius the Great and his son, the not-so-great Xerxes. Astutely though, the Persian conquerors allowed their defeated foes to retain their own religion, or beliefs of

another ancient religion, Hinduism, is still today a major religion. However, Zoroastrianism is not. It was Persia's (Iran) official religion for over 1,200 years, from 600 BCE up the time of the Arab Muslim conquest in 650 CE. Now, there are only about 190,000 followers. Zoroaster was a man who lived about 1,000 years before Jesus Christ. He thought of himself as a seeker after truth and wisdom; just as did any philosopher, but he preached a form of metaphysics that was religious in nature. Zoroaster claimed the universe was forever split between light and darkness, with light representing good and darkness evil. People were at liberty to go towards the light or dark, this sounds a bit like the Star Wars where Luke had the goodie "Force" with him while chief baddy, Darth Vader, gloried in the "Darkside".

[Figure: Zoroaster, from a 1906 Persian print]

Early on, Zoroastrian had two Gods. One was the chief of the light and the good, Ahura Mazda. The other, representing the peak of darkness and evil, was Ahriman. This dualistic religion over time gradually moved to monotheism with Mazda recognized as sole chief God. Zoroaster is sometimes known as Zarathustra; a name given greater prominence by the writings of Nietzsche and by the music of Strauss in his Opus 30. The Zoroastrian God, Ahura Mazda, is also known as the Wise Lord. Mazda, who now creates cars, started off by cranking up the universe, while allowing for good and evil in the process. This has great resonance with the later religion of Christianity. Did early Christian Biblical authors do a bit of copying of this concept? It also has similarity with Taoism's idea of light and dark. Zoroastrians did not allow artistic holy images of any type. This ruling is also a feature of later Islam. Since much of early Muslim conquest was of the Persian, Zoroastrian, Empire, could this no-imagery rule have been copied? Zoroastrianism's sacred text is The Avesta. It teaches that the elements are pure and that fire represents God's wisdom. The Parsis, a sect of this religion who escaped persecution in Persia, exist now in India and number about 50,000.

[Figure: Ahura Mazda (right) gives the ring of kingship to Ardashir I, Naqsh-e Rustam, Iran (3rd century CE)]

African religions We've now covered development of religions in the middle and Far East, what about Africa? About 85% of Africans today are either Christians or Muslims. The former predominate in sub-Saharan Africa and the latter is very heavily represented in countries bordering the Mediterranean and in the Horn of Africa (Red Sea coastline). An estimated 15% are mostly of indigenous religions and Bahai.

South America Early South Americans, Aztecs, Incas, Mayans, Toltecs and others had naturalistic Godly beliefs that were part and parcel of everyday life. Their Gods had to be appeased or appealed to by animal or human sacrifice. Spanish and Portuguese conquerors brought Catholicism to South America. They also brought, eventually, many African slaves. Some African beliefs translated in amended form to South America, largely as a result of the slave trade. Candomblé is probably the main one of this type. It has about 2 million followers, mostly in Brazil. The principal form of devotional expression is through dance, not surprising since the name Candomblé means, "dance in honour of the Gods". Oludumaré is top of the Candomblé Godly tree, serviced by lesser deities called orixas. Every person is believed to have his own orixa.

Other parts of the world Ancient religion in other parts of the world, such as Australasia and Arctic regions, was based on nature and mysticism. It still is to some extent. Australian Aborigines believed in ancestral creator beings. These brought into being living creatures and natural features like rock formations and water holes. The creator beings were thought to have roamed through the land naming and creating as they went. The time of creation was known as dreamtime.

The Maoris of New Zealand originated from Polynesian stock and their religion was similar to that of Polynesia. It identified with many Gods of nature and, as with Australian Aborigines, believed dreaming important.

The Sami (reindeer herders) and other far northerners have traditionally engaged in animism which included a form of bear worship.

Now to move away from both the east, and the south. It's time to look towards the west. Europe up next.
