Chapter 17

Christianity

In terms of numbers of adherents Christianity trumps every other religion currently and in the past. It has 2.4 billion followers. Catholics have the most followers, at 1.3 billion, followed by Protestants, 920 million. The rest are mostly of the Eastern Orthodox church.

The Christian Bible

This is the holy book revered by Christians. It is central to the Christian faith. The Bible is in fact several books, comprising of both the Old and New Testaments. The old really is old because it was probably written in Hebrew or Aramaic between 1200 and 165 BCE. And the New Testament is only relatively new. It was written almost 2,000 years ago. Books of the New Testament total 27: four Gospels; the Epistles, mostly by St Paul; and the Revelation of St John. The Old Testament has more books. Catholics and Protestants count 39 but some other Christian denominations, Coptic and Ethiopian, add an extra 4.

There was more than one author of the Bible, probably about 40; not surprising given it was written over a period of about 1,300 years. Even by some biblical standards, no one lives that long. Moses, he of the famous ten commandments and leader of the Jewish flight out of Egypt, is thought by Abrahamic religious adherents, to have written the first five books of the Bible, (see the claim explained here that this is impossible: https://listverse.com/2014/09/08/10-theories-about-who-really-wrote-the-bible). At a distance of 3,000 or so years we cannot be quite certain of the exact timing or precise authorship. When describing the Bible as consisting of several books this seems apt, because of the word's origin. The word "Bible" comes from Roman Latin, which in turn derives from the Greek ta biblia = the books. We have more on the Bible a little later but for now concentrate on Christian beliefs.

You could also argue Christianity really began with Abraham, maybe 1,500 BCE, or perhaps Adam, 4,000 BCE (by Biblical counting). In the start-up frame we also have John the Baptist. He, a relative of Jesus, began his preaching and baptizing before Jesus got underway. He announced the coming messiah, i.e. Jesus. John, sometimes known as John the Forerunner or John the Immerser, later got carried away and lost his head in foolishly denouncing Herod, the local chief, for divorcing his wife and marrying Herodias. As a result, he really did lose his head.

The Church of Christ Takes on Many Variations

Here are assorted Christian sects, probably not all of them:

Catholics

Full title: Roman Catholicism

The biggest of the Christian religions, with over 1.2 billion

headings.text: The Church of Christ Takes on Many Variations

pages.text:
[Figure: The Vatican, Rome, HQ of Roman Catholicism]

Expanded detail below

Protestants

Many variants below fall under the broad umbrella of 'Protestantism'

Expanded detail below

Anabaptists

[Figure: Martyred Dutch Anabaptist, Dirk Willems, 1569 CE, saves his pursuer]

These believe that baptism only works when the baptisee really wants to be baptised and says that he really does believe in Jesus. Faith in the Gospel must come before Baptism, for the Anabaptists. Anabaptists literally means again Baptists. Perhaps though it should mean later Baptists' because the baptisee must be an adult. Anabaptists think this is when a person can confess sin and properly embrace the faith. Children are considered not to be able to do this, thus they should not be baptised. Swiss Ulrich Zwingli, in the early 15th century, came up with this idea. Because it was against both Protestant orthodoxy and the Catholic church Anabaptists were heavily persecuted by both in 15th and 16th centuries. Today there are about 4 million Anabaptists. They are closely linked to Amish and can be referred to as Mennonites.

Amish

[Figure: Amish]

These are of German and Swiss origin. They believe in a literal interpretation of the Bible and are one of about 25 very slightly different Amish communities. The Amish are closely related to Mennonites, with some distinct differences. Amish don't like modern technology and try and avoid it, that's why they frequently use horses for transport and working the land. They also have little contact with the world outside their community and dress very traditionally. All these traits are not found in Mennonites. Together with Mennonite and Brethren groups Amish are mainly located in Pennsylvania USA. These are known as the Plain People.

Anglicans

[Figure: Canterbury Cathedral, Archbishop of Canterbury base]

Originated in the 16th century English Reformation when Protestantism broke away from the Catholic Church. It is the main branch of Protestantism. Its mother church is the Church of England with the Archbishop of Canterbury at the head. A worldwide group of churches fall under the Anglican umbrella.

Baptists

[Figure: Font of St John's Baptist Church, Colsterworth, England]

An avenue of Protestantism that insists believers must be baptized by a process of total immersion in water. Just a little sprinkling does not do the job for Baptists. But some Baptists, known as Reformed Baptists do believe that babies can be baptized. Some Baptists trace their origin to John the Baptist - forerunner of Jesus Christ. The Baptist sect could be seen as a 17th century offshoot of Congregationalism. Early Baptists were one of two groups; Particular Baptists and General Baptists. The former believed in the doctrine of particular atonement and the latter were a bit freer. The Generalists thought Christ had died for all.

Calvinists

[Figure: John Calvin, 1509 to 1564 CE]

John Calvin, kicked off this version of Protestantism. He was a Frenchman who died in 1564 and was counted as one of the leading Protestant reformers of his day, although he has a rival here - Martin Luther. His work the "Institutes" set out his beliefs, founded on a rather adaptive interpretation of the Bible in a humanistic way. Appeal to the heart rather than bludgeon people with too much reasoning, rites and rituals was his view. He said salvation was only possible through God's grace, not via good works. He believed in original sin and in predestination, so, for Calvin, God had already decided, probably some billions of years ago, who was to be saved. Living a moral life only shows that a person just might one of the lucky ones, but God had already made his decision before you were born, so, tough, you just have to hope for the best. There's no way that God's divine decision making can be influenced.

Christian Fundamentalists

[Figure: Charles Hodge, Princeton (1797 to 1878)]

This developed in the USA late on during the 19th century. Charles Hodge, a Princeton USA theologian, helped establish Fundamentalists ideas. The movement was a reaction against the revised Christian theology, known as modernism, following on from Darwin's theory of evolution. The latter put a very big hole in the ship of Genesis. Subsequently, the ship was hardly able to get out of the dock. The Fundamentalists thought Darwin fundamentally wrong, ergo the Biblical ship was completely unscathed. They believe in the historical accuracy of the Bible, including Genesis, with the 7-day timescale for all creation. They also think the 'second coming' is imminent. It is not clear exactly how long is imminent, given early Fundamentalists first thought the coming was imminent over one hundred years ago. Of course, something can forever be imminent. Many Fundamentalists do not smoke, drink, dance, go to the cinema or theatre. They do engage in congregational singing though. Do they watch TV and what about mobile phones, iPads, laptops etc? None of these are mentioned in the Bible.

Christadelphians

[Figure: Christadelphian Hall, Llandudno, Wales]

This word comes from Greek meaning 'brother of Christ'. It kicked off in the USA during the mid 19th century thanks to John Thomas. Some early Christadelphians used their beliefs as an argument against military service during the time of the American civil war. Just like Jehovah's Witnesses the C's do not believe that man has an immortal soul. There are thought to be about 50,000 Christadelphians in 120 countries.

Christian Scientist

[Figure: Title page of the first edition of Science and Health, 1875, by Mary Baker Glover (later Eddy)]

'Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures', a book by Mary Baker Eddy in 1875 set this one going. It was a reaction to Darwin and evolution. She said that Christian Science was: "...the law of god, the law of good." She and her followers founded the Church of Christian Scientist. Its principle intent was to re-start the "primitive Christianity and its lost element of healing." Mary argued that sickness was just an illusion. It could be sorted out by prayer. For Christian Scientist all is in the mind. CS considers Jesus to be divine (i.e. has Godly attributes) but not a deity. There are about 400,000 CS worldwide.

Church of Christ Scientist

Another name for Christian Scientist.

Church of the Latter-Day Saints (Mormons)

[Figure: Salt Lake Temple, Salt Lake City, Utah]

Mormon is the common name associated with this sect, but this title embraces some slightly different, although far smaller denominations, up to 12. The 'Community of Christ', with 250,000 members, and the 'Apostolic United Brethren', who have around 10,000 followers, are two of these smaller Mormon denominations. The 'pure' church's real name is "Church of the Latter-Day Saints", or the LDS Church. The churches are in fact mostly temples.

Apparently in 1819 the angel called 'Moroni' paid a visit to a 14-year-old American, Joseph Smith. Moroni told Joseph of ancient writings setting out God's work for Americans. The angel visited Joe three times and told him to get on with it. Purportedly, the angel turned up brandishing a sword on his last visit and threatened to kill the cowering Joseph if he did not follow instructions. This, understandably, spurred Joe into action. He found those Godly records, interpreted them, then wrote them up into the 'Book of Mormon'. Apart from his book, Joe was also well known for his lust for the opposite sex, sometimes quite young girls. This might explain why he believed in polygamy, although this was apparently on orders from God. He knew a lot of women very well, and ended up with 40 wives. The youngest, Helen Kimball, was 14. Early on in his marriage to Emma, he seduced Fanny, his wife's 16-year-old housemaid. Other men's wives were not safe from his attention. This sexual selfishness caused him to have to deal with a court case against him. William Law, on 23 March 1844, filed a suit against Smith for committing adultery with Smith's foster daughter. Writing in the Salt Lake Tribune newspaper in 2014, Mormon psychologist, Kirsty Money said: "Joseph may have erred in his practice of polygamy". The 'may have' suggests the possibility that he may not have erred. Poor Joe Smith upset a number of more traditional Christians and probably quite a few husbands and fathers. As a result, while in prison, he was attacked by a mob and killed in 1844. This murderous action was a copy of the Christian mob treatment handed out to that astonishing woman, Hypatia. She was mob tortured and murdered in Alexandria, some 1,500 years before Joe's demise. The comparison with Joe is very unfair on Hypatia. In nearly all respects she was head and shoulders above Joe Smith.

After Joe, Brigham Young, from 1847, was the LDS Church President and governor of the territory, later state, of Utah, USA. Brigham gave the LDS a great boost, especially in Salt Lake City. He was also, like Joe Smith, strongly supportive of the state of marriage, having 55 wives. Brigham was really very busy: founding Salt Lake City; working away as state governor; and presiding over the whole Mormon community. Even so, he must have been able to spend some time with his many wives - they bore him 59 children. The poor chap, fancy having to remember the names of those 55 wives and 59 children, exhausting work for his brain. "Latter-day" - those earlier saints missed the cut. Mormons believe in total immersion baptism and in confirmation. There are about 16 million Mormons today.

Church of United Brethren in Christ

[Figure: Church of United Brethren symbol]

This evangelical church started up in Indiana, USA in the 18th century. It has historic links to Mennonites and Methodists. After splits between liberals and conservatives it first merged with the Evangelical Church then the Methodists to become the United Methodists Church.

Congregationalists

[Figure: John Wycliffe reading his translation of the Bible to John of Gaunt, by Ford Madox Brown, 1847-48]

This one is of English origin and oldish, having started off in the late 16th century with founder, Robert Browne. They opposed both the Catholic church and the structured Protestantism of the Church of England. They took up and developed up the reforming ideas centuries old, i.e. those of of the Lollards, John Wycliffe, a philosopher/preacher, and later Martin Luther. As opposers Congregationalists were, along with other groups, called Puritans at first. Governance is a key difference in Congregationalism. Each church is required to look after its own affairs, independently of any other higher, human command. The authoritative governing structure of the Church of England and Roman Catholics is an anathema to them. Sometimes they are called Independents, especially in Wales. Congregationalists were a bit more prominent in Victorian times. In 1972 some Congregationalists' merged with Presbyterians. However at least three groups remained in the Congregational fold: the Evangelical Fellowship, the Federation of Congregational Churches and the Fellowship of Independent Evangelical Churches.

headings.text: Church of United Brethren in Christ

pages.text:
Coptic Catholic Church

[Figure: A Coptic pendant cross, 6th to 7th century]

These are a location orientated Catholic sect, mainly in Egypt (over 8 million) and Sudan (500,000). The word Coptic comes from the Greek for Egyptian. The Coptic church closely associated with the smaller Eritrean and Ethiopian Catholic Churches. All use a liturgy called the Alexandrian Rites. Coptic language is spoken in this Rite by, you've guessed it, the Copts of Egypt and Sudan. The other two speak Ge'ez in their liturgical services. The Coptic church HQ is St Mark's Cathedral, Cairo, Egypt. A place that recognizes the claimed Coptic founder as St Mark.

Eastern Orthodox (excluding Russian and Greek Orthodox)

[Figure: Eastern Orthodox Church Cross]

This is a biggy. It's estimated there are more than 200 million members. Sometimes churches under this general umbrella is referred to as 'Orthodox Church'. This term includes: Church of Constantinople; Church of Antioch; Church of Russia and Church of Poland and Church of Greece among others. The BBC describe the Orthodox Church in this way: "It is made up of a number of self-governing Churches which are either 'autocephalous' (meaning having their own head) or 'autonomous' (meaning self-governing). The Orthodox Churches are united in faith and by a common approach to theology, tradition, and worship. They draw on elements of Greek, Middle-Eastern, Russian and Slav culture." The big chief is the Patriarch of Constantinople. Eastern and Western Christians began to split up following the seventh Ecumenical Council of 787CE. They very finally and resentfully divorced after the Fourth Crusade in 1204. During this time Constantinople was sacked by the Crusaders. Eastern churches keep to the language of the local community while Western, Catholic, churches use Latin. One distinct difference with most other Christian religions is the Orthodox cross. This has three cross bars. The bottom one is slanted and is commonly said to be a foot rest for Christ. The shorter, top bar is for Pontius Pilate's inscription in Latin, Greek and Hebrew saying "Jesus the Nazorean, King of the Jews." This is usually shortened to 'INRI'.

Episcopalians (Episcopal Church, United States)

[Figure: Episcopal Church coat of arms]

headings.text: Eastern Orthodox (excluding Russian and Greek Orthodox)

pages.text:
Like several other sects this one is based mainly in the USA where it started up in 1785. It became separate from the Church of England after the American Revolution. Its beliefs and practices are extremely close to main stream Church of England - Anglicanism. It's an American branch in a way. The Episcopal church can occasionally describe itself as Protestant yet Catholic, so attempting to keep a foot in both major camps. One difference is that it ordains both women and gay people. There are over 1.5 million Episcopalians, nearly all are in America.

Ethiopian Tewahedo Church Orthodox

[Figure: Ethiopian processional cross, 15th century]

In its title the word 'Tewahedo' means made one' in the language of this church, Ge'ez. It's a reference to the unity of Jesus who combines both human and Godly characteristics. The first Ethiopian church member was, apparently, a eunuch. The Ethiopian Orthodox church is closely associated with the Coptic church and its Alexandrian liturgical rites.

Evangelicals

[Figure: Leith Anderson, President of the National Association of Evangelicals, 2006 to 2019]

This is a broad title which embraces many Protestants denominations including Methodist, Baptist, Mennonite and Pentecostal. The Protestant origin goes back to at least the early 1700's. Luther, Calvin and Zwingli were influencers. Others, hundreds of years before these, also were heeded, such as John Wycliffe (Oxford University philosopher/theologian of around 1360) and Peter Waldo (French religious leader of about 1170, a believer in simplicity in religious observance and poverty in life style). Their core beliefs are founded on three Latinised, Biblical concepts: Sola Scriptura, by scripture alone - meaning pay sole heed to the Bible, both old and new testaments. The Bible tells all that's needed; Sola Gratia, by grace alone is the way to get salvation, emphasizing that God is in charge; finally, Sola Fide by faith alone, being saved by grace through faith. Does this mean that these latter two 'alones' make a couple, hence neither are alone! And in fact together with the former alone they make a trinity.

Friends of Man

[Figure: Frederic-Louis' tomb near Geneva. Is the imploring lady asking to be one of the 144,000 lucky ones?]

Quite a recent one this, starting off in 1919 by the writings and preachings of the long titled Frederic Louis-Alexandre Freytag. Friends are found mostly in Switzerland and France. They have a precise figure in mind about the number of people allowed in heaven - 144,000. This is OK though, because with only 71,000 members all these have a good chance of making it. The Friends don't believe in a Godly trinity. It's all one for them. They are apparently strong on the Bible. Members are vegetarians, so maybe not be quite so overly strong on the Bible which refers to meat eaters. Two unusual feasts are celebrated by the Friends, that of the Army of the Lord on 18th April and about 6 months later there's the feast of the Little Flock.

Greek Orthodox

[Figure: The iconostasis screen]

A biggish church with about 25 million members, half of whom are in Greece. Greek Orthodox is a part of the family of Eastern Orthodox churches. The founder is thought to be the Apostle Andrew. It grew out of the Eastern Roman Empire - Byzantium. The old capital, Constantinople, now Istanbul, remains a special place for Orthodox Christians. The main differences with Protestantism and Catholicism is in the way they worship, language used and, in the belief that the Holy Spirit is involved in everything. They also reject the supremacy of the Pope and don't accept the Pope's decisions on religious issues are infallible. The nave and altar in GO churches are separated by an iconostasis. This is a wall of religious paintings of Jesus and saints. Traditionally, only men are allowed behind it, in the altar section.

Hutterites

[Figure: Jacob Hutter, 1500 to 1536]

Hutterites are sometimes called 'Hutterian Brethren'. They are associated with Anabaptists and Mennonites. Like them they are firm believers in the literal truth of the Bible. Hutterites came about during the 16th century Reformation when founded by German Jacob Hutter. They believe in communal living and the 45,000 members of today are based mostly in North America and Western Canada.

Jehovah's Witnesses

[Figure: JW HQ, Warwick, New York]

This is another Christian sect from the USA. It originated in Pittsburgh during the 1870's, as the Bible Student Movement. They only adopted the name 'Jehovah's Witnesses" in 1931. A group of elders in New York oversees the movement and its doctrines. They have a fairly unique view of the soul - that it does not exist. This goes completely against orthodox Christian beliefs. There is a mistranslation of the old Hebrew and Greek word as soul when, according to JWs it means 'life'. After Armageddon, just those good and faithful JWs will make it to everlasting life, as immortal 'spirit beings' but apparently there is a limit of 144,000. The Bible, Revelation 7 and 14 are the source of this figure, which is disputed by most other Christian denominations. Jehovah's Witnesses are famous as Biblical door-to-door salesmen, also for refusing medical treatment involving blood. They claim: "Both the Old and New Testaments clearly command us to abstain from blood." and, "God views blood as representing life. So, we avoid taking blood not only in obedience to God, but also out of respect for him as the giver of life." Of course, medically, when an operation is required, blood is going to be involved. The person needing the operation may die without it. This has caused a few headaches when parents try and insist their child does not have the recommended operation. They are very strong on promoting and explaining the Bible, requiring members to go out and tell others about it. Their meetings take place in a "Kingdom Hall". One of their claims is: "When bad angels married women on Earth they had sons who were giant bullies. Violence was everywhere. But Noah was different. He loved and obeyed God." JW think secular societies are morally corrupt and under Satan's influence. They've made various predictions of: Christ's Second Coming; the advent of God's Kingdom and Armageddon. So far none of these have happened, although with Climate Change looming ever larger, the latter might come about. JWs are anti the idea of the Trinity and don't observe Christmas or Easter, thinking these to be pagan festivals. There are about 8 million evangelic JW followers and maybe 12 million more non-evangelicals.

Lutherans

[Figure: Martin Luther (1483 to 1546)]

[Figure: ML nails his 95 Theses to the door of Wittenberg's Castle Church]

Martin Luther cranked this one into life in 16th century Germany. There are estimated to be more than 74 million adherents. See a fuller description below under the heading: During the Reformation Martin Luther, ditched Catholicism'

Mennonites

This is a broad-brush alternate title. The Mennonites refer to those Christian groups called Anabaptists. Its name comes from Menno Simons (1496 to 1561) who preached and wrote in Holland and elsewhere. Mennonite beliefs were enshrined in the Dordrecht Confession of Faith in 1632. Mennonites are great believers in pacifism.

Methodists

[Figure: John Wesley, founder of Methodism, preaching in Ireland, 1789 (attributed to Maria Spilsbury). Methodists believe Jesus Christ died for everyone, not just a few. This is the doctrine of unlimited atonement.]

So called because of the methodical way in which they practiced their Christian faith. We have John Wesley (1703 to 1791) to thank, mainly, for launching Methodism. His brother Charles helped as did George Whitfield. The church is one of the big ones, having 70 million members worldwide. In Great Britain it has 6,000 churches with 25,000 members. John Wesley said he had a spiritual experience: "I felt my heart strangely warmed. I felt I did trust in Christ, Christ alone, for salvation; and an assurance was given me that he had taken away my sins." The experience encouraged John to preach. He proved to be a most skillful operator. Methodists are known as non-conformists, well they are to some in the know. This means they do not recognize the authority of the Church of England or keep to its rules. Interestingly though, John Wesley himself thought it should remain within the Anglican Church saying: "I live and die a member of the Church of England." There have been a few past schisms resulting in minor branches such as: Primitive Methodists; Wesleyan Methodists and United Methodists Church. Today these have mostly joined up into the present-day church which is world-wide with a claimed 80 million followers in 1956.

Moravian Church

[Figure: Count von Zinzendorf, 1700 to 1760 CE]

Jan Hus (1372 to 1415), a Czech, started up the Hussite movement which later became the Moravian Church (Moravia was formerly a region in the Czech republic). For his troubles The Catholic Church burned him at the stake for heresy in 1415. Bohemia and Moravia both had majority Hussite followers until wars resulted in the Hapsburg empire in the 1620's forcing people to return to Catholicism. In 1727 refugees from Moravia, seeking to avoid persecution, landed up in land provided by Count Nickolaus von Zinzendorf in Saxony, Germany. They called their new base Herrhut, meaning 'under the watch of the Lord'. This is now the main base of the Moravian Church, but there are churches in other countries, including Britain. The church is also called 'Unitas Fratrum' - Unity of Brethren. The church says, as one of its beliefs: "In the light of divine grace, we recognise ourselves to be a Church of sinners. We require forgiveness daily, and live only through the mercy of God in Christ Jesus our Lord."

Mormons

See Church of the Latter-Day Saints no. 12 above.

Pentecostals

[Figure: Pentecost: the Holy Spirit descends on the apostles (engraving, 1575)]

Another from the USA. This started up in the early 1900's. It emerged from beliefs that the second coming of Christ was imminent. The word, Pentecostalism, comes from the Greek Pentecost meaning the Jewish Feast of Weeks. But it also refers to the Biblical Book of Acts, where Christians received gifts from the Holy Spirit. Pentecostals are very strong on the literal truth of the Bible and they think Baptism is an essential link to God. The early proponents were William J. Seymour and Charles Parham. There is no authoritative structure of this church branch and Pentecostals are split, some believe in the Trinity other do not. A number of slightly different sects fall, loosely, under the Pentecostal umbrella, including the Nigerian founded Redeemed Christian Church of God. There are estimated to be more than 200 million of one sort or another Pentecostalists.

Presbyterians

[Figure: John Knox (1510 - 1572)]

Scotland is to the fore with this Christian sect, although it has since spread to other countries. It was started up in Scotland by John Knox in the 16th century. He had an eventful life, being a galley slave for a while and engaging in several arguments with the Catholic, Mary, Queen of Scots. She asked him by what right did he rebuke her so openly. John responded: "...I am a worm of the earth, and yet a subject.... But I am a watchman, both over the realm and the Kirk (church) of God." The name Presbyterian comes from its form of church government. Here a group of elders do the general governing. "Presbyter" means elder. There are no Bishops or tiered hierarchy. The Bible, again, is the most important in their church because it was given by God, say Presbyterians. They believe God has control over all and has already picked out some people to follow Jesus Christ but not others. Who are the fortunate chosen?

Puritans

[Figure: Old Ship Church, Hingham, Massachusetts, USA]

The name tells all. These were reformed protestants who, in the 16th and 17th centuries, considered that both the Church of England and Roman Catholic church needed purifying. The reforms that began under Elizabeth 1st were well short of the mark for Puritans. They disliked the church structure with its Bishops and wanted a more localized authority. Their followers believed in a purely Biblical led approach to their entire way of life. Puritans were closely akin to Presbyterians, Congregationalists and Calvinists. A big sideways impact was the huge colonisation movement. By 1631 21,000 had emigrated to New England, USA. Puritans were a major political party in the English Civil War (1642 to 1651). Oliver Cromwell was a Puritan and during this time became Head of State after King Charles 1st was executed.

Russian Orthodox

This is estimated to be more than 200 million of one sort or another Pentecostalists.

Salvation Army

[Figure: William Booth (1829 to 1912), founder of the Salvation Army]

This is an army promoting Christ and his teachings through the Bible. It is a derivative of Methodism and founded in 1865 by William Booth. They say: "At the Salvation Army, we are dedicated to doing the most good.", and "The Salvation Army, an international movement, is an evangelical part of the universal Christian Church. Its message is based on the Bible. Its ministry is motivated by the love of God. Its mission is to preach the gospel of Jesus Christ and to meet human needs in His name without discrimination." The Salvation Army is unique in having what it calls, officers, soldiers as well as adherents. There are 1.5 million of these in 131 countries. It is very much hands-on giving solid, practical help in areas such as running shelters for the homeless, helping the unemployed, fighting human trafficking, disaster relief and other good deeds. They are more heavily into action than words.

Scripture Union

[Figure: A lamp unto my feet: Roman oil lamp (Psalm 119:105)]

This world-wide movement main aim is to get the young particularly but also adults to know more of God through the Bible. Joseph Spiers kicked off in 1867 in London. He spoke to 15 children in an Islington house. This led to the Children's Special Service Mission (CSSM) which later on became the Scripture Union.

Swedenborgian

[Figure: Emmanuel Swedenborg (1688 to 1772 CE)]

This one came about in 1787 when a Swedish Lutheran leaning theologian, Emmanuel Swedenborg, claimed a divine revelation. Emmanuel claimed that God had explained the Bible in such a way to show that the second coming of Jesus Christ was definitely on the cards. He also had seen the Last Judgement. So, Emmanuel set up this, his New Church. It's also got other titles: Swedenborgian, Church of New Jerusalem and The Lord's Church, among others. The various churches have between them less than 10,000 members.

Quakers

Really quite unusual this one because it espouses no particular creed. Unitarianism is a kind of 'one size fits all' approach to religion. While its roots are Christian with a bit of Jewish it welcomes all varieties of believers. People are accepted to their get-togethers who might be Muslim, Jewish, Buddhist or even atheist. Unitarians promote inclusivity, that means supporting freedom of speech, equality of race, gender and belief. People should also hold the natural world in deep respect, for Unitarians. On top of all these basics, people then apply reason to get to wherever they are going. In the process, when pondering new information and fresh ideas, people should be prepared to change their minds and switch the direction of their personal journeys. After the first Unitarian church opened up in 1774 there are now reckoned to be 170 congregations in the UK. Quite a few famous people have been Unitarians: novelists Charles Dickens, Elizabeth Gaskell and Kurt Vonnegut; poet and actress Sarah Adams; 3rd President of the United States, Thomas Jefferson; aircraft pioneer, Frank Lloyd-Wright; film star Paul Newman and inventor of the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee.

United Christian Church

[Figure: Photo of a United Christian Church, church building]

This one cranked up, as UCC, in 1878. It is another American Protestant offshoot, from Pennsylvania. The UCC broke away from the Church of the United Brethren in Christ because members rejected the doctrine of 'total depravity'. The latter meant humans were endowed with original sin and were unable to influence God's decision about where they ended up, no matter how hard they might pray. Originally the flock were steered by the Rev. George W. Hoffman. For some years in the early days of UCC, they were known as Hoffmanites. Important rituals are Baptism, the Lord's supper and feet washing. Any type of baptism is OK with UCC. They believe in the Trinity. There are reckoned to be about 770 members in Pennsylvania. There are also some in Cambridge, England.

United Reformed Church

[Figure: United Reformed Church, symbol of a cross and fish]

This is the one that came to life after a merger of Presbyterian and 75% of Congregational churches in 1972. The formal merger took place after a historic House of Commons Bill passed in that year. Another merger was with the long titled Re-formed Association of Churches of Christ in 1981. In yet a further, bigger, attempt at integration in 1982 the URC proposed a covenant with the Church of England, Methodists and Moravian church. The Church of England turned them down. The reforming nature of this church resulted in the URC allowing the conduct of same-sex marriages in 2016. The URC is reckoned to have a membership of about 56,000 in 1,400 congregations, but it has been in serious decline, losing 21% of members between 2013 and 2018.

Unity Church

[Figure: Unity Village, Missouri, headquarters of Unity]

This is a spiritual movement, formerly the Unity Church, which began in the late 1800's. Myrtle Fillmore and her husband claimed they cured her tuberculosis. Her husband, Charles did something similar to heal his injured leg. This happened Kansas City, USA. Their farm is now Unity Village and HQ of Unity. The original philosophy is Transcendentalism, now known as 'New Thought', basically saying human thoughts have creative power. Unity believes all people are inherently good. It gets its message across in a lot of spiritual literature.

7th Day Adventists

[Figure: Ellen G. White (1827 to 1915), a founder of the Seventh-day Adventist Church]

What's unusual about the 7th Dayers is the 7th day. This they count as Saturday which they treat as the Sabbath, the day of observance. Saturday is the 7th day in both Christian and Jewish calendars. Added to this is their emphasis on the second coming of Jesus Christ, hence we have their name, 7th Day Adventists. It was properly set up in 1863 inspired by its main founder, Ellen White, but it follows on from the USA Millerite Movement of the 1840's. It has a hierarchical structure with the General Conference at the top followed by divisions, union conferences and local conferences. It has 7,500 schools in 215 countries and about 20 million members. 7th Day Adventists lays great emphasis on mental, physical, social and spiritual health, and it actively promotes religious freedom.

As we've already seen, the largest Christian groupings are Catholics, Protestants and the Orthodox churches. The many denominations above are small variants on basic Protestantism although, as explained Mormons, Unitarians and Jehovah's Witnesses each have a slightly larger difference. They do not believe in the Trinity - i.e. God the Father, God the Son and God the Holy Ghost. There's only one God for them.

But for Christianity clearly the main event was Jesus, born 00 CE. He was a human who was also a God. Jesus, died and rose again. The promise of eternal life is essential to Christian theology. Jesus showed the way.

St Paul, originally Saul, was important as the alleged first historical witness, John the Baptist aside, although St Paul did not meet Jesus in the latter's lifetime. Saul claimed to have an encounter with the risen Christ and was then converted. He wrote lots of stuff. This comes before the gospels were written. An important idea promoted by Paul was that Jesus had risen from the dead. Christianity is based a lot on Paul's writings. This, the earliest author of the New Testament did not know he was writing part 2 of the Bible. Saul, after his conversion designated him St Paul, was that NT author. He scribbled away around 55 CE.

Saul was born a Roman Jew, in Tarsus, modern Turkey. He had a miraculous insight on the way to Damascus and immediately converted to a Trinitarian version of Godly belief. This differed widely from the pagan polytheism of Rome and was at a slant to the singular monotheism of Judaism. After seeing the light on his Damascene journey newly minted Paul became a serial letter writer, passing on his revealed understanding to all and sundry. His letters, more famously known as Epistles, were dispatched to various mysterious 'ians' and other peoples: Corinthians; Galatians; Ephesians; Philippians; Colossians and Thessalonians, among others. These 'ians' were appropriate recipients of Paul's messages. The name Ian is Scottish, meaning "Gift from God".

The Pauline Epistles set out the earliest groundwork of Christian theology. They offered some differentiation from the religion of Judaism. It was Paul what done it. He brought Jesus to the fore, believing and promoting the resurrection of Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 15). Through his preaching and Epistles, he got Christianity well and truly on the road. Sadly though, the New Testament Bible does not list all the replies Paul got to his letters. Some must have been challenging and perhaps even rude. But the evidence of continuance shows Paul was not put off. He soldiered on, using gallons of ink to get his message across.

Christian Beliefs

It is difficult to be precise about all Christian beliefs because there are so many varieties of Christianity; each is a bit different to the others. These various Christian sects generally take a slightly different view on often a minor belief area, or on what rituals should be conducted. However, there are core beliefs that nearly all Christian sects accept. For Christians:

Jesus is both man and God, this is unlike the other two Abrahamics, Judaism and Islam, who think Jesus was just a prophet;
Jesus was the son of God, sent to save mankind from sin;
Jesus rose from the dead and ascended into heaven;
There is life after death, either in a heaven if you've been good, or in hell if you've been bad;
The Bible is God's holy work.

They also believe that there is only one God, but within a holy Trinity of God the Father, God the Son and the Holy Ghost. Three Christian sects do not acknowledge the Godly Trinity: Jehovah's Witnesses, Unitarians and Mormons.

Christianity is seen as synonymous with the Father, God the Son and the Holy Ghost. Three Christian sects do not acknowledge the Godly Trinity: Jehovah's Witnesses, Unitarians and Mormons.

Some Commonality

One thing common to Abrahamic religions, not just Christians sects, is that dastardly Prince of Evil satan, also known as the Devil, Beelzebub, the fallen angel and in Islam Shaitan. What's not clear is that although Satan is top of the tree when it comes to evil entities he is still only given the accolade of "the Prince of Evil", that title suggests there may be someone even higher up the scale of wickedness, a King or Queen of Evil, or even an Emperor of Evil. Satan is reckoned to have fallen out of favour with God before humans were on the scene (Ezekiel 28:14-18 and Isaiah 14:12-17). This must have been a really difficult period for him because he did not have anyone to tempt. Since his fall, Satan and God have been at loggerheads. Why these two don't just sit down and thrash things out is not explained in the Bible. Many unbelievers will also think that a supremely powerful God need not accommodate Satan in any way. He could insist on Satan becoming a good angel or shove him in a fiery pit. Also common among most Christians is the Eucharist, also known as Holy Communion, the Divine Liturgy and Lord's Supper. It's a ceremony reenacting Jesus' last supper and involves, often, the consumption of bread and wine.

Back to Uncommonality

Anglicanism is seen as synonymous with Protestantism, although it also has some mild Catholic leanings. This is not surprising since it is based on the Church on England, which split from the Catholic Pope because of Henry VIII's marriage wishes. The exact distinctions between out and out Protestants and Anglicans are indistinct. It is a subject of debate. However, Protestants are more protestant than Anglicans. Both stem from the time of reformation and Martin Luther. Anglicans have a secular head of church, the English monarch, courtesy of Henry VIII. Therefore English, Welsh, Scottish and Irish Protestants are Anglicans as are many others around the world, usually in countries of the old British Empire. The Archbishop of Canterbury is seen technically as "the first among equals". He chairs meetings of the greats in Anglicanism at the ten-yearly Lambeth Conference.

Differences Between Catholics and Protestants

Baptism
Confirmation - a strengthening of faith
Holy Communion or Eucharist - where Catholics receive a wafer at mass, representing a spiritual link with Jesus Christ
Reconciliation or penance - where Catholics go to a priest, in the Confessional Box, and confess their sins. They then receive a penance, usually requiring a number of prayers to be said, and absolution
Anointing of the sick - done by a priest, using holy water
Holy Orders - by which a bishop ordains a priest
Holy Matrimony - marriage of a man and woman within the Roman Catholic faith

These are set out in written form in the "Catechism'. This list of Catholic sacraments is not the same for Protestants. They only have two: Baptism and Holy Orders. Curiously, despite matrimony is not counted as a Protestant sacrament, Anglican Vicars will commonly wed people.

Riches of Catholicism

When it comes to relative wealth the Catholic church easily trumps Protestantism and probably every other religion. There's the splendor that is the Vatican, with its buildings, the gold, silver and art treasures, the unique Pope mobile, and not forgetting those specially tailored vestments worn by its chiefs - the Pope and the Cardinals, other clergy, staff and guards. They dine pretty well too. All this demonstrable wealth is worthy of any major historical monarch or Emperor. What would that humble carpenter's son, Jesus, make of it? Has he given special dispensation to Vatican camels, so they can squeeze through the eye of a needle? The Vatican also tops every other religion in terms of the governmental status endowed on its location in Rome. It is the only church HQ that benefits from being a city-state.

During the Reformation Martin Luther Ditched Catholicism

During the Reformation Martin Luther ditched Catholicism, because of its adulteration, as he saw it, of the Bible's purity through addition of sacraments, traditions and Papal edicts. He Protested (hence supporters were Protestants) and identified just a small cadre of essentials for his idea of religion. Martin came up with snappy Latin slogans to emphasise his simplistic, evangelical, teaching:

Sola Scriptura - the sole supremacy of the Bible as God's authoritative teaching;
Sola Fide - salvation is through faith;
Sola Gratia - God's benevolent favor, generosity and forgiveness of sin;
Solus Christus - claiming that Christ is the only mediator between God and man. That shuts out those Catholic intercessors; the saints and the blessed Virgin Mary;
Soli Deo Gloria - simply glory is to God alone.

These five were included in Martin's 95 Theses. He dramatically nailed these to the door of Wittenberg Cathedral in 1517, with all this he founded the Protestant variety known as Lutheranism and kicked off the Reformation.

In the 1600's King Henry VIII saw some merit in the embryonic, European Protestantism. He decided that England should switch from rigid Catholicism and the supremacy of the Pope.

Of course, his decision was made on a very pragmatic, wholly self-interested, basis. He did not want the Pope to interfere with his marital affairs. If Henry wanted to ditch a current wife and get a new one, that should be up to Henry not the Pope, so the King thought. Henry made himself Head of the Church of England thus giving himself both the secular and spiritual power to do whatever he liked. This was the start of a process which eventually shifted the official religion away from Catholicism to Protestantism. Thomas Cranmer and a bevy of other religious reformers, played a big part in furthering the cause of Protestantism, as did Edward VI. Bloody Mary, in her short reign of 1553 to 1558, tried hard to return England to Catholicism, through 274 religious executions.

Her successor, Elizabeth 1st, known as Good Queen Bess, although a Protestant with Catholic trimmings, encouraged religious tolerance, at least partly. Her devout Catholic cousin, Mary Queen of Scots, would not have referred to her as Good Queen Bess. They had a humdinger of an argument over which was the true Godly religion. Mary became so irate she lost her head over the issue.

[Figure: Catherine of Aragon]

It might be argued that many English people who are currently Protestants are so because of Henry's marriage wishes. Maybe though Catherine of Aragon should get the blame, or is it the honour. She started off the whole process by failing to give Henry a male heir and, with her increasing age, losing out in the beauty stakes to the younger Anne Boleyn. Luckily for her she was popular with the common man. This may have helped her keep her head on her shoulders. Catherine was put aside for Anne, who did not last long. She eventually headed off to pastures new when Henry sought to see more of yet another woman, Jane.

Where Catherine and Anne had failed Jane Seymour succeeded, giving birth to eventual King Edward VI, but she died in the process. It was her son, Edward, who really put a firm, decisive Protestant boot into English Catholicism.

[Figure: A young Edward VI, Reign 1547 to 1553, By William Scrots]

Poor Edward, he became King at just aged 9 years old, and died at age 15. He would have been subjected to heavy influence from his advisors. Perhaps it's his advisors who should be noted as chief booters. But times have changed. Nowadays the Church leaders seem to get on quite well despite various differences, including that of their Church's structure.

Clergy Rank Order

The Catholic church has a very distinct hierarchy. First there's the Pope. Following on from him we have Cardinals, Bishops, Monseigneurs, Priests and Deacons. These clerics are in Division one.

The first Division are ordained and deliver sacraments, all are men. In Division two there is a supporting group of nuns, monks, friars and brothers. These mostly do good deeds or live quietly and pray a lot, or are supposed to. Within the lesser ranks there's some variations in titles. Nuns can become Mother Superior or Reverend Mother and eventually Abbesses - later in charge of nuns. Helping administer Cathedrals are secular Canons. These last are the only ones allowed not to be celibate, which seems likely to have caused problems.

[Figure: Pope: "Sorry to hear you've had so much rain recently in Canterbury Archbishop. If it helps I Noah man who has an Ark."]

How a New Pope is Appointed

The top man gets to be installed through a ritualised process. A fresh Pope excitement arrives in a cloud of white smoke. That's the signal the College of Cardinals have finalised their vote for a new Pope. They go through this voting process once the old Pope has departed, usually to a location interview with his God.

[Figure: Cardinals in conclave in the Sistine Chapel, 1903 (Achille Beltrame)]

The College meet in secret in Rome's Sistine Chapel. A Cardinal is promoted to Popehood once someone has received a majority vote, normally having to get two-thirds of the votes. The ballot papers are then burnt with an added substance to produce white smoke. The smoke signals to the world that there is a new Pontiff.

[Figure: The Vatican, Rome, Official residence of the Pope, head of the Catholic Church]

The new guy, it's never a woman - heaven forfend - has to take on a traditional name, usually John, Paul, Pius or Benedict. You don't get any Pope Harry, Oliver, Charlie or Jack and certainly not Aaron or Muhammed.

Popes are considered to be the infallible successors to the apostle Peter. As such, they can canonize people. This does not mean they shoot them with a large caliber gun. They make them saints, a title in recognition of an especially good and holy person. Popes have been making saints for at least the last 1,000 years. After Popes had for centuries canonized just a handful of people, in the 1860's Pius IX upped the ante and awarded 52 sainthoods. This is nowhere near the record of Pope Francis. He generously gave out 838 sainthoods from 2013 to 2019. His papacy continues so the number is likely to increase.

The main guy for Protestants is the Archbishop of Canterbury. Bishops vote him into power. His standing and authority are not at the same level as the Pope. Second in line of authority is the Archbishop of York. After these two the rank order is: Bishop; Suffragan Bishop; Canon; Vicar; Curate (sometimes known as Rector, Pastor or Minister).

[Figure: Canterbury Cathedral, founded in 597 CE, rebuilt 1077 CE]

The references to "Canon" and "Suffragan Bishop" can be explained thus. A Canon, with capital C, refers to a type of priest within a Cathedral chapter. They might get annoyed occasionally but do not go off with a bang. There's also a general reference to canon law. A Suffragan Bishop is a sort of understudy, sometimes referred to as an assistant bishop.

More on the BIBLE

It's important to look at the Bible in more detail because it is a fundamental sacred text of the Christian faith. It has almost an equal importance in Judaism and to a lesser extent Islam too. We need to understand why this is such an important book and what issues are associated with it.

The 40 authors of various books of the biblical canon known as the Bible wrote in different time periods, in fact over several centuries. The first book was the "Old Testament", this was written at least 500 BCE but probably even earlier than this. Old Testament books start with Genesis the last book is Malachi. Numerous other books were written, including those of the New Testament, which starts at Matthew and completes with Revelation. However, Jews and Christians disagree about which books of the Bible are in the "true" version and which should be on the outside.

The Jews Hebrew Bible is called the Tanakh, counting 24 books. Eastern Orthodox Christians think 51 books are the right number for their Bible. Catholics and Protestants believe that 46 and 39 respectively are the correct books. For Muslims, parts of the Torah are taken as God's revelation and more clearly articulated in the Qur'an.

The New Testament has 27 books and is exclusive to the Christian arm of the three Abrahamic religions. These three agree only in very broad terms on the content and relevance of the Bible.

The various Biblical books were amended from time to time. Disputes took place over what was sacred scripture (i.e. the divine word of God) and what was merely good guidance. A number of texts were debated for centuries as to whether or not their origin was divine. Some of these didn't make the cut for Protestants, but did for Catholics. And there are differences between various Christian and Jewish versions. For example, Judith and Maccabees are in the Catholic and Eastern Orthodox versions of the Old Testament and not in either the Protestant or Jewish versions.

The final composition of what is now known as the Christian Bible, appeared to emerge by the 4th century AD. It was at first thought that the definitive biblical canon was determined at the Council of Nicaea in AD 325 (this was the first ecumenical council of Bishops) but we know now that the Council did not fully complete the job. Athanasius, Bishop of Alexandria in AD 367, made the first list of what were called Biblical canon.

Athanasius was a controversial figure, condemning Arianism, the reigning orthodoxy of his time, as heresy. Arianism denied the Trinity, just as do some modern Christian denominations.

Athanasius was exiled five times by four different Roman Emperors. But he stuck to his guns and prevailed in the end. It was his views that prevailed on what were the correct Biblical texts. All the amendments and disputes over content meant it took nearly four centuries after Jesus for Christians to decide exactly what it was, through his Bible, that God was telling them. 'Exactly' is an exaggeration. There has been never ending disputes over Biblical interpretation.

Jerome wrote a Latin version of the Bible in 382CE, translating from the Jewish Hebrew. More than 1,200 years later, in 1592CE, Jerome's work became the main basis for the Clementine Vulgate; the new, official Catholic Bible. This was superseded by the Nova Vulgata in 1979. In between times there was the Stuttgart Vulgate, which included the Epistle to the Laodiceans. This alleged Pauline letter is missing from earlier Vulgates.

The most famous version of the Bible is probably the King James. This book was an English translation of the Latin Bible and first published in 1611 CE. The KJV consists of 80 books; 39 of the Old Testament, 14 in the Apocrypha and 27 in the New Testament. Altogether there are over 783,000 words.

In 1898 Gideon International was founded with the aim of putting a Bible, usually a KJB, in every hotel bedroom. The scheme has helped the Bible to become the most printed book of all time. In the 21st century about 100 million Bibles are printed each year.

One modern version of the Bible is the 'New International Version, study Bible'. It was first printed in the 1970's and claimed in 2019 to be the world's most popular Bible. One quote from it: "Like all translations of the Bible, made as they are by imperfect man, this one undoubtedly falls short of its goals." This apparently acknowledges the many holes that can be picked in the Bible. God, apparently, gave his message to mankind through the Bible, but did not make it clear enough. A curious situation, with a supremely powerful, all-knowing God. Surely He could get it right first time?

Joining and Leaving Christianity

Any non-Christian can attend Christian churches, engage in its rites without any formal ceremony of introduction to the faith. Sometimes they may be offered the sacrament of baptism and/or confirmation.

Those who are Christians and later give up their faith, that is become apostates, are not, in modern times subject to any sanction.

It's of interest that the King James Bible thinks such people should be killed. The Old Testament, Deuteronomy 17:3-5 says: "Then shalt thou bring forth that man or that woman, which have committed that wicked thing, unto thy gates, even that man or that woman, and shalt stone them with stones, till they die." The New International Version of the Bible clearly does not consider the possibility of atheism. It thinks apostates will believe in one or other God, but not the right one: "...and contrary to my command has worshiped other gods, bowing down to them or to the sun or the moon or the stars in the sky and this has been brought to your attention, then you must investigate it thoroughly. If it is true and it has been proved that this detestable thing has been done in Israel take the man or woman who has done this evil deed to your city gate and stone that person to death." Fortunately, these biblical instructions are not enacted in the 20th and 21st centuries. If they were an awful lot of stones would be needed because many tens of millions have given up the Christian faith and become, mostly, atheist or agnostic. Even more hundreds of millions embrace different faiths to Christianity.

The Numbers Game

A study by the Pew Research Centre in 2015 made predictive changes in the level of beliefs by 2050. The biggest net changes anticipated are:

A drop in Christian believers of 66 million;
An increase in unaffiliated (atheists, agnostics and humanists in the main) of 61 million;
And an increase of 3 million in Muslims.

One big reason for this change is the expected much superior birthrate of Muslim parents. Pew Research says between 2010 and 2015 Muslim births were 31% of all babies born in the world. This far exceeded the Muslim share of world population, which stood at 24%.

What's Been Good and What's Been Bad About Christianity

Christianity, as practiced by its two main arms, Catholicism and Protestantism has had its commendable and not so commendable, in fact appalling, moments over the 2,000 years of its history.

The Good Bits

Comfort for individual Christians: Many believers have gained solace, as set out in Chapter 2: the comfort blanket; safety deposit box; forgiveness and absolution; a listening service; hope, and promise of a blissful afterlife. These do not need to be real or based on truth for people to derive benefit from believing. Large numbers of individual believers have consistently performed good works within their communities.

Both Catholic and Protestant organisations spend large sums on charitable projects. In the USA St Jude Children's Research Hospital receives about 2 billion dollars. This to research a variety of diseases, including cancers. Catholic Relief Services, with about 1 billion dollars, help the poor and needy around the world. The Economist magazine estimated that in 2010 the American Catholic church spent 4.7 billion on charities. However, this was only 2.6% of their estimated total income of 171.6 billion dollars. The USA figure is thought to represent 60% of the Catholic church's estimated global annual income, which would put this at about 290 billion dollars. The Catholic church's charitable work is carried out in other countries, not just the USA, but what this represents as a % of income is unknown.

The Not-So-Good Bits

headings.text: What's Been Good and What's Been Bad About Christianity

pages.text:
Finance: Whether all Catholic income has been fairly spent is clearly not the case. Claims of mismanagement of Catholic finances has resulted in court cases in both the USA and Italy. In August 2013 the Economist magazine told: "Of ALL the organisations that serve America's poor, few do more good work than the Catholic church: its schools and hospitals provide a lifeline for millions. Yet even taking these services into account, the finances of the Catholic church in America are an unholy mess. The sins involved in its book-keeping are not as vivid or grotesque as those on display in the various sexual-abuse cases that have cost the American church more than $3 billion so far, but the financial mismanagement and questionable business practices would have seen widespread resignations at the top of any other public institution."

The Catholic church's finances in Italy also have received severe adverse media reports. In November 2015 the UK's Guardian newspaper's headline was: "Vatican hit by new claims of financial mismanagement and lavish spending", and followed up saying: "Journalists claim to have exposed millions in lost revenues and senior officials pouring church funds into their already-lavish apartments....... two controversial new books describe a Vatican awash with cash that is woefully mismanaged."

Sexual abuse of children and vulnerable adults: Insistence on celibacy of its clergy has caused the Catholic church lots of problems over the centuries. Quite a number of its clergy have found it impossible to keep to this unnatural human condition. Pope Adrian II had a wife and daughter who lived with him. Popes Pius II, Innocent VIII and Clement VII all had illegitimate children. There were various other backsliders but top prize may go to Pope Julius II. He had 3 illegitimate daughters. These were all Popes of many centuries ago. In more recent times Popes have either been more easily able to be celibate, or their office has been more expert at covering up. Towards the bottom end of the priestly hierarchy there's been huge issues involving abuse of children. The history of child abuse in Catholic institutions is a long one. Until relatively recently the general reaction by those Catholics with some authority has been to cover up, or ignore. One story illustrates what may have happened in many Catholic schools and places where Catholic clergy held some authority. In 1974 Brother Ted Dowlan, of the Christian Brothers, was removed from St Patrick's College, Ballarat, Australia after he admitted abusing boys. He then went on to work in four other schools and continued his abuse of children. Cardinal Pell was informed in the early 1970's of Dowlan's abuse at St Patrick's. He was told by two priests and a couple of students. He failed to inform the headmaster or the local Bishop Mulkearns.

At the time Pell was a senior priest who had a responsibility to keep his Bishop informed. Pell said that in hindsight he should have done more. Pell also knew of another abuser, a notorious paedophile priest Gerald Ridsdale. He abused hundreds of children over many years. A Royal Commission found it implausible that Pell did not know what was going on. They said: "We are also satisfied that by 1973 Cardinal Pell was not only conscious of child sexual abuse by clergy but that he also had considered measures of avoiding situations which might provoke gossip about it."

Child abuse in the Anglican Church: The Anglican church is no better when it comes to incidents of child abuse by its clergy. We have knowledge from Australia, because of the Royal Commission detailed investigation. They uncovered that more than 1,100 complaints of child sexual abuse were made against hundreds of Anglican church clergy and laypeople between 1980 and 2015.

In England, because of the number of abuse cases coming to light, the UK government set up an Independent Enquiry into Child Sex Abuse in 2014. 3,300 complaints of abuse had been made by 2016. 20% of these were by clergy. According to the Daily Mail newspaper, in 2020, the Church Of England faces a bill of £200 million to compensate victims of abuse. Whatever the figure might be it seems certain to run to millions of pounds.

The Anglican leader, Archbishop Justin Welby, apologized over both the church's past racism and child sex abuse. About the former he said: "When we look at our own church, we are still deeply institutionally racist. Let's be clear about that." At an enquiry into child sex abuse in 2018 he remarked: "I want to put on record again - I don't know how to express it adequately - how appalled I am and how ashamed I am of the Church for what it did to those who are survivors and are coping with this." The Independent Inquiry into Child Abuse said, in October 2020, that the Church's failure to respond consistently to victims and survivors of abuse often added to their trauma. Prof. Alexis Jay, Chairwoman said: "Over many decades, the Church of England failed to protect children and young people from sexual abusers, instead facilitating a culture where perpetrators could hide and victims faced barriers to disclosure..."

Abuse has not been confined to Australia and England. Since the 1960's child abuse scandals involving dozens of Catholic priests in 28 countries have come to light. This includes more than a thousand cases of reported abuse by Catholic and Protestant clergy in just a few states in the USA.

For years, church leaders seemingly tried to discreetly cover up priestly scandals, or deliberately fail to fully investigate. This may suggest that what is known publicly is just the tip of the iceberg.

In February 2019 Pope Francis admitted to abuse of nuns by Catholic clergy saying: "Pope Benedict had the courage to dissolve a female congregation which was at a certain level, because this slavery of women had entered it-slavery, even to the point of sexual slavery - on the part of clerics or the founder." and then, "It's not that everyone does this, but there have been priests and bishops who have." In response to this on top of mounting allegations, globally, of both child and adult abuse he set up a meeting with cardinals and bishops to look at what action was needed. The conclave was also to consider whether the issue of mismanagement and cover up by senior clergy. In 2017 Pope Francis met Chilean victims who had suffered sexual abuse by Catholic priests and apologized personally to them.

Attacks on and killing of alternate believers: Pope Francis is not the only Pope to apologise for the past misdemeanors of the Catholic church. It is probably Pope John Paul II who holds the record for the number of apologies, although most of his were for past misdemeanors by Catholicism. In 1992 he said sorry for the church's treatment of Galileo. This was the first of more than 100 apologies made by John Paul. These included remorse for Catholicism's attack on other religions and their believers over centuries, back to before the time of the Crusades, and through the Inquisition up to Hitler, the holocaust and Nazism. In the latter period, Pope Pius XII never condemned the Nazis persecution of the Jews. And remained silent when Jews in Rome were rounded up by Nazis. John Paul said: "We forgive and we ask forgiveness. We are asking pardon for the divisions among Christians, for the use of violence that some have committed in the service of truth, and for attitudes of mistrust and hostility assumed towards followers of other religions."
