Chapter 18

Problems with the Bible

The Bible, what's the hard evidence?

The Bible is so absolutely tied into Christianity it's important to know whether there is evidence of the truth of it, particularly of some of the key, oldest sections. The BBC has broadcast two separate series looking at some aspects. Both have similar names. The first: "The Bible's Buried Secrets", was a 2008 USA production, narrated by Liev Schreiber.

It concluded:

Origins of Israel:

The stories of Adam and Eve, Noah's flood, Abraham and Moses cannot be corroborated by any archaeological findings.
Similarly, nothing's been found to confirm the mass exodus of the Israelites from Egypt. Some archaeologists think that a small group did get away from Egypt; however, these were apparently Canaanite slaves, not Israelites. Israelites might have been Canaanites who migrated to lands Biblical Joshua conquered.

headings.text: The Bible, what's the hard evidence?

pages.text:
In a second BBC series Hebrew Bible expert Dr. Francesca Stavrakopoulou was commissioned to look at some aspects. She made the documentary series aired in 2012: titled, yet again, "The Bible's Buried Secrets". Her focus was on the Kingdom of David, the Garden of Eden and God's Wife. Intriguingly, she spoke of the evidence that in ancient religions there was a Goddess, Asherah, who it is suggested was the consort or wife of the Jewish name for God, Yahweh. The Ugaritic culture considered she was the wife of El, Akkadians said she was wife of their God Anu. The Bible does not mention that God had a wife, but if he had a son?

There are many other issues with or from the Bible, aside from above, and those noted in the previous Chapter. Here are some more:

Written over many centuries, approaching 1,000 years, by many different people (perhaps over 40). Not completed until 4th century CE, at least. The amended Vulgate version of the Bible was not finalised until the fifteen hundreds (CE);

Some books made it into the final Bible, others did not. This was not clear cut, because there are differences between Jewish and Christian versions of the Bible. Even different Christian denominations also dispute the exact composition of the Bible.

Why can't a supremely powerful God ensure his Earthly creatures get the text right and have it written up in one go?

Several creation and flood stories were written before the biblical ones. Highly likely the biblical creation and Noah's ark and other stories are just that, stories, and were "borrowed" from ancient pagan religious tales, particularly that of the Sumerian gods Marduk and Tiamat. There is also possible copying from other, earlier traditions, including Zoroastrianism.

The early Greek philosophers could have inspired the concept of the eternal, unchanging being. Anaximander 520 BCE suggested the Apeiron, an infinite and indefinite universe, then there's Xenophanes. Around 500 BCE he originated monotheism and proposed one supreme God. We have Anaxagoras, about 460 BCE, with his idea of the eternal substances, and Parmenides - everything is part of one unchanging whole. Some or all of these stories were probably known to the early biblical writers.

Other Gods and other beliefs have influenced its writing, especially the Old Testament; The original OT God was Yahweh, or the vowelless YHWH (called a tetragrammaton, the four-letter word for God in the Hebrew bible) Was God El? The Jewish God may have been derived from the Canaanite supreme God El. At the time Jews began to worship YHWH other than El there were other Gods about receiving support, Baal, Molek and even that Goddess, Asherah. It took a while for Yahweh to reach the exclusive, top position. In the "Oxford Companion To World Mythology" David Leeming said: "It seems almost certain that the God of the Jews evolved gradually from the Canaanite El, who was in all likelihood the 'God of Abraham'."

There were differences drawn between the two early Jewish states. Judah (where people had gone into exile and then returned) and Israel, where people had not been exiled. In Judah the one God was called Yahweh whereas in Israel God was known as Elohim.

Eve blamed and Satan gets away with it. The underlying message could be interpreted as women being wicked, and maybe in league with Satan.

Commandment 10: "... You shall not covet thy neighbour's wife, nor his ox or donkey." This implies ownership by the neighbour of these, that includes he owns a wife and there's no equality command such as: "thou shalt not covet thy neighbours husband." This does not support modern views of equality of gender. Some religions, especially Islam, still treat women differently to men.

Judaean centric in nature. The Bible concentrates largely on the Jewish story, what about the rest of mankind? Then there is the very heavy emphasis on men, the many people who have contributed and amended the biblical text were men. Women are conspicuous by their absence. That's half of humanity ignored and it presents a perfect excuse for religious zealots to treat women as second-class citizens.

Jews, "God's chosen people", what have the Jewish race been chosen for? Historically, this seems to be to suffer persecution and vilification for thousands of years. Arguably Jewish people have been more consistently badly treated, over a longer period of time, than any other people on Earth. Perhaps the horrible culmination of this ill treatment was the 6 million Jews who were systematically exterminated in World War II death camps.

In Exodus 14, and Israelites crossing the Red Sea the "Red Sea" should be translated more accurately as the "sea of reeds". This was the site of the famous battle. The Egyptian chariots were likely to be bogged down and useless, if indeed there was any attempted battle. There was no parting of the waves. One of many false bible stories.

If the Bible is God's book why does he allow false stories in his book?

The well known Nativity story is very thinly described in the Bible. Of the four gospels only two mention it, and the little they seem to tell is contradictory. Luke says pregnant Mary and Joseph traveled to Bethlehem on a donkey to register for the Roman census. But in Matthew's version Mary and Joseph did not travel. They were already living in Bethlehem. Scholars think one reason for this divergence is that the stories were actually written about 90 years after the event! If God wanted his Bible to be definitive he surely could arrange that the story of his son's birth was accurately and consistently described.

Miracles make no sense, if you consider how supremely powerful and beneficent God is supposed to be. Why resuscitate only Lazarus, what about the billions of other humans who have died? Why heal just the one leper. How about helping all the sick and ailing who exist today and throughout mankind's 300k history? Why perform a party trick, turning water in to wine, when countless thousands have suffered from lack of water, right up to modern times? Why endlessly regenerate five loafs and fishes to feed a few, what about the rest of starving humanity? Curiously, miracles, if they meant to impress us, seem to be conveniently 2,000 years away from the present time. That is, apart from the odd weeping Irish Madonna and the occasional French peasant woman who has had a odd dream. There is no hard evidence for miracles. If God really wanted us to believe in them, then a Being of his purported power and supreme intellect could easily make this happen.

Biblical commandment "Thou shalt not kill", but then God sanctions lots and lots of "smiting". The Noah story probably takes top prize. In the Old Testament, Genesis 7:23, we are told that, apart from Noah and his Ark, God destroyed every living thing - men; women; children; animals; birds on Earth. Later, Azrael (the Archangel of death) kills all Egyptian first born. In Sodom and Gomorrah all the people, children too, were turned to salt (as already mentioned). There're the massacres at Jericho and other cities recounted in the Bible. But, perhaps these people didn't count in Gods eyes. They weren't Jews and God was clearly furious with their actions, so, many had to suffer. Fortunately, these stories are not true, in the main. There's a lack of hard evidence according to some archaeologists, although a few war stories may be based, and much embellished, on historical fact. They appear to be written up in a way to justify cruel slaughter through war. Whether true or not, are these fair and just actions and are they examples of a supposedly gentle and loving God, a God of all human kind, not just Jews?

Here's a few Biblical verses telling of God's apparent love and compassion: 1 John 4:16 (NIV) "And so we know and rely on the love God has for us. God is love. Whoever lives in love lives in God, and God in them." Psalm 86:15 (NIV) "But you, Lord, are a compassionate and gracious God, slow to anger, abounding in love and faithfulness." Isaiah 54:10 NIV "Though the mountains be shaken and the hills be removed, yet my unfailing love for you will not be shaken nor my covenant of peace be removed, says the Lord, who has compassion on you."

Abraham's love and obedience to God is tested by said God. In the Old Testament, Genesis 22 of the Bible He required poor Abraham to burn alive his first-born son, Isaac (or Ishmael). The event is remembered on the 1st of Tishrei in the Jewish calendar and from the 10th - 13th of Dhu al-Hijjah in the Muslim calendar. Apart from the main, totally cruel message this story invokes, notice here the sub-text: "first born" - this tells us that the other children are not so important, and "son" - women count for even less. What does this say about both the God and the believer?

Differences between the Old and New Testament

What Impression do we receive of God from the OT? God makes regular appearances throughout the Old Testament. He is very much hands on and in constant contact with his main men - women generally only have bit parts. Eve of course was an exception. In this process he is getting his message across, often in a very dramatic manner. Control, threats and retribution are continuing themes. Sadly, it becomes very hard to understand God's actions. They are certainly far from the image of the gentle, loving and merciful God who is apparently typified in the New Testament, that is apart from the NT story of not just allowing his son to be tortured and killed but actively ensuring it happened.

Mistranslation from Hebrew

The Latinised versions of the Bible, KJV is the most common, have incorrectly translated an important word from the original Hebrew. They have said the Hebrew word almah ("baby") in Isaiah 7:14 means virgin. In fact, the correct meaning is young maiden. In which case there might not be a 'virgin birth". Maiden can just mean 'an unmarried woman'.

Different understandings of the Bible at different time periods

The earliest possible Old Testament translation, from ancient Hebrew, was the Septuagint. This was translated in about 50 CE into an archaic language, a form of Palestinian, colloquial Greek. It was thought to have slightly doctored or added to the original Hebrew. We do not today have anything like a complete understanding of what this was saying. The apostle Paul apparently used it in his utterings. The later Vulgate may have partly been based on the Septuagint. If so, this may not be an accurate description of original Hebrew meanings. How can we be sure that the even later KJ, at a distance of 1600 years, was a faithful translation of original Old Testament writings? The word almah may not be the only issue.

According to the Bible God allows Satan to take away Job's wealth, children and his health. This is supposed to "test" Job's loyalty to God. Job had done nothing wrong to warrant this severe punishment. This is a further anti-example of God's fairness and kindness.

Why does God allow Satan to do dirty deeds, such as encouraging Eve to give the Apple of knowledge to Adam, against God's wishes; trying to tempt Jesus. If God is all-powerful why does he not completely fetter Satan? It is always humans who are punished by God, not Satan. No doubt some theologians would say, "Ah, but God does not allow Satan into heaven. That's a severe punishment." Has anyone asked Satan about this? He might find heaven boring. He's seems to be able to roam around everywhere at any time, and have lots of fun trying to tempt people into being naughty, or worst, that's if he exists of course.

Stoned to death for collecting firewood? Bible verses Numbers 15:32-36 "And while the children of Israel were in the wilderness, they found a man that gathered sticks upon the sabbath day. And the Lord said unto Moses, The man shall be surely put to death; all the congregation shall stone him with stones without the camp. And all the congregation brought him without the camp, and stoned him with stones, and he died; as the Lord commanded Moses." Someone trying to light a fire, to keep himself warm and cook food warrant the death penalty? Is this remotely fair by any stretch of the imagination?

There's also Exodus 35:2 of the Bible, in the KJV "Work shall be done for six days, but on the seventh day there shall be a holy day for you, a Sabbath of rest to the LORD. Whosoever doeth work on it shall be put to death." Boy, with than one it's a wonder that humans have not become extinct.

Here's another couple of Biblical strictures that strictly followed could result in a chunk of humanity becoming deceased: Leviticus 20:13 "If a man also lie with mankind, as he lieth with a woman, both of them have committed an abomination: they shall surely be put to death; their blood shall be upon them." and eating shellfish? - an abominal thing to do - Leviticus 11:10 "And all that have not fins and scales in the seas, and in the rivers, of all that move in the waters, and of any living thing which is in the waters, they shall be an abomination unto you." Leviticus has it in for homosexuals but oysters and whelks are pleased.

It's worth mentioning the fundamental focus of Leviticus. Here's as told by the New Study Bible: "The key thought of Leviticus is holiness - the holiness of God and man. ...In Leviticus spiritual holiness is symbolized by physical perfection. It....requires priests without deformity (Chs 8-10). A woman's hemorrhaging after giving birth (Ch. 12) is an issue, as is sores, burns or baldness Chs. 13-14), a man's bodily discharge (15; 1-18); and specific activities during a woman's monthly period (15: 19-33) which breaks with his spiritual wholeness." So, all women who have had a period, all men who are bald and everyone who has ever had sores or pimples are spiritually defective? This is not worthy of serious comment.

The OT mentions 20 OT prophets who have lived for more than 200 years. Seven of them had, apparently, lived for more than 900 years with Methuselah topping the charts at 969 years. There is no evidence that these people existed or lived to such extreme ages. Current medical science does not support this longevity. Is this another example of deliberate Biblical error, or simple story telling? The original writer could have meant his text to be a story. He may never have intended the over-zealous, the unquestioning followers, and the leaders of the flock, to take his story literally, some two thousand or so years later?

There are no prizes for guessing how many of the 20 longest living OT prophets were female. None of course, giving further support to the view that the claimed God is heavily male biased.

New Testament, what father deliberately manufactures a scenario that He then uses to justify sending his son (Jesus) suffer a painful death? Why is it necessary for a supremely powerful deity to decide that (a) mankind; all of it, past present and future are born with "original sin". Then (b) God decides that the only option to save them from this sin is to have his son killed.

This makes it appear as though God is beholden to some greater power whose weird laws he must take heed of. This great 'evil' thing requires God's son, the messiah, as a sacrifice. If this is not so, then why is the God who designed all humans, and incapable of making a mistake, unhappy about what they do, or in the case of original sin, haven't done, but get charged with it regardless? Did Gabriel really try and talk God out of this? - see Chapter 18a.

What on Earth, or heaven, is "original sin" about? Although the exact phrase does not appear in the Bible there are references to it, some claim: Psalm 51:5 says that everyone comes into the world as sinners: "Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity, and in sin my mother conceived me." Ephesians 2:2 states that people who are not with Christ are "sons of disobedience." It is not a common doctrine to all Abrahamic religions, but is a favourite of Roman Catholicism. Why do billions of humans get blamed for something -what?- they could not or did not do?

The "free will" argument just does not hold water. (See also Chapter 3, re free will) Free will is not specifically mentioned in the Bible. Some theologians claim it can be derived from the Adam and Eve story. These two were apparently given a choice by God, hence they had "free will". How does this fit in with the all-knowing, super-capable God? God, as traditionally described, kick started the entire universe. He drew up detailed plans for everything: galaxies; suns; planets; Earth; evolution and mankind; He knew exactly what He was doing. In any case, He is master of both space and time. That means from the very beginning, that is before the Big Bang some 13.8 billion years ago, He knew in minute detail, how people would turn out and what they would and would not do. He could either travel forward in time to have a look at how things pan out. It could be he does not need to travel in time because, for him, time is all one, past, present and future is now for God. He therefore can know what will happen, before it happens in the human time-frame. If he didn't like what he was seeing, God could go back to the beginning and amend his programming to ensure we turned out differently. He didn't, of course He didn't. He would never need to make changes because He is incapable of making a mistake, we are told. Therefore, we humans must be just as he planned. We must be the flawless products of this Godly design. That is, we do what God wants us to do. God is responsible for all our actions and inactions, the good the bad and the ugly. He made us and He knew exactly how we would turn out. There can be no free will if God is as all powerful and all-knowing as the religious claim, and despite Alvin Plantinga's clever analytics. All of this tortured logic does depend on the very doubtful possibility that there is an Abrahamic type God.

What's this thing about evil? If God doesn't like it why does this supremely powerful being allow it to exists, if it does? The impression given by the Bible and add-on, Christian interpretative holy writ, is that evil is a super-sinister, universal force that even God has to pay attention to. Perhaps it's like "Dark Matter", there's a lot of it about, unseen and undetectable, but it has an enormous impact in our universe! Have a look at Chapter 3 for more about evil.

What about the 298,000 years of human history before the Bible? Where was God? Where was his message to his pre-biblical people? Is it the case that any humans who preceded Jesus, or even Abraham, do not register with God?

Where do the intelligent, upright hominids who preceded Homo Sapiens fit into the Godly scheme of things? Homo Erectus, Heidelbergensis and Habilis had brains, although smaller than HS. They used stone tools, just like HS. And some practiced ritual burial, an indication of a spiritual belief. These hominids existed at least 2.5 million years prior to Homo Sapiens arrival. Our Neanderthal cousins lived alongside us and had brains the same size or bigger than ours, what has God done with them?

Prof Israel Finkelstein, an Israeli archaeologist, has said that some royal buildings, previously attributed to the time of David and Solomon, are now correctly dated to the 9th, rather than 10th century and therefore could not have been constructed by Solomon.

Professor Francesca Stavrakopoulou, an atheist and Professor of the Hebrew Bible and Ancient Religion in the Theology and Religion department at Exeter University, says (1) Moses never existed; (2) The exodus of Jews from Egypt never happened; (3) A great whale, or fish, did not swallow Jonah. "When you take a historical approach [to the Bible], looking at the archaeological evidence for events or people described in the Bible, it is hard to find corroborating evidence to support biblical claims about the past."

[Figure: Moses with the tablets of the Law (Gustave Doré, 1866)]

Professor Stavrakopoulou was also not at all enamored of the New Testament saying: "The God of the New Testament is not interested at all in humanity; he's not really present in the New Testament. It's all about Jesus." She also amusingly said, well amusing for some, "The Bible was written by men with Daddy issues." In answer to Francesca some Biblical supporters say lack of evidence is not evidence of lack. They also mention some Biblical stories are allegorical. Question: Why would a supremely powerful God not make things clear?

In Support of Christianity

In support of Christianity Ravi Zacharias puts forward a strong contrary view. He claims Christianity is the only religion that meets the four key tests of: origin; meaning; morality; and destiny. Ravi Zacharias says: "It's the only one (religion) that takes those four questions with corresponding answers that are truthful and coherent answers that stand the test of time"

The problem with this answer is that are so many holes that can be picked in it over the question of "truth" and 'coherence' especially, but also "morality" and 'destiny'.

Summary, so far, of Issues with the Bible

So, we are asked to believe we have a God whose main message to humans is contained in His holy Bible. The timing of this text ignores 99% of the period humans have existed on Earth. It was written and amended in parts by many men, over many centuries. HIS Bible is full of mistakes and horror stories. It is also heavily biased, it almost ignores everyone other than Jews, mainly male Jews.

It was the post-biblical writings and speeches of Paul that really fostered the gentiles - non-Jews - cause. The Bible is focused mostly on a small area of the middle-east and one small tribe in this area - Israelites, Israeli's or Jews. The rest of the world is largely outside God's vision. Importantly, but unsurprisingly, we have no evidence that the Bible stems from God. Yet despite these huge problems we are asked to believe it and follow its teachings (whatever they might be).

Philo of Alexandria, 20 BCE to 50 CE, was an early Jewish theologian and philosopher who admired Plato, he and others, have tried to re-interpret some of the Bible in an attempt to find a higher (much higher) meaning. Philo's musings almost constitute a total re-write, nothing like the original. Is this because he is embarrassed by early scribes' interpretation of God's literary instruction?

Stories of the Bible

headings.text: Summary, so far, of Issues with the Bible

pages.text:
There are lots of well-known biblical stories, as already mentioned. The point is are all these stories, no more than that - stories? Are they some creative writer's (there were quite a few authors) figment of imagination and nothing more? If they are more than pure fiction, then the next stage up in possibility is the parable or illustrative religious lesson. It's hard to go further than this latter possibility, i.e, to contemplate that they are not just parables, they represent literal truth. And there is scientific evidence to suggest some stories have untruthful components, as pointed out by Professor Stavrakopoulou, and Liev Schreiber.

So, what Godly lessons might be inferred by one other of the biblical stories. There's one so famous it also has a song written about it: "Joshua at the battle of Jericho".

Joshua 6:1-27 tells of the action by Joshua's army to follow up on God's promise to give the land of Canaan, and its main city, Jericho, to his Israelite people. It involved the use of ram's horns, a lot of marching around city walls carrying the Ark of the Covenant, and the help of a prostitute spy, Rahab. Most importantly it also meant application of the Godly law of herem - destroy all, slaughter all (except Rahab).

Let's see what this story meant for one fictional family in Jericho...

Jericho

The two children, Patma, aged 6, and her little brother Vartac, 4, played in the dusty, narrow street outside their red, mud-brick house. Moments before they had said goodbye to their father. He had left home earlier than usual. The children liked that he had given them many more hugs and kisses than usual before leaving. They wondered why he had taken the big axe out of his carpentry workshop, and went away carrying it over his shoulder.

Their mother, Sanka, had told them to stay close to home. They sensed their mother's anxiety and were more subdued than usual. It was noisy this morning. There was lots of shouting. Small groups of men ran past the children without stopping to smile and talk to them as they usually did. Patma and Vartac were bouncy and cheerful. People liked them and often gave them dates or other tidbits, but not today. The children were puzzled, what was happening? Suddenly the familiar, friendly figure of Menair came striding up. He stopped when he saw them. "You must go home and hide." He said. "Why?" Asked Patma, "There might be some strange, nasty men coming. Go home and hide now." replied Menair in a loud, firm voice. This frightened the two children so much they both raced the short distance home. Their mother was waiting anxiously for them. "Mum, Menair said some nasty men might be coming and we should hide." Said Patma. "Don't worry just get under the table, I'll put a cloth over it." Sanka said hastily, but not in a sufficiently reassuring voice. Her tone frightened the children so much they did as they were told, too afraid to argue.

After a little while they could hear shouting outside. The sounds got louder and more frantic. Then there was some screaming. The door of their house was suddenly slammed open. Vartac held Patma's hand tightly.

They could hear their mother, Sanka, pleading with someone. Patma slowly slid aside the table cloth. She saw two fierce looking men. Both held swords. The biggest, a bearded man with a helmet, grabbed her mother by the throat. He raised his sword and snarling something in a strange language he thrust it through her body. The two children screamed and climbed out from under the table, racing to their mother. Sanka fell to the floor with a red stain growing larger on her clothes. Patma cried out, "Mummy!" Vartac stood weeping beside his mother not understanding why she did not move. The younger and slighter of the two men said: "That's enough Boltran. We can leave the kids." Boltran growled fiercely: "No, Joshua and the priests said God wants everyone to be killed, men, women and children." Saying this he lifted up the crying Vartac by his hair. As he drew back his bloodied sword Patma pleaded, "Please, NO...."

Joshua's army, at God's apparent instruction, slaughter every man, woman and child in Jericho (Rehab, the prostitute, was rewarded with her life for aiding the mass-murder). The Canaanite's had lived in Jericho for 500 years before Joshua's arrival. Joshua carries out similar massacres at several other cities, with God's support, according to the Bible. Today, the instigators of such dreadful events would be condemned by the United Nations and international law; the perpetrators would be subject to war crimes tribunal hearings.

Fortunately, archaeologist William G. Dever says Joshua really didn't fight the Battle of Jericho. So, like many stories in the Bible, Jericho was just another story. Phew, good, that means innocents, like Patma and Vartac, were not cruelly slaughtered! Many stories of the Bible, like Joshua and the battle of Jericho, are well known to most Christians. Some of them would be horrifying if the events were of more recent origin, perhaps with some gruesome shots on TV, and via smart phone videos. Their distance in time, together with the mystique of both their locations and characters, allows people today to be generally unfazed by them. The stories then become unthinkingly sanitized and loosely accepted.

Jericho - The Walls Blown Down

[Figure: Jericho: the walls blown down. Julius Schnorr von Carolsfeld, 1860]

An example of Biblical mass murder, apart from Jericho and Joshua, is the well-known story of Sodom and Gomorrah. The book of Genesis tells of this horror story. But like Jericho, this tale is also sanitised by time. The event seemingly occurred more than 3,000 years ago. At this distance, it's harder to get disturbed about what may have happened. Our emotions are not assailed by dramatic photos or TV pictures of the dead, particularly of all the children who would have been killed in the purported massacres. And we don't want to visualize this. It's much too unpleasant and difficult to reconcile with a kind and loving God. So, the full realizable horror of a story that describes the wiping out all the inhabitants of these towns is avoided. Many people just don't want to think about it. It's much easier just to accept the story and then get on with your life.

Dismissive choice

Dismissive choice has some similarities to selective amnesia. The key difference is while the latter has a negative connotation dismissive choice is mostly positive. People will often be selective in the parts of the Bible they choose to focus on. A favourite is the New Testament stories of the helpful miracles of Jesus: raising Lazarus from the dead; feeding the 5,000 etc. For both clerics and followers these signify the generally acceptable and ethical parts of the Godly story; goodness, kindness, forgiveness and mercy. The death, blood and thunder of much of the Old Testament might be less attractive. These contradictory, wrong and cruel stories are dismissed in favour of the more desirable ones.

Comfortable Familiarity

Many of the OT stories are well known to most Christians: Noah and his ark; The Tower of Babel; Jonah and the whale; Joseph sold into slavery by his jealous brothers; Moses and the burning bush and lots of others. They are comforting through their familiarity. The comfort is appreciated and their truth goes unchallenged. No one has yet managed to produce conclusive evidence that these are other than Stories.

Creative interpretation

Theologians and Church leaders are brilliant at this. When modern knowledge shows some biblical stories to be blatantly untrue, then it is often claimed the stories are merely allegorical. They are not to be taken as gospel, it is said.

So, despite the evidence, or lack of it, that's how quite a few reasonable and pleasant people may hold on to their beliefs. They are sometimes supported, and their belief encouraged, by governments and political leaders. These have found it useful to encourage belief.

Christianity, a weapon of politics and Empire building

The Bible underpins all Christian belief. It's a fundamental holy text for today's 2.4 billion Christians. This book has helped Christianity achieve an enormous impact on world history for the last 2,000 years.

Christianity and its Bible has been a handy political weapon. In 313 CE the Roman Emperor Constantine was the first to try and use the growing Christian faith in this way, on a large scale. He thought insisting on a common faith, Christianity, could be a unifying force across his vast, disparate realm. It was Constantine who called the First Council of Nicea, in 325CE. This resulted in the first clear statement of Christian belief - the Nicene Creed. He also made Sundays a day of rest.

Since Constantine governing structures have often used Christianity as a supportive and controlling prop. It's been an instrument of Empire building by European nations from the early middle-ages. This helped establish Christianity in places like Africa, South and North America, Australia, New Zealand and the far east; most of the world in fact.

From Constantine and later the Crusades - war between Christians and Muslims - the Christian God has regularly been invoked, sometimes by both sides in a conflict. Even in modern times antagonists have claimed that God is on their side. The British Prime Minister, Winston Churchill, said this at the start of World War 2, in in his first speech as PM, in 1940: ".....to wage war, by sea, land and air, with all our might and with all the strength that God can give us." Before the German, air armada blitz, again in 1940, he said: "Upon this battle depends the survival of Christian civilisation."

Churchill's main antagonist, the Nazi Adolf Hitler, also appealed to God's support or claimed to have it in his book Mein Kampf he wrote: "I believe today that my conduct is in accordance with the will of the Almighty Creator."

The full Christian story is a long one. Diarmaid MacCulloch covers it quite thoroughly in his 1,100-page tome: "A History of Christianity."

What's on offer overrides all misgivings

Finally, almost, for many believers the advantages of belief, as described in earlier chapters, helps swamp any niggling misgivings that believers might have. There are just a few more issues to raise in a subsequent chapter. There's the question of the soul, eternity, heaven and hell and an imagined conversation between God and Archangel Gabriel concerning God's plan.

chapters.title: Eternity, The Soul, Heaven and Hell, - again, Creation and Jesus
chapters.summary: Eternity and how God avoids boredom (tongue firmly in cheek!) The soul, what, why, where and when is it? Heaven and Hell, a few more little problems. God and Gabriel discuss G's grand plan (tongue even more firmly in cheek).

pages.text:
Chapter 18a

Eternity, The Soul, Heaven and Hell again, Creation and Jesus

Eternity

Eternity lasts for quite a long time. God's there throughout. Does He get bored?

Here we have, many claim, not just a supreme being but THE Supreme Being. This Supreme Being, in His traditional monotheistic God mode, knows everything; can go anywhere and anywhen. He is all powerful and exists for ever. At least, that is what most of His adherents claim of Him.

How does such a being retain interest in continued existence? Nothing is impossible to Him. His capabilities can't be stretched. No one is in his league. He is incapable of forgetting anything. God knows what's going to happen before it happens. For Him existence just goes on and on and on, forever and ever. Looking at the Trinity, three as the one, means He does not have family, nor does He have friends. No one is on His level so it's impossible for Him to have interesting discussions with anyone. He, apparently, doesn't do jokes or laughter, so there is no refuge in humour for this Abrahamic God. What does He do for recreation? He has many universes for His playground, but how can He utilise these to relieve potential tedium?

[Figure: Infinity symbol illustration]

We can investigate a little here. Let's again employ the Tardis, our time travelling machine, to visit God in his heaven nearly 14 billion years ago. We find that He's been thinking about what to do to pass the time. Our detectoring reveals that He is about to take His cue from the leisure activities of one of the beings He will create. i.e. God moves ahead 13.8 billion years on the space/time curve of one of his universes to take a quick look at what some humans eventually do at the weekends. Sadly, he notes, some even do this on Sundays.

God discusses his idea with someone close to Him. With the help of the Tardis, We are back in time to just before the Big Bang. We hear this conversation between God and his angel-in-chief Gabriel:

God: "Gabriel, I've taken a look into the future, I see that these humans I'm eventually going to bring into existence spend a lot of leisure time playing something called golf." "What is golf Lord?" asks Gabriel. God: "Apparently golf is a healthy, outdoor activity with an opportunity for serious socialising on the 19th tee. The basic idea seems to be to knock a ball into a hole."

"Yes Lord?" queried Gabriel, not quite seeing where this was heading. (as senior advisor Gabriel is allowed to forego the "My" which would normally precede the "Lord" when addressing God) God: "Well, I thought that I could turn a suitable galaxy into a golf course. Then you and I could have a game occasionally." Gabriel: "Ah, I see, very good idea Lord. Of course, you are the Supreme Being with unlimited powers so no doubt you could easily construct an excellent golf-course. In fact, it would instantly become the best in all the universes." (Gabriel had been God's right-hand angel for countless billions of years. He knew when a bit of flattery was in order; even if he did not fully grasp the topic under discussion.)

"Yes, of course" God replied, completely unaware that he had made a very small joke.

God went on: "We could play with rounded, dimpled and extra dense asteroids and try potting them in a galaxy wide course of 18 black holes. Strategically placed Red Giant stars would act as bunkers." "On second thoughts," said God pausing, "Close up, black isn't really my colour." God hesitated a fraction and then continued: "I know, I'll make them white holes instead of black holes." Gabriel: "Lord, are you sure you want to be seen as preferring white to black? This will become a serious PC issue with later humans. They may eventually discover your golfing galaxy and be dismayed at your preference for white."

"Nonsense" said God briskly, "there's going to be a lot of black in the universe. Nearly all the stuff between the stars will be made of something called "dark matter". That's near as dammit black. No one should complain because the black holes in just the one galaxy are white." God continued, "Come to think of it, I'm not keen on "Red" either. Bit of a hellish colour that. But I won't make the bunkers white, in case the PC crowd get agitated, I'll turn all the Red Giant stars (the intended bunkers) into Cerise Giants." and in a triumphant tone God goes on: "Hardly anyone will know what colour cerise is so they won't be able to accuse Me of colour discrimination."

[Figure: A golf flag, ball and hole]

[Figure: A fiery sun]

God and Gabriel would have a fairway to drive off on each hole of their galactic, star flung, course. Naturally, poor Gabriel would be on a hiding to nothing. God can achieve a hole in one with every shot, even on the 570 million light-year par 5.

Many, many years after setting up this course, God and Gabriel are in the celestial clubhouse bar.

headings.text: Eternity, The Soul, Heaven and Hell again, Creation and Jesus

pages.text:
"Nice round again Lord. That's the 2 millionth and second time you've beaten me. As usual, you scored a hole in one at every hole." Gabriel paused then continued: "You really are the holy one, aren't you?" God, not having a sense of humour, but sensing that something is not quite right with Gabriel's last remark replied: "Gabriel, am I missing something here, Did you attempt to make some sort of joke just then?" and, with a flash of slightly misplaced inspiration: "Do my socks need darning?"
Look out on a clear night with a powerful telescope. Focus top left of the Milky Way, four galaxies on, you might just make out a Cerise Giant star or two and the white holes.

The Soul

Let's examine this ephemeral, floaty, mystical essence through the five Ws analysis: what; why; where; when and who.

What is it?

The soul is thought to be a non-physical essence of self. It can exist after the body has died and is in effect immortal.

All the current major religions: Christianity; Islam and Judaism believe MH (Modern Humans) have a soul. There is quite a lot of theological discussion as to when the idea of a soul was introduced into Abrahamic religious belief. Some say the idea was borrowed from ancient Greek and other cultures. Plato, 2,400 year ago, thought MH had immortal souls.

[Figure: Charon, ferryman of the dead (Gustave Dore, 1861)]

For Christians, it was Origen, around 200 CE who first expounded the idea of a soul, claiming it was created in every human by God. The Hebrew word 'nephesh', in the Bible, is often translated to mean soul, but not consistently. The old religions (sometimes referred to by snooty monotheistic moderns as "pagan") also believed there was some sort of spirit that allowed an existence after death, even if they did not name this spirit a soul. The soul cannot be seen, touched or in any other way detected. No bodily dissection, X ray, CT or ultrasound scan or any other type of medical examination has every produced evidence of the existence of a soul. It is only some religious people who suggest what a soul is and claim that it exists in every MH. There is not a shred of hard evidence for it, unless spiritual mediums or some people's dreams are to be given that description.

Why claim there is one?

Why does the concept of a soul pervade nearly all religions? The existence of a soul, of sorts, is absolutely essential if any major religion is to have believers. The soul offers the engaging prospect of eternal life. And each religion, apart from some ancient ones, promises a very pleasant perpetual existence if only the believer keeps to certain rules during his/her time on planet Earth. There is no body, after death to enjoy the eternal life with, but the soul is a perfect vehicle to propel believers to heaven, nirvana or whatever endless delight is on offer. As an essential part of their sales pitch, religious chiefs have to convince potential followers that they each have a soul.

Where is it?

It resides [cannot say "lives", in place of "resides" because this would imply that a soul can die] within each human, apparently, and continues when the physical body dies.

When does it come into existence?

Now this is a good one. The issue is when does the ephemeral soul associate with a human body. Is this at the point of birth or is it at conception? Maybe neither of these, but perhaps at some other stage during foetal, physical or mental development? There is potentially an issue with abortion, or miscarriage. Does the soul hook up at some stage after conception, but before the expected time of birth? This conjecture is only relevant if there is a soul.

Who has a soul?

Do animals other than humans have souls? If not, at what point in human evolution were souls attached to the body? Were souls only given to modern humans (MH)? MH have been around for 300,000 years. But their cousins, the Neanderthals have some similar characteristics to MH. They were bipedal. They had large brains, generally larger than MHs. And arguably Neanderthals had some form of spiritual belief. So, were they given souls in some mysterious way? What about all the intelligent, bipedal hominids who preceded both MH and Neanderthals: Homo Erectus; Homo Heidelbergensis; Homo Ergaster and Homo Hablis, to name but a few. Did these have souls too? If non-MH had souls, do they still exist somewhere in a heavenly, or hellish type location?

Perhaps though the provision of souls is dependent on brain size. The size choice imposed by the supreme deity could limit souls to MH and maybe Neanderthals. But if brains are vital to the decision awkward issues can arise. What effect, if any, does abortion, or any other cause of death of a foetus developing in a potential mother's womb, have on the soul? What happens with MH who are born with much reduced mental capacity, because of some form of physical disability? If they do not have a soul that is doubly unfair situation. They would be denied not only a "normal" human life but also a hereafter one.

There is not just a sole question to be answered about souls, there's lots of issues.

Heaven and Hell

Heaven

[Figure: A happy emoji and an unhappy emoji linked by a double tipped arrow]

headings.text: When does it come into existence?

pages.text:
Heavens above! Heaven is a place of eternal peace - apparently. It's where the souls reside of those rated good enough to get through its pearly gates. In heaven these souls are said to enjoy peace forever. Do we want everlasting peace, and not much else? Is "peace", interspersed with regular God worship, all there is to be had from achieving heavenly status? Are humans to eternally forgo all the pleasures they enjoy once heavenly eminence is attained? - No eating, drinking, sex, TV, cinema, theatre, dinner parties, computer games, reading, cooking, rugby, football, badminton, fishing, cycling, walking, or bridge, and no texting or even gardening. Holidays at exotic locations or any location would be a no-no.
Heaven has never even been reported as having a golf club, although God may have his own personal one. Do heavenly rules allow people, or their souls, to chat to family and friends? We don't know, but this seems unlikely. Apparently, there's no laughing either in Heaven. It's all devoutly serious. Even smiles are frowned upon. Frowns are frowned upon too. Boring is too weak a word for heaven, a new word must be invented.

Artists, when picturing heaven, traditionally depict people in saintly mode encapsulated within glowing clouds. These righteous persons are usually shown with clasped hands pointing reverently upwards. Their fingers are sometimes aimed at a stern looking, white haired man glowering down from a cloud. The salvationista have a slightly vacant, puzzled look on their faces. Perhaps it's just dawned on them what heaven is all about. How many weeks can the average person last in this traditional pious pose? Surely not for ever and ever.

Many religions, including pagan ones, have more inviting "heavens" than the Christian one. The Vikings version, Valhalla, with its promise of endless quaffing, singing and wenching would surely win any vote when the dull, solemn, reverential Christian Heaven was the alternative on the electoral card. Even women may prefer Valhalla. They could become beautiful Valkyries, riding white horses, singing Wagner, and choosing the fate of men in battle. Women with absolute power over men, maybe a feminist dream come true! Come back Odin, all is forgiven. We really need a religion that gives a wide choice of afterlives, just as proposed in Chapter 21, Design a God.

With a nod to dyslexia and pluralism, those Christian theologians might have almost got it right. Rather than removing to a place of eternal peace, i.e. Heaven, we in fact revert to the eternal pieces from which our body matter is composed. When we die we are usually cremated. Our bodies return to dust and eventually further decay into particles less than dust. These particles, in new molecular forms, find their way into the earth, air and cosmos itself. We are all composed of fundamental, basic atoms and sub-atomic particles, exactly as stars, planets and inter-stellar matter. As Carl Sagan once said: "We are star stuff." As star stuff, all the pieces that make up us are in essence eternal. We may not be at peace but we are certainly in pieces.

Hell

Hell's bells! We've had Heaven, but what about Hell? This is meant to be a place worse than Heaven, although there could be some contention about this. Traditionally, Hell is where bad souls go to because their bodily precursors had not towed a goodly line. It's a hot location where the damned are eternally tortured, apparently. The King James Bible, Old Testament, mentions Sheol, on 31 occasions. Sheol is translated as "Hell", mostly, but also refers to "the pit". Modern versions of the Bible try to be slightly less frightening; for these Sheol is "the grave". Tortured in the grave though is not any better than being tortured in Hell.

In that old favourite Bible version, the King James (KJV), Revelation 21:8 makes it terrifyingly clear what will happen to those who do not follow Biblical instruction to the letter: "But the fearful, and unbelieving, and the abominable, and murderers, and whoremongers, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars, shall have their part in the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone: which is the second death." If strictly applied this will really reduce the numbers going to heaven in a very big way. At the same time Hell is in danger of being clogged up. We may not have too many "sorcerers", unless this is a miss-spelling and in fact refers to people who place their tea cup on a saucer, but in human history there's been lots and lots of unbelievers and idolaters, then the 'abominable' can be a broad church, personal viewpoint dependent. We also have 'liars', which person can claim they have never, ever, told a fib? Hell must be a really big place and the heating bill enormous to cope with, what is probably the vast majority of humanity.
Islam refers to Jahannam, a sort of Hell. Here, in the afterlife, evildoers are punished on a scale commensurate with how bad they've been in life, that seems a bit fairer than the Christian Hell where you get the full works regardless, although Dante thinks there are 9 levels of Hell. In Islam at the end of creation the dead will be raised. The soul is then weighed in terms of good or bad. Then souls have to pass over a test bridge to paradise. This widens for the good and narrows to a knife edge for the bad. Falling off this bridge is not a sensible thing to do, it's straight to Jahannam.

There is no mention of hand-rails, so it obviously gets extremely difficult if the bridge is very narrow and if the soul does not have a good sense of balance. Infidels even suffer in the grave, before going on to Jahannam after judgement day.

[Figure: Muhammad, Buraq and Gabriel observe "shameless women" being punished in Jahannam for being prostitutes - historical Islamic illustration]

Apparently, the soul of a dead infidel is wrenched from its body then interrogated by the angels Munkar and Nakir. Being infidels, they are certain to fail the interrogation and then suffer torment in the grave. Eventually they are eternally physically and spiritually tortured in Jahannam.

In the Jewish tradition there is place called Gehinnom (see also Chapter 16). This is akin to a very superior washing-machine for the soul. Baddish souls are thoroughly cleansed in Gehinnom. The sparkling clean soul is then ready for entry to heaven. Gehinnom may not be very pleasant for the soul. It has to endure a full wash cycle - on high heat and fast spin for the really bad soul. But this is only to be endured for quite a limited time. It is as nothing when compared to the Christian Hell or Islamic Jahannam.
Dante's vision of Hell deserves explaining. His 14th century epic poem sets out nine circles of Hell (inferno in Italian, Dante's native tongue). Each succeeding circle represents an increase in wickedness. Which circle souls end up in depends on what bads people did in life. In the first circle souls tick over in Limbo - not too bad at all. This one is for the unbaptised and those pagans who have been quite good. Treachery is reckoned the most heinous sin and for that people land up in circle 9. You just don't want to be end up there.

[Figure: Sandro Botticelli's La Carte de l'Enfer (The map of Hell and the 9 Circles) drawn in the 1480s - showing Dante's nine descending circles of Hell in a cone-shaped diagram]

Here are the 9 in order of degree of badness from not so bad to appalling: First Circle - Limbo; Second Circle - Lust; Third Circle - Gluttony; Fourth Circle - Greed; Fifth Circle - Wrath; Sixth Circle - Heresy; Seventh Circle - Violence; Eighth Circle - Fraud; Ninth Circle - Treachery.

Heaven and Hell, a key problem

Imagine someone getting into heaven and looking down on a friend, or maybe family member, who had fallen foul of Revelation 21:8. Says the heavenista: "Look, there's George in absolute agony again." How can that person be serenely content in heaven, enjoying eternal peace, knowing that others are suffering eternal agony, sometimes for very minor misdemeanours? Is this evidence of a kind and loving God?

The Bible - again

headings.text: Heaven and Hell, a key problem

pages.text:
The Bible, in spite of all the problems identified in Chapter 18, is at the heart of Christian faith. Much of it is also central to Judaism and Islam. All three great Abrahamic religions believe the Bible stems from God and is a divine guide to how people should live their lives, although the three religions do dispute the meaning of some parts, for example, Christians think Jesus is the son of God while both Jews and Islamists believe he was a prophet. Apart from this issue, there are quite large chunks of the Bible that are tricky to decode by present day readers. For example, when it comes to the ten commandments, very few of the texting generation have any difficulty in avoiding the temptation of coveting their: "...neighbour's... manservant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his ass" (Exodus 20:17). Not many present-day neighbour's have man and maid servants. Oxen are a bit thin on the ground too nowadays. All neighbours have asses though, some are asses too, but possibly the biblical writer did not intend the alternative, modern day meaning of "ass". So, because most of the Bible was written several thousand years ago, interpretation of its meaning in a current context has been an ongoing issue.
Some Christians, particularly Creationists, take a radical view. They maintain that all the words of the Bible are from God and therefore should be taken literally. This, they think, applies to the entirety of both New and Old Testaments, regardless of what Darwin, evolution, cosmology, science generally, simple human compassion or common sense says. Are the Creationists correct? Is the entire Bible the word of God? If it is, how far should it be literally interpreted and applied now, in modern times?

There is no uniform agreement as to the answer to this conundrum in the broad Christian community. Disputation on matters of theology; particularly Biblical interpretation; have often been violent in nature. Violent religious conflict is almost a defining feature of Christianity, up to the middle ages at least. These vicious disputes were not only with those of other beliefs but also with Christians who may have held slightly different views of Christianity.

1,700 years ago, the prolific Roman historian Ammianus Marcellinus in his "The Later Roman Empire" said: "No wild beasts are so deadly to humans as most Christians are to each other." Marcellinus was even handed though, alongside his critique of Christians, he also had a go at Roman Emperor Julian's paganism. Julian was particularly keen to placate Roman Gods through large scale animal sacrifice. Marcellinus said that Julian "drenched the altars with blood of an excessive number of victims, sometimes offering up a hundred oxen at once..."

[Figure: A bust thought to be of Ammianus Marcellinus, soldier and historian (c.330-400 CE)]

Ancient language translation, is it right?

Dispute between Christians can also arise from mid-translation. There can be argument about the correctness of the translation of Biblical text from ancient Hebrew. Splitting hairs and holding strongly opposing views is a favourite human pastime. That is why we have a multitudinous line up of Christian religions (see Chapter 17). Although Christianity probably takes first prize, factionisation is not confined to Christians. It's common currency in other major Abrahamic religions. While each religious faction may dissent from each other, for one reason or another, they all have in common their certainty. They each know, without doubt, that their particular religion or religious sect is the correct one. Theirs's is the only one that really knows what God means to convey through his Biblical or other sacred text.

How do we decide for ourselves which of the wide variety of biblical based "truths" we should accept, if any at all? We need to go straight to source for clarity on some of the central issues here. It's time to listen in again on another conversation between God and his chief hench-angel, Gabriel. On this occasion, we hear their discourse on the key topics of creation and the role of Jesus. These two biblical issues, one from the Old and the other from the New Testament, are closely linked.

Of all the archangels, Gabriel is renowned as the guardian of truth. It has always puzzled Gabriel that God made him his chief confidant despite knowing this.

[Figure: The Archangel Gabriel, engraving by Martin Schongauer, about 1490]

headings.text: Ancient language translation, is it right?

pages.text:
The exchange here takes place quite some time after God created his cosmic golf course.

God: "Gabriel, I've quite enjoyed playing golf with you these last three million years, though I must say you don't seem to make any improvement. You still drive off with a bent arm and your putting is appalling. However, that aside, I find I need something more than golf to occupy me."

Gabriel, in a humble, contrite tone: "Sorry about my golf Lord, what are you considering now?"

God: "Well, I'm adding something to my original grand plan, which was to start up a new universe. Now, it will be one with the right conditions to allow humans to evolve."

Gabriel: "Yes, Lord, I recall reading your great plan. Wasn't your universe going to kick-off with an almighty, no pun intended Lord, explosion? Then 13.8 billion years later humans were to be on the scene? Incidentally, I wondered why you didn't make that evolutionary period a nice round number, like 10 billion years. That would be much easier to remember."

God: "Get with it Gabriel. If I made it "a nice round number" as you put it, humans might smell a rat. For the same reason you may have noticed that I'm going to make the circumference of a circle equal to 3.14159 and a bit of its diameter, instead of simply "3". I know this may seem a little irrational, but you can't make a Pi without having something left over. Also, humans will eventually evolve a very bright fellow with a name like a beer mug. If I didn't have some odd numbers in the maths he certainly would catch on that someone had been fiddling the laws of physics and cosmology. One more thing. The kick-off for my new universe is not, "an almighty explosion." That sounds like I might be blowing myself up." "I've penned a clearer and snappier name than that - the Big Bang. Do try and get it right."

Gabriel, somewhat bemused by this, hesitantly said: "I think I understand Lord."

God, forcefully: "No you don't. I can tell. Look, there's going to be billions and billions of humans eventually. If they all got into heaven we wouldn't have room to swing a cat up here, so, I can't make it too easy for them to believe in me. Simple relational numbers will give the game away immediately. They'll know then, without having to make any effort of faith, or even go to Sunday school, that I must exist. I want them to work hard at getting to know of me. I don't want to set up the universe in a way that makes it too obvious that I exist. So, the numbers have got to be both difficult and awkward. There will even be something called quantum, which is so tricky it's sort of magical. Even the beer mug guy will have trouble sorting that one out."

Gabriel: "Ah, what brilliant logic, as always, Lord."

God, unsuccessfully trying not to appear pleased at this praise, briskly carried on: "Now, to get back to my main point. I've decided I don't want to wait 13.8 billion years to see what these interesting humans get up to, so I'm going to speed things up a bit."

Gabriel injected: "So will you put everything together in, let's say, 5 billion years - sorry (remembering God's desire for odd numbers), I meant, say 5.76 billion years?"

God, slightly irritated at being interrupted: "No, I'll do it even sooner than that. I'll make the planet Earth and the first humans, Adam and Eve, within a week."
Gabriel responded in some awe: "Good God, even for you, isn't that pushing it Lord. Besides, what about all the stars, planets, moons, comets etc in the universe. If it takes you a week to make just the Earth then the rest of the cosmos is going to take a lot longer. There will need to be lots of stars, not just those two lights in the firmament that you plan to make on the 4th day of creation (Gabriel had just read God's plan at warp speed)."

God smirked knowingly at this and said: "Ah-ah, that's where I have a cunning ruse! Of course, even the early, rather primitive humans, must be able look up into the sky and see twinkly lights that many generations later they will call stars. So, at first, I will do something simple and temporary to fool them. What I plan to do initially won't take very long. I will put into geo-stationary orbit the right number of very large candles. These will be placed about 40 miles above the Earth surface. There will still be a slight atmosphere even at this height. But the wind will only be enough to make the candles flicker, not blow them out. The flickering will look like the twinkling that will later occur with stars."

Gabriel: "Yes, pre-historic humans won't be sophisticated enough to be able tell they are candles rather than stars, but later ones will with their telescopes and other instruments. What then Lord?"

God: "Well, we have many thousands of years before humans will be able to detect the candles. During that time, I'm going to have the entire host of angels gradually replacing the candles with proper stars. They'll be set at the right distances and correct expansion speeds. When they've finished that job, I'll get the angels to go to work on Earth. They'll stuff dinosaur bones, the skeletons of ape-like humans, and other apparently ancient plants and animals into the Earth's rock strata. With all this, by 2011, of Gregory's calendar, human cosmologists will believe the universe is nearly 14 billion years old. Geologists, thinking they are so smart, with their isotropic and carbon dating techniques, will believe that the Earth is billions of years old too - 4.558 billion to be exact. It will be just those few astute Creationists who, despite all the apparent evidence to the contrary, will have sufficient faith to believe in the true cosmic timescale, i.e. 5,600 years. Bishop Ussher will be encouraged by me to calculate this timescale. As a reward, creationists will be the only ones to have a chance of making it to heaven. This way we will be able to keep the numbers down and avoid being overcrowded up here."

Gabriel: "If it's only Creationists and their like who will get to come up to us, won't that mean there will be a disproportionate number of Americans in heaven from the USA's deep south?"

God: "Yes, but that can't be helped."

God stopped for a moment to gather his thoughts and then continued: "Coming back to the angels, they need something constructive to do." "You can't get much more constructive than building a star." - Gabriel interjected knowingly. "Yess-s" said God, slightly distractedly. After pausing he continued: "At the moment those angels just lounge about putting on gold make-up, preening their feathers and strumming harps." God frowned as he recalled the discordant harp playing that permeated every nook and cranny of heaven. He went on: "That damned constant tinkling noise gets on my nerves."

Gabriel: "But you don't have any....."

God, impatiently: "Yes, yes, I know I don't have a nervous system. I was merely speaking meta.. meta.."

"Metaphorically I think you mean Lord." interposed Gabriel in a carefully polite tone.

"That's the one." replied God briskly. "Anyway, the angels can get on making the basic stars; planets; comets and asteroids. You archies (God's collective term for his archangels) can have fun too. I'll let you do the interesting stars: white dwarfs; black holes; red giants; pulsars; that sort of thing. You can even set off the odd supernova too." - He added generously. "I will concentrate on galaxies. I've got some interesting shapes in mind, although for speed most will be simple spiral galaxies."

Rubbing his hands together, self-satisfied, God added: "That's this universe sorted. I've already written a detailed plan covering not just the first week but the first 5,600 years of Earth's history. I want you to read it again now Gabriel, this time with more care, then give me your views."

Gabriel, a few nanoseconds later (he was quite good at bending time): "I've read it again Lord and am a little concerned about some aspects."

"Oh, what are they?" said God with some surprise.

Gabriel: "Well, for starters, right at the beginning I see Adam and Eve will be evicted from their home just because Adam eats an apple that you don't want him to eat. Wouldn't a simple ticking off be more appropriate than eviction?"

God: "The point is, it was Me who asked them not to eat that apple. They knew that but wanted to know more."

Gabriel: "And so you think a much harsher punishment is warranted than this very minor misdemeanour would ordinarily attract?"
God: "You've got it in one Gabriel. But of course, eviction is not sufficient punishment in this case. I give these two people everything. They defy me and are the first humans to do so. They are representing their entire race and should be more respectful."

Gabriel: "Yes, I've noted that the whole of humanity is to be branded with "original sin" as a result of the A & E department operation. Surely Lord this is excessive in the extreme. Many billions of humans will be punished for something they didn't do and had absolutely no control over. Even if Eve had picked every apple from your tree and baked apple pies with them all without offering you a single slice, that would not warrant what you are imposing."

God: "Gabriel, I think you are forgetting just who is the Supreme Being here."

Gabriel: "Deepest apologies Lord. Naturally I would never intend any offence. I would though like to make a further point."

God, his fuse getting shorter, snapped: "And what is that?"

Gabriel hesitated, then replied in his most reasonable voice: "Adam and Eve and every human are to be punished for this "crime" but the perpetrator, Satan, thinly disguised as a snake, gets away scot free?"

God: "You know I have to be very careful when dealing with Fred (God always uses Satan's first name). He's a mischievous devil but very powerful. Were he and I to have a serious set-to the whole of reality would become twisted."

Gabriel quickly picked up on this: "And your plan isn't really twisted?"

Fortunately for Gabriel, God took his reply as a statement rather than a question: "Exactly, it's actually quite straightforward. And on the original sin issue, if you've read the fine detail of my plan you would have noticed that I've allowed humans a way out."

Gabriel: "Yes, I was coming to that. You intend that your only son, Jesus, should become a temporary human. He is then to suffer horrible torture and a slow and agonising death. What has any of this to do with Jesus? Someone steals one apple and as a result your son has to be killed as a form of expiation for all people, who also had nothing to do with it. I find this hard to understand Lord."

God: "It makes for a great story and really impresses the humans. They talk about it for thousands of years afterwards. Humans even celebrate Jesus' immaculate birthday every year. Admittedly, in time the birthday celebration mostly involves heavy duty shopping and debauchery, but I can live with that. And then there's Easter with all those chocolate eggs and the consumption of billions of hot-cross buns. So this story has quite a following."

Gabriel: "But you only have one son Jesus. He, apparently, adores you. Why hurt him?"

God: "Stop making such a fuss. Jesus is not only going to absolve mankind from the apple sin he's got to go down to Earth and pass on righteous messages from me to these humans. In any case, he needs to get out and about more. The experience will toughen him up, but He'll soon be over it. Why, I'm going to beam him back up here at the end of his Earthly visit, so he won't have to worry about return travel arrangements."

Gabriel felt compelled to continue despite being aware he was on dodgy ground: "Lord, yes I know you will raise Jesus up, but only after he's been dead for three days! Why not do it three days before his intended death?"

God, impatiently and forcefully: "Gabriel, you really must try and see the bigger picture here. If I raised him before he died that would completely destroy the dramatic impact I'm trying to achieve. And then there would be no more Easters either. Think of all those people who will eventually work in the chocolate Easter egg and hot-cross bun industries. They would be without a job."

Gabriel made a last desperate attempt to delay God's plan and get Him to re-consider: "Lord, I know you've been working really hard recently. This plan of yours is...is...amazing and clearly the result of a lot of effort. I think you deserve a holiday. Let me knock up a planet with sandy beaches, warm blue seas, waving palm trees and mountain views in the background. You could chill out on the beach for a week. In the second week we could decamp to your galactic golf course and hold a tournament with all the archies."

Gabriel decided that the point had come where he had to play his last high card: "You are very good at golf remember." - he said with heavy emphasis.

God hesitated for a moment, then with a note of finality in his voice: "I'm much too busy to go on holiday, despite the temptation of winning the golf tournament. Gabriel, I know that you think my plan is nonsensical but you'll see, it will all work out in the end. I'm planning some really big fireworks when the curtain eventually comes down on humankind. I think you will enjoy the spectacle."

Gabriel, dispiritedly giving up said: "Thy will be done Lord" and very quietly, under his breath, added: "not only Will will be done; Jesus and other humans too."

The Blue Qur'an: A rare 9th to 10th-century Islamic manuscript written in gold on indigo-dyed parchment, approximately 1,100 years old. Probably created in North Africa for the Great Mosque of Qairawan in Tunisia. Each page features elegant Kufic script. Islam derives from the Arabic word meaning submission or surrender. Muhammad had over 23 years of revelations from the archangel Gabriel, which became the Qur'an. His visions began in 610 CE, although Muhammad did not fully come to grips with his religious role, even with his wife Khadija's help, until later.
[Note: Page 12 appears to be largely a continuation/repetition from earlier pages with some corrupted OCR text. Based on the visible content in the image, this appears to be discussing Christianity, Islam and Muslims as followers of Allah. I'll capture the legible content while noting the fragmentary nature.]

Islam refers to the religion of Muslims, who are the followers of Allah (God). Christians believe in Jesus Christ, whereas Muslims also see Jesus as an important prophet but not as the son of God. Rather, Muslims believe Muhammad to be God's final prophet. The Qur'an is central to Islamic faith, as revealed to Muhammad over 23 years through the archangel Gabriel. Muslims believe Allah (God) is one and the same as the Abrahamic God worshipped by Jews and Christians, though the three religions interpret God's message and requirements differently.

[Figure: Resurrection of Jesus Christ by Raphael, painted 1499 to 1502 CE - showing Jesus rising from the tomb with divine light]

The resurrection of Jesus Christ is central to Christian faith. Christians believe that Jesus was crucified, died, and was buried, but rose from the dead three days later. This event, commemorated at Easter, represents victory over death and sin, and provides hope of eternal life for believers. The resurrection is seen as proof of Jesus' divine nature and God's power over death itself.

However, critics question various aspects of this narrative. Why wait three days? Why allow the suffering in the first place if resurrection was planned? And what about those who lived before Jesus or never heard of him - are they condemned through no fault of their own?

The story has persisted for over 2,000 years, inspiring billions while raising fundamental questions about justice, mercy, and the nature of salvation. Easter celebrations in 2018 and beyond continue this tradition, though for many the religious significance has been overshadowed by chocolate eggs and commercial interests.

Christians see the Bible as prophetic guidance, while Muslims view Muhammad as the final prophet, and Jews await the Messiah. Jesus is variously seen as: son of God by Christians; a prophet (but not divine) by Muslims; and not recognized as Messiah by Jews. Islam does not view Jesus as the son of God but as a significant prophet and servant of Allah (God). All three Abrahamic faiths - Judaism, Christianity and Islam - trace back to Abraham and worship the same God, though they differ fundamentally on interpretation, practice, and the role of various prophets and holy figures.

Friends of Allah (God).
