pages.text:
Chapter 19: Islam

This is the third and most recent of the three Abrahamic religions, in terms of the defining date of its holy book, the Qur'an, also called the Koran. After Christianity, Islam is the second largest religion in the world with about 1.8 billion followers in 2018. It's a monotheistic, Abrahamic religion because it has the same origins as the other two in the prophet Abraham, and recognises Adam. Islam acknowledges other important people referred to in the Jewish Torah and Christian Bible as prophets: Noah; Ishmael; Moses; Joshua and David among others. It sees Jesus as yet another prophet, although a very important one. Islam does not view Jesus as God. The Torah and Bible are considered to be significant Godly guides but only as precursors to the final and definite words of Allah (God). For Muslims, these definitive words are contained in their holy book, the Qur'an.

[Figure: A page of the Blue Qur'an: gold ink on blue-dyed parchment, about 1,000 years old]

The word Islam is generally thought to mean submission to the will of Allah and Muslims are the followers of Islam. The Muslims' holy book, the Qur'an, means revelation. Expanded, this becomes the revelation of Allah's will.

The Prophet Muhammad and the Qur'an

The Qur'an derives from visions that Muslims believe the prophet Muhammad had over 23 years concluding in 632 CE. These visions were of the archangel Gabriel who orally communicated Allah's divine messages. The visions began in 610 CE as he meditated in the cave of Hira. At first Muhammad did not fully understand what the visions were. He discussed these with his wife in Mecca.

Muhammad was born in Mecca in about 570 CE to the Quraysh tribe. His father died before he was born and his mother died when he was six. He was raised by his grandfather and then his uncle. At about 25 he married Khadija, a wealthy widow. Muhammad is said to have been a trader and successful merchant. He was troubled by the social problems of his time and sought answers by meditation.

After his first vision, Muhammad began to preach, initially in his hometown of Mecca. His message was not well received by the city's ruling elite who saw him as a threat. In 622 CE Muhammad and his followers migrated to Medina (then called Yathrib), about 200 miles north of Mecca. This migration, called the Hijra, marks the beginning of the Islamic calendar. In Medina, Muhammad's following grew and he became both a religious and political leader.

headings.text: The Prophet Muhammad and the Qur'an

pages.text:
Muhammad and his followers eventually returned to Mecca in 630 CE and took control of the city. By the time of his death in 632 CE, much of the Arabian Peninsula had converted to Islam. The Qur'an, as it exists today, was compiled by Muhammad's followers after his death, based on his recitations and notes.

Originally the Qur'an was written in old, classical Arabic, a Semitic language; different to modern Arabic. This has required much needed explanation and some dispute over the true meanings of a number of surahs. Some expert commentators say the early verses of the Qur'an were appropriate to only the earliest Muslim communities. They go on to say that these beginning surahs were cancelled out or abrogated by Muhammad himself in his later text. Yet other Muslim scholars say no abrogation occurred. There is not a 100% consensus in the Islamic community. As a result, various sects have arisen over these and other differences.

Islamic Sects

Islamic sects are several. Sunni (85%) and Shia (10%) are the main two. Their differences go back to disagreement about the Caliphate succession following the death of Muhammad. There are also variants on Sunni and Shia, such as:

Wahhabi, Ibadi, Sufi, Salafi, Ahmadi, Alawite, Kalam, Ash'ari, Maturidi, Jahmis and Hizmet.

Sufism

Sufism is a little different in that it is a form of mystical Islam which goes back to the 8th century. Some claim it is not exclusively Islamic. There are thought to be millions of Muslim Sufi today, although they can be at base Sunni or Shia Muslims. Sufi believe in recitation and chanting to achieve a form of ecstasy so that the word of God is more easily assimilated. They think there is a network of saints who act as teachers to pass on divine knowledge to Sufi followers. Sufi have questioned the rituals and strict theology of orthodox Islam. This may explain why some Muslims believe Sufi not to be truly Islamic. Sufi followers have even been killed because of this. Saudi Arabia has prohibited Sufi books and punished those caught practicing Sufism. Some Muslim influencers' dislike of Sufism may have led to the rise of Wahhabi and Salafi Islamic sects. These two are similar.

[Figure: The Kaaba in Mecca, the focus of Muslim pilgrimage (photograph, c.1910)]

Wahhabi and Salafi

Wahhabi and Salafi are more rigid and traditional than other sects, especially Sufism, and can advocate jihadi (holy war) violence. Wahhabism has a powerful base in Saudi Arabia and has been exported from there in recent times to other countries by use of Saudis' vast oil-based wealth.

Muslim Clergy, or not

Islam is unlike Christianity in that it does not have clergy and a church. This can make it difficult to find an authoritative doctrinal interpretation. It also means it is awkward for Governments who may want to discuss issues, especially connected to terrorism. Islam has people called Imams, but these are not the equivalent of Priests or Vicars. They are simply teachers and Mosque leaders at prayer. There are also Mullahs, an honorific title given to someone who acts as a teacher and judge with expertise in Muslim law, more of a Professor of religion than a priest. Ulama are a type of Mullah who are highly trained and acknowledged interpreters of the Qur'an. An Ayatollah is a high-ranking Iranian Shia Muslim. He is an expert in Islamic law and the Qur'an.

Women in Islam

Historically, Muslim women have not been treated as men's equals. Some Islamic scholars have justified this by their interpretation of the Qur'an and example from the life of Muhammad. He had an estimated 15 wives and 4 concubines in his lifetime. The Qur'an allows Muslim men to have up to 4 wives, but Muslims can also make use of slaves, from conquered non-believers. The Qur'an has been used to justify this practice in recent times. Isis, was a proponent of sex slavery. This organisation was a violent, extreme Muslim movement that gained territory by force of arms in parts of Syria and Iraq from 2014 before its final defeat in April 2019. It was classified as a terrorist organisation by the United Nations. Isis treated thousands of Yazidi and Iraqi women as sex slaves. Yazidi and other captured men were routinely butchered. Sometimes this was done by beheading, which was deliberately caught on camera.

[Figure: The Blue Mosque, Istanbul, built under Sultan Ahmed I, 1609 to 1616 CE]

Traditional Islamic Rules for Women

Traditionally, there are a number of Islamic rules and customs that treat women differently from men:

Increasingly, in recent times, the role and treatment of women has come under scrutiny in some Muslim societies. In early 2018, there was a limited movement by Iranian women against wearing the headscarf. In the twenty-first century the issue of women's involvement in leading the salat - prayers, has been debated but there is a long way to go here. In the Islamic religious establishment female Imams (prayer leaders) are rarer than Erasmus' white crows.

Sharia Law and Modern Society

Most discussion and dispute concerning women arises over Sharia laws to do with marriage and divorce. Sharia law presents another and a more fundamental problem: what is its role in secular societies? Many such societies, mostly western, have large Muslim populations, but they also have a secular based legal system. These legal systems are likely to have been honed over centuries and at base have international commonalities and acceptance. All this debate has resulted in the slow emergence of a form of Islamic feminism.

LGBT and Islam

In early 2019 the Sultan of Brunei fully adopted the draconian version of Sharia law. This meant those found guilty of gay sex would be stoned to death. The penal code also allows the removal of a hand and foot for those guilty of theft. LGBT people are subject to discrimination and potential maltreatment in many Muslim dominated countries. This is the complete antithesis of the more liberal views and laws encouraged by the United Nations. In September 2015, 12 United Nations organisations issued a joint statement that called for an end to violence and discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex people. It asked its member states to repeal any discriminatory laws that they had.

The attempt to teach children something about LGBT in some areas with large Muslim population in England had caused public mass protests and even threats against teachers. In April 2019, the English Education Secretary, Damian Hinds, wrote to all school heads saying the policy of educating children about LGBT was to help children leave school "prepared for life in modern, diverse Britain." He left it to schools to consult locally and decide age-appropriate level for this type of teaching. The Muslim Council of Britain has moved a little to give women a more equal say. It recognised that women must be given a greater role in Mosques by setting up the 'Women in Mosques Development Programme' in 2019. They also bravely elected their first women leader, Zara Mohammed in January 2021.

Violence in the Name of Islam

As a religion Islam has a unique claim to prominence in the early years of the 21st century. In recent times it is by far and away the religion that most inspires both individual and group terrorists' attacks in its name. Every other main-stream religion does not get anywhere near Islam in this regard. Even if the death and injury caused by all other religious extremists are added together, Islam still tops the pile by a very big margin.

Terrorism

headings.text: Violence in the Name of Islam

pages.text:
In the 10 years or so since 2010, there have been over 100 terrorist incidents around the world supposedly associated with Islam. The terrorists do not think of themselves as terrorists. They believe they carry out Allah's will. They conduct their killings and woundings of innocent men, women and children in the name of Islam, or rather, in support of their version of Islam. Sometimes these terrorists shout "Allahu Akbar" (God is greatest) when carrying out their mayhem.

More than 40 countries have suffered from terrorist attacks in the last 15 years, these include: Afghanistan; Australia; Bangladesh; Belgium; Bosnia; Burkina Faso; Cameroon; Chad; China; Denmark; Egypt; Finland; France; Germany; Great Britain; India; Indonesia; Iraq; Iran; Israel; Ivory Coast; Jordan; Kenya; Lebanon; Libya; Mali; Morocco; Netherlands; Niger; Nigeria; Norway; Pakistan; Philippines; Russia; Tajikistan; Saudi Arabia; Somalia; Spain; Sri Lanka; Sweden; Syria; Turkey; Tunisia; United Arab Emirates; USA; Yemen.

China is so concerned about the perceived threat from its Uighur, Muslim, population that it has created nearly 400 what it calls 're-education camps' from 2018 to 2020. This to 'educate' people to give up on Islam and accept the strictures of the Communist Party. Over one million Uighurs are said to have been in such camps. Many people thought this was wrong. In August 2018 the United Nations called upon China to free Uighurs from these camps. China said Xinjiang, the province containing Uighurs, faced a serious threat from Islamic militants. It rejected criticism of its policies.

Many Islamist inspired attacks are anti-western in nature or anti-anything not Muslim. Christians have been deliberately targeted and killed, with hundreds of Coptic Christians murdered in Egypt in the 10 years up to 2018. Indonesia saw 202 people, mainly tourists, killed in bombings by Jemaah Islamiyah, a radical Islamist group. At the Christian Easter festival in April 2019, a local Sri Lankan Islamic terrorist group, National Thowheed Jamath, carried out simultaneous deadly assaults on Christian churches and top-class hotels. Westerners frequented the latter. More than 250 people were killed and more than 500 injured in these attacks.

In October 2020, the beheading of a history teacher in Paris, by an Islamist terrorist, caused a widespread outcry in France. This was seen as an attack on entrenched French values, particularly freedom of expression. President Macron called the victim, Samuel Paty, "The Quiet hero."

Sectarian Violence

Quite a few attacks though are by one Muslim sect against another. Sunni Muslims against Shias, and vice-versa. Sufi Muslims have also been killed as not true Muslims. More than 30,000 people have died in Iraq 2014 to 2017, mainly because of sectarian violence between Sunni Muslims and the Shia majority. Isis Sunni Muslims have conducted most killings. Sufi Muslims have been targeted in Pakistan, which has a large Sunni majority. 64 Sufi were killed in 2010. The 4 million Pakistani members of the Islamic Ahmadi sect have been officially declared non-Muslim. Muslim gay rights activists in Bangladesh have been killed.

Some attacks are by disaffected individuals, others by those claiming allegiance to a group such as Isis; The Taliban; Al-Shabab; Al-Qaeda; Boko Haram, Jemaah Islamiyah, Al Muhajiroun and Hezbollah. These are the principal groups but there are others. The teaching of a particularly conservative branch of Islam, Wahhabism, has been associated with many attacks. In July 2013, the European Parliament in Strasbourg identified Wahhabism as the main source of global terrorism.

Conflicts at National Level

[Figure: The Twin Towers, New York, 11 September 2001]

Excluding the 2001, 9/11 attacks on the USA, which killed 3,000 people, these forms of terrorism are relatively small-scale, but there have been national conflicts too involving Islam.

From the time of the Crusades at least, nations have engaged in forms of religious warfare that involves Islam. Islam could either be on one or both sides of these international conflicts. In the latter part of the 20th century several Muslim Middle-Eastern countries have had wars with Israel. These have already been described. Then there've been the various wars between western nations with Iraq, Afghanistan, Syria, Libya and Tunisia. These have generally been called non-religious. Western nations, usually led by the USA have tried to engage in regime change. They are likely to have encouraged some radical Muslims to respond in the form of what is usually described as terrorist attacks.

At a national level, Islamic countries have often vied violently with each other. A common religion and common reverence for the Qur'an has not stopped Muslims killing other Muslims on a large scale. From 1362 CE the Turkish Ottoman Empire conquered, by force of arms, many Muslim countries in the Middle East and beyond. In defeating non-Muslim populations, it cleverly used the sword only to gain the initial upper hand. Conversion of the conquered populaces to Islam followed by a subtle process, mostly involving the offer of advantage. There was one major exception to Ottoman conversion subtlety - Armenia. In the first World War, conquest of Armenia, from 1915, an estimated 1.5 million Armenians, mainly Christians, were systematically exterminated. This was a deliberate act of genocide. The Turkish government of about 2010-2020 disputes the figures. In any event such massacres ended when the Ottoman Empire finally came to a close during the course of World War 1.

Iraq was at war with both Iran and Kuwait during the 1980 to 1988 conflict. At the time Saudi Arabia supported Iraq. Iran is mainly Shia Muslim, while Saudi Arabia is principally Sunni. These two Islamic nations have engaged in proxy warfare in Yemen and Syria for at least 4 years from 2015. By the end of 2018 many thousands of Yemeni Muslims had died, a growing number as an indirect result of a foreign backed civil war. The BBC estimated 85,000 Yemeni children under age 5 had died of starvation. This far exceeds the estimated 60,000 killed directly as a result of the conflict.

By far the worst most recent conflict in the Middle East is the continuing complex civil war in Syria. The Syrian Assad regime is backed by Russia and Iran. Opposing forces consist of several different groups, including Isis and Kurdish forces. Initially, anti-government rebel forces were supported by the USA, Saudi Arabia and some other Middle-Eastern nations. A major group emerged, Isis, which had carried out several terrorist attacks in Syria and Iraq and against western nations.

The USA, particularly, with some support from France and Great Britain, have carried out many air attacks on Isis, first in Iraq and then in Syria. Isis had carried out a number of gruesome beheadings of westerners in Iraq and Syria. Turkey has been targeting Kurdish groups in Syria. The continuing factional war in Syria has been a disaster for the country. An estimated 400,000 people have died, with over 5 million fleeing the country as refugees. A further 6.5 million have been displaced internally.

The Kurdish Question

The Kurds, who are mainly Sunni Muslims, have been attempting to establish their own autonomous region, cutting across Iraqi, Iranian, Syrian and Turkish borders. An estimated 36 million Kurds live in these countries. This attempt to establish a new Kurdish nation has resulted in further conflict and many deaths. More than 3,000 Kurds, Iranians, Iraqis, Syrians and Turks have died 2015 to 2017. All were Muslims.

Muslim dominated countries appear to find it hard to get on with each other. Dispute at a level below that of outright war is a feature of their relationships. Such clashes have involved most Middle-Eastern nations. Apart from those already mentioned, this includes smaller Gulf States like Qatar, the U.A.E., Bahrain and Kuwait.

In 2017, the UK Labour Party leader, Jeremy Corbyn, said that the UK policy of regime change in Syria, Iraq and Libya had destroyed state authority and provided sanctuaries for al-Qaeda and Isis. The biggest player in the regime change aims was the USA.

Western nations cannot claim any moral superiority in the context of conflict between nations with similar religions. World Wars one and two were massive clashes between allegedly Christian nations, millions died. England, a primarily Christian nation, has been at war, on and off, with one or other European nation, all Christian of one type or another, for many centuries past. It is only in the last seventy or so years that there's been relative peace, some conflict in the Balkans aside after the break-up of Yugoslavia.

Islam and Terrorism in Great Britain

Let's take a look at what impact and reaction there has been to Islamic terrorist action in one country, Great Britain. There are around 2.8 million Muslims in Great Britain, representing about 4% of the population. Many were born in GB. Most have originated from countries of the old British Empire.

In 2017 Great Britain suffered more Islamic inspired terrorist attacks than any other country in Europe. In three attacks 35 people were killed. These were part of the near 90 deaths from Islamic terrorism since 2005 up to 2018.

Three Major Attacks

Three of the biggest attacks in this 13-year period were:

1. July 2005, London Underground and bus attacks: 50 people killed, hundreds injured. Four people aged 30 to 18 carried the attacks using rucksacks full of explosives. Their leader, Mohammed Khan, posted a video before the attacks praising Al-Qaeda and founder Osama Bin Laden.

headings.text: Islam and Terrorism in Great Britain

pages.text:
2. March 2017, Westminster Bridge attack: Lone wolf Khalid Masood, a 52-year-old Muslim convert, drove a van deliberately at people and then used a knife to kill a policeman. Three people were killed and 29 injured. Masood was born Adrian Elms. He was said to be intelligent and popular at school but as an adult, he bitterly complained to his mother about his childhood. He had life chances, was married with two children and had several jobs, one as a teacher of English to foreign students. Throughout his life he was prone to rage and violence. This led to several convictions. He became a Muslim convert and was radicalised, probably by members of the Al Muhajiroun terror group, when serving a term in prison.

3. May 2017, Manchester Arena suicide bombing: 23 people died, including an 8-year-old girl, and 800 were injured. Salman Abedi, a 22-year-old Muslim, carried out the attack. Abedi was born in Manchester. His parents were highly religious, deeply conservative Muslim refugees from Libya. They had been members of the Libyan Islamic Fighting Group. The UN Security Council said this group had links to Al-Qaeda. Abedi had dropped out of Salford University and did not seem to have joined clubs or organisations. Abedi had made trips back to Libya and is thought to have gone to Syria. His backpack bomb was quite sophisticated. He may have come into contact with Abd Azzouz, an expert bomb maker. Azzouz lived near Abedi's family in Manchester and was accused of running an Al-Qaeda network. Abedi's sister, Jamona, said she thought Abedi had become angry at the American bombing of Syria and wanted revenge. Isis claimed that the Manchester bombing had been carried out by one of its soldiers. An eleven-year-old Muslim girl, Sara Hussein, spoke out movingly against this attack. She said that she wished she had a time machine so she could go back and explain to Abedi how wrong he was. In August 2020 Abedi's brother, Hashem, was jailed for 55 years for his part in the bombing.

Muslim Council of Britain Response

[Figure: Muslim Council of Britain logo]

Muslim Council of Britain: In response to the killings in Britain various Imams (Mosque leaders) and Islamic organisations have said that Islam is a religion of peace. Before the horror of 2017, the year 2016 saw the Muslim Council of Britain and other Islamic organisations hold The London Conference on Islam and World Peace.

The conference made these statements:

WHEREAS Muslims strongly believe, as emphasised by the Qur'an, that Islam is a religion of peace (Q2:208), that Allah (God) invites to peace (Q10:25) and that Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was sent by God as a messenger of peace and mercy to the world and to all humanity (Q21:107); and

WHEREAS life is the greatest treasure and gift of God to humanity and that Islam emphasises the sanctity of life (Q5:32), prohibits mischief and disorder on earth (Q7:56), and enjoins justice and kindness to all (Q16:90);

CONSIDERING the lack of global peace today and that different parts of the world, especially Muslim-majority countries, are afflicted with serious conflicts and warfare that have adversely affected the lives of millions of innocent people, including women and young children and that there have been many unjustified wars and acts of aggression perpetuated by both state and non-state actors against innocent people in different parts of the world in the last century and still continuing in this century;

CONSIDERING that some Muslim-majority countries have been confronted by conflict and warfare for so long that young children and adolescent youths in those countries have not known anything in their lifetime except a life surrounded by warfare and wanton destruction of life and property

After all the good points made in the "whereas" and "considerings" some of the things this conference concluded was: "Islam is a religion of submission to God, service to humanity and promotion of peace and human welfare." Another main conclusion stated: "While the Qur'an states that Islam is the religion brought by all the Prophets sent by God to humanity and therefore the religion recognised by Him, it also acknowledges the freedom of everyone to follow their own convictions. Q2:256 clearly states that there is no compulsion in religion."

The Prevent Strategy

Ten years before The London Conference on Islam and World Peace came The British Government's 2006 Prevent Strategy. This has three main aims:

[Figure: Book cover: The Enemy Within - A Tale of Muslim Britain by Sayeeda Warsi]

Baroness Sayeeda Warsi: The government's Prevent Strategy was strongly challenged by Baroness Sayeeda Warsi, a former British Cabinet Minister. In her 2017 book "The Enemy Within". She said: "There are far more Muslim doctors in Britain than terrorists, yet the community is not defined by the reputation of its daily life-savers, it's defined by the reputation of ad hoc life-takers." She also argued that Muslims are killing many more Muslims in Muslim countries than they are killing Brits. These points could be interpreted, probably unintentionally, suggesting that just a few deaths in Britain by people claiming to be Muslims are not too bad and they are no reason to view all Muslims in a negative light.

It is certainly fair to say the many should not be defined by the few, but a few deaths do matter, especially to the family and friends of those killed and injured. It also does not help the argument that Islam is a religion of peace by pointing out that Muslims are killing many more Muslims abroad than they are people in Britain.

She also said the intelligence services needed to look at factors other than ideology as to why some Muslims were prepared to kill the innocent. This is a reasonable point; all underlying factors do need to be examined, such things like: degree of inclusiveness; victimisation/unfairness in the workplace; and everything that stems from hardened Islamophobia - this includes a tendency to encourage ghettoisation.

Terrorists' Motivation

It is sometimes claimed that the terrorists were so because they were disturbed, unsuccessful people. Masood (of the Westminster Bridge attacks) had a distinct violent streak. It may be one motivating factor behind his action, but it's probably not the only one. It was after his conversion to Islam that he turned to random murder for the first time. It's certainly the case that terrorists were disturbed people in some way. However, there are many, many people who are not Muslims who might be classed as disturbed or who have a grievance with either their life, Government or society generally. They are not the source of fairly regular deadly attacks.

The common factor in the attacks, internationally and in Great Britain, is the religion Islam.

In the case of the Manchester bombing, the perpetrator, Abedi, had no apparent reason to be disgruntled. He had life chances in Britain. After fleeing from Libya, he was picked up from the sea by a British warship, then given asylum with his family in Britain. He had a home and was given the chance of higher education at Salford University (he dropped out). Indications are that his strong, particular, Muslim beliefs made him think killing innocent, non-Muslim Mancunians was the right thing to do.

Why do some Muslims believe they should carry out attacks against non-Muslims? It appears they have been radicalised so to believe this is what Allah wishes. Abedi seemingly thought so. It looks likely that a number of Muslim terrorists follow the instruction of Qur'an 9:5 "fight and slay the Pagans wherever ye find them" and Qur'an 47:4. "So, when you meet those who disbelieve, smite at their necks till when you have killed and wounded many of them, then bind a bond firmly." There is also the apparent promise of paradise for the killer, with 72 virgins to enjoy. This is not mentioned in the Qur'an but is referred to in a hadith by Ibn Kathir in the 14th century: "The Prophet Mohammed was heard saying that the smallest reward for the people of paradise (meaning of course only men) is an abode where there are 80,000 servants and 72 wives, over which stands a dome decorated with pearls, aquamarine, and ruby...." Do the virgins get any say in this arrangement and what are that many servants going to do all day? Who are the servants any way? Is this arrangement fair to women and the servants?

Integration and Muslims

Integration and Muslims: Baroness Warsi said, with some justification, that integration in Britain is a middle-class pastime. It can be argued that a form of integration - beginning with acceptance of common values - must be aimed for, no matter how difficult. This could have at its core those issues that Baroness Warsi has encouraged Muslims to consider.

She said Muslims should not follow rigid, conservative views saying: "You're not a terrorist, but are you fit for purpose? That includes everything from their attitude to women, minorities, LGBT communities, education, and the child exploitation issue."

Integration goes well beyond this of course. It's a two-way process. Muslims should have equal opportunities in the jobs market, education and all other spheres of activity. They need to have fair representation at every level of local and national government. On their part Muslims should fully accept and support democratic, secular, government; the supremacy of English/Scottish law; equality for both women and the LGBT community. In addition, they must accept, without hindrance, those with other or no beliefs.

The Role of Education

Education is a key factor in encouraging an integrated society. All pupils should be taught in non-religious schools. Any religious education must include all major belief systems, including secularism and humanism. Evolution has to be taught, creationism can be mentioned, but not as a truth. Teaching equality of race, gender, religion and age would be an essential element of schools' curriculum, in all schools.

[Figure: Diagram showing interconnected concepts: Faiths, Gender, Sexual Orientation, Secularism, Free speech, Atheists Humanists, Age, Politics - all connected around "Secularism" in the center]

For integration to work there needs to be much more "joining in". Smaller communities, like Muslims, should be able to freely retain their own unique identity and be able to freely engage in cultural and religious activities, such as attending their local mosque or taking part in Ramadan. At the same time, it would help if minorities took a greater part in the common national pastimes of the country they live in, for example gardening and popular sports. How about many more Muslim women playing football and rugby, two very British sporting activities? Instead of headscarves they could wear head bands or scrum caps and long shorts and socks.

Final Thoughts

Islam, like Judaism and Christianity, is one of the great Abrahamic faiths that has shaped world history and continues to influence billions of people today. It is a religion with a rich intellectual tradition, beautiful art and architecture, and has contributed significantly to human knowledge in fields such as mathematics, astronomy, medicine, and philosophy during its golden age.

However, like all religions, Islam faces challenges in the modern world. The tension between traditional interpretations and contemporary values, particularly regarding women's rights, LGBT rights, and secular governance, remains a significant issue. The problem of violence carried out in Islam's name, whether through terrorism or sectarian conflict, is undeniable and requires honest examination and action from both Muslim communities and wider society.

The vast majority of Muslims worldwide are peaceful people who wish to live in harmony with others. The challenge for the 21st century is how to preserve religious and cultural identity while embracing universal human rights, how to maintain faith traditions while accepting secular pluralism, and how to build bridges of understanding in an increasingly interconnected world.

Integration, education, mutual respect, and open dialogue offer the best path forward. Muslims should be able to practice their faith freely while also accepting the principles of democracy, equality, and human rights. Non-Muslims need to combat prejudice and Islamophobia while also being willing to have honest conversations about difficult issues. Only through such mutual effort can we build societies where people of all faiths and none can live together in peace and prosperity.

Chapter 20

The 4 Horsemen of new Atheism - plus 1 Horsewoman?

[Figure: The 4 Horsemen (Durer, 1498), plus 1]

This is a reference to four successful authors and debaters whose works really took off not long after the devastating attacks called '9/11'. These took place in 2001 in the USA. Nearly 3,000 people were killed.

Their works might, just might, be the slow burning fuse setting off a religious apocalypse, but it's clear that religion is far from coming to an end yet, if ever. The 4 set out their criticism of religion and, powerfully articulated the case for atheism, or very thin agnosticism, in these books, among others:

Richard Dawkins - "The God Delusion";
Daniel Dennett - "Breaking the Spell";
Sam Harris - "The End of Faith, Letter to a Christian Nation";
Christopher Hitchens - "God is not Great".

Since these 4 came to prominence, Susan Blackmore, with her ideas on consciousness, and memes might be added, as a horsewoman of atheism.

Richard Dawkins

[Figure: Photo of Richard Dawkins]

Richard is an evolutionary biologist and a very successful author. He was Oxford University's Professor for Public Understanding of Science for thirteen years, from 1995 to 2008. He has won a number of awards. His main claim to fame though comes from his books which attack religious belief. These have been the subject of films and TV programmes. The main point he makes is that there is no evidence supporting any form of religious belief. He particularly has it in for religious extremists: "Religious fanatics want people to switch off their own minds, ignore the evidence, and blindly follow a holy book based upon private 'revelation'."

Of many penetrating observations by Richard is: "one of the truly bad effects of religion is that it teaches us that it is a virtue to be satisfied with not understanding." and, "It's a tragedy that people are being actively led astray by medieval or pre-medieval superstitions and bronze age myths written down more than 2,000 years ago." About the Bible, he points out one of the blatant mistakes, concerning the Catholic Church's claims of Jesus resulting from a virgin birth. Richard says this is simply wrong.

It's because of a mis-translation from Isaiah into Matthew. The original Hebrew referred to "young woman" but it was translated into the Greek word for "virgin". In his 1996 book, "The Blind Watchmaker", he argues forcefully against the 'intelligent design' claimed proof of a God. Evolution, selection and mutation are not something that is guided by a supernatural being according to Richard. He pointed out that Charles Darwin, in 1859, explained natural selection was the process by which all life evolved. See TED 2002, Militant Atheism, here he talks about Creationism as opposed to evolution. His best seller: "The Selfish Gene" adds more support to Darwin and introduces the 'meme', an ideas replicator.

Richard's later, 2006 book, 'The God Delusion' takes a big swipe at more attempted proofs of God's existence. There are six main points by way of explaining his arguments against the attempted proofs of God's existence:

Throughout time, it has been hard to explain why everything looks like it has been designed by a designer.
It's a natural urge to say a designer made everything.
Ultimately a designer causes more problems, especially because who designed the designer?
Natural selection is that problem solving theory. Creationism is a trick.
We cannot fully explain how everything got here.
Just as it took scientists time to discover Natural Selection, it will also take time to discover where everything came from and the weak theories we have now are at least better than anything a theist has ever produced or will produce.

His astutely framed logic offers serious refutation of Godly existence.

Richard gave an example of the possible range of beliefs on a scale 1 to 7. Here, 1 (one) would be for those who have absolute, certain sure belief and 7 complete non-belief. He has been careful to explain that he is not quite an atheist, saying he was at 6 on his 1 to 7 scale. This 6 score, he said, represented for him the very low possibility a God existed, to the same extent of his belief there are fairies and unicorns. Richard is a wafer-thin agnostic then! He explained his belief was passionate, rather than fundamentalist. In a 2007 entry on his website headed: "How dare you call me a fundamentalist", Richard wrote: "No, please, do not mistake passion, which can change its mind, for fundamentalism, which never will. Passion for passion, an evangelical Christian and I may be evenly matched. But we are not equally fundamentalist. The true scientist, however passionately he may 'believe', in evolution for example, knows exactly what would change his mind: evidence! The fundamentalist knows that nothing will!" His general stance against all religion is summed up by his comment: "Religion is a virus of the mind."

Daniel Dennett

[Figure: Daniel Dennett (1942 to 2024)]

Dan's specialist areas were: philosophy of science, philosophy of mind and philosophy of biology. He was an atheist and secularist. Like Richard Dawkins, he too was associated with Oxford University. After studying under Gilbert Ryle, he received his Doctor of Philosophy there in 1965. Again, like Richard, he was given numerous awards.

His book "Breaking the Spell" sets out a cogent argument that religious belief is a natural phenomenon. That's because it has had an evolutionary advantage and it is a part of the human psyche to lean towards some form of supernatural belief. He credited the work of anthropologists Pascal Boyer and Scott Atran. These demonstrate the human tendency to believe in spirits and ghosts. Dan clearly expressed his views on religion and the unfounded sureness of its chief proponents: "I for one am not in awe of your faith. I am appalled by your arrogance, by your unreasoning certainty that you have all the answers." and, "I am confident that those who believe in belief are wrong. That is, we no more need to preserve the myth of God in order to preserve a just and stable society than we need to cling to the Gold Standard to keep our currency sound." What Dan was saying here is relevant to all religions and societies throughout history. States of all persuasions have used religion a device to keep people in check. He also said religions are natural phenomena, re-designed by humans over thousands of years. View his TED talk, TED2006, "Let's teach religion, all religion, in schools." Just teach facts, not values, he said. His talk was basically about the key role of evolution in refuting the claim of Intelligent Design.

pages.text:
In "Darwin's Dangerous Ideas" Dan said: "I think Darwin's idea of natural selection is the best idea anybody ever had." In addition, argued that evolution can account for the origin of morality. He co-authored a book in 2013 with Linda La Scola: "Caught in the Pulpit: Leaving Belief Behind". This was based on fascinating research into clerics who were actually atheists in secret. These clerics kept their jobs on the basis that they were doing some good by providing the comfort that religion can bring to people. They also had a non-altruistic attachment to their jobs, with the finance, homes and security that their church provided.

Dan accepted that people can gain from religious beliefs, whether or not their beliefs are mistaken. He wrote: "I have known people whose lives would be desolate and friendless if it weren't for the non-judgmental welcome they have received in one religious organisation or another."

Sam Harris

[Figure: Photo of Sam Harris]

Here's the third horseman. Sam's major tome is: "The End of Faith, Letter to a Christian Nation". He's an American neuroscientist and philosopher. His trenchant criticism of religion can be gleaned from some of these things he's said: "The problem with faith, is that it really is a conversation stopper. Faith is a declaration of immunity to the powers of conversation. It is a reason, why you do not have to give reasons, for what you believe." He added: "We have names for people who have many beliefs for which there is no rational justification. When their beliefs are extremely common we call them 'religious'; otherwise, they are likely to be called 'mad', 'psychotic' or 'delusional'...... Clearly there is sanity in numbers. And yet, it is merely an accident of history that it is considered normal in our society to believe that the Creator of the universe can hear your thoughts, while it is demonstrative of mental illness to believe that he is communicating with you by having the rain tap in Morse Code on your bedroom window. And so, while religious people are not generally mad, their core beliefs absolutely are."

Christopher Hitchens

[Figure: Christopher Hitchens (1949 to 2011)]

This determined, and fiercely combative atheist wrote an international best-seller: "God is Not Great". In which he claimed religion poisons everything. Curiously, he was respected by some believers. As he was suffering from terminal cancer, an informal group promoted "Everybody pray for Hitchens day". Not unexpectedly, the prayers were insufficient because Christopher died of cancer related pneumonia in December 2011.

His personality, wit and debating expertise made him a favourite for media interviews and TV. Some quotes that encapsulate his anti-religious stance: "To terrify children with the image of hell, to consider women an inferior creation - is that good for the world?" "Owners of dogs will have noticed that, if you provide them with food and water and shelter and affection, they will think you are God. Whereas owners of cats are compelled to realize that, if you provide them with food and water and shelter and affection, they draw the conclusion that they are Gods." "Human decency is not derived from religion. It precedes it." and finally: "Many religions now come before us with ingratiating smirks and outspread hands, like an unctuous merchant in a bazaar. They offer consolation and solidarity and uplift, competing as they do in a marketplace. But we have a right to remember how barbarically they behaved when they were strong and were making an offer that people could not refuse." Maybe a little bit unfair this last about the gentle souls of the TDF crowd - see chapter 22.

Susan Blackmore

[Figure: Photo of Susan Blackmore]

Prof. Sue Blackmore is a freelance writer, lecturer and broadcaster. She is an atheist with a keen interest in the mind, consciousness and memetics - the theory of memes. Following up on Richard Dawkins concept of memes her several books include 'The Meme Machine'. A meme she describes as "that which is imitated", or "information that is copied". Further explaining that at the base of human evolution there are two replicators on the planet: 1. Genes; 2. Memes. She adds a new, third replicator, the "teme", something that propagates via new technology.

Just as the 4 horsemen, Sue is a great admirer of Charles Darwin and his Genesis-shattering discovery - evolution. The evolutionary algorithm she explained, as have others: "If you have variation, selection and heredity then you must get evolution." Her key word is "must". As with the 4 horsemen, there is no mention by Sue of a God's involvement in this process. In an interview by Robert Kuhn she said: "I couldn't find any evidence of life after death." And, "...certain things won't work. You know, inventing spirits and souls." (see the 5 W's analysis of souls in Chapter 18a)

She has interesting, and somewhat original views of self, free will and consciousness: "Actions do exist and also their consequences, but the person who acts does not." - see YouTube, August 2017. Jordan Peterson, God supporter, who said the Bible, was a route for fallen humanity, engaged in debate with Sue in the Big Conversation, June 2018. Sue appeared more credible, and relaxed than the author of "Twelve Rules for Life". Jordan's best seller includes the charming Rule 12, "Pet a cat when you encounter one on the street." Yes indeed, but to avoid alienating canine supporters, and his daughter Mikhaila, let alone Sikko, his loved, clever dog, Jordan sensibly does include the petting of dogs.

Chapter 21

Design a God

If there is a Supreme Deity, a God of the sort described in Abrahamic religions, many would say He does not operate in quite the way many would wish. HE has been much too laissez-faire for most peoples liking. What's he done about all the bad things that have happened in the past and continue to occur? Nothing identifiable is the answer. Think of human history, the many, many wars, their associated destruction and wasted lives. Then there's the disasters; disease; poverty; famine; repression; fear; brutal treatment; inequality and restricted freedom? A number of these harmful occurrences are the result of mistreatment by some humans of other humans, although the vagaries of climate, plate tectonics, cosmology, micro-organisms and accidents play their part too. And while we are listing all the bads of life, we should remember that humans have not only quite often made life miserable for their fellow kind, they've also had a detrimental effect on the planet, through relentless exploitation of all its resources including other inhabitants. We've also managed to speed up Climate Change. Rapid global warming is causing more problems for humankind.

[Figure: The plague of boils, Toggenburg Bible, 1411 (often used to picture the Black Death)]

Just two of the diseases that have left a big, adverse, mark on humanity are the Black Death of the 14th century and much more recently the Coronavirus, COVID 19.

In the 14th century the Black Death killed 50 million people, 60% of Europe's population, and possibly 200 million worldwide. COVID 19 virus caused havoc the world over in 2020 but actual deaths were nowhere near that of its Black Death predecessor 600 years earlier.

[Figure: Illustration of the coronavirus (SARS-CoV-2) particle, with its crown of spike proteins]

Up to January 2021 COVID 19 deaths worldwide were about 2.5 million. That is only 1.25% of the Black Death total.

To sum up, there's been a never-ending litany of events, and personal circumstances, which have resulted in so much despair; so many painful, early deaths and too many miserable, tragic and sometimes very short human existences.

Though, to be fair, it's by no means all been bad. Lots of people have led interesting, happy, long and fulfilling lives. Even these, and those people who might be considered the fortunate ones: the relatively rich; the healthy, the successful and contented have not got away scot-free. No one goes through life without problems at some stage. At the very least, the process of dying, or of some loved one dying, is generally considered to be an unwanted experience. But we all die.

Where has the traditional God been when all this nastiness has been going on? If he did set up the universe and if He created and loves humans as most mainstream religions claim why hasn't he made life much easier for everyone?

Theologians and devout religious people often say that "We cannot know God's will", in answer to His failure to prevent dreadful occurrences. This assumes that no matter what happens it will all be for the best in the long term. Such an approach is not helpful in many circumstances. Tell the "God's will" argument to a mother who has to watch helpless as her much loved child dies slowly of some fatal disease; perhaps in pain and debilitated for years before the final moment comes. Only the blinkered, extreme religious devout, can thank God in these circumstances.

We can confidently say our traditional God is most notable by His absence from the lives of men and women when they are most in need of Him.

Another thing, He is also far too serious. He lacks a sense of humour and lightness of touch. HE never sees the funny side. Laughter completely eludes him; despite he designed us, purportedly, and should be aware of its importance to humans.

Of course, all this presupposes that there is in fact some sort of God. It may be, though that He exists purely as a thought in a human brain - a stream of elementary particles, faintly flickering among the neural pathways of religious people. That certainly explains why He is so insubstantial and uninvolved. - just a thought!

So, if any current God is not much cop, why don't we have a new one? Is this possible? - well yes, it is, sort of, maybe.

What do we want from our new God? If we are to have a different deity, ideally, we want one who is considerably more active and sympathetic than the traditional monotheistic one, HE needs to be a super-being who will ensure nasty things do not happen; to anyone, ever.

Designing Our New God

Humans will be slightly re-designed so that their natural state is a tendency to adhere to these laws.

The new God will head up a new religion, with all the best traditional trimmings to keep humans intrigued and amused. There will be interesting rituals and rites to pursue. These will be designed to be more enjoyable and entertaining than those of any current religion. Humans find it essential to their religious belief to engage in some form of ritual, often associated with eating or not eating some sort of food', like eating fish on a Friday, or not eating pork - ever. Then there must be some designated special days, perhaps with dressing up parades or giving/receiving presents and general jolly making. To allow humans to feel comfortable with their newly designed God a specific food ritual will be made desirable, but not compulsory. It will be a requirement to eat peanut butter on toast for breakfast every Monday. This will be no problem for those who like peanut butter. For those that don't, it will be just one more thing to endure on an already disliked day of the week, Monday. And once Monday is over, all can be rosier for the rest of the week. In fact, our new God will ensure that this is so.

We will also establish a specific Godly emblem. This will be a circlet of carrots and butterflies on a star shaped greenery background. The emblem will emphasise our new God's environmental stance and healthy eating credentials. We will have feasting and drinking at celebratory days mid-winter and mid-summer. This will allow people plenty of time to recover in between and give them something to look forward to. These summer and winner festivities will provide the retail trade and entertainments industry a boost.

On God's side of the contract humans will be made bullet proof against serious diseases, accidents and all other unpleasant events. The average length of a very happy life will be 150 years. Death will become a truly comfortable, transitional, going-away-on-an-endless-holiday type experience. All defunct bodies will be composted and used to grow carrots and greens. These vegetables will help humans see the light and be in keeping with the Godly emblem. However, on the right side of the line humans will still retain what they think of as free will.

Why can't we have such a Supreme Being who looks after us like this? Well, good news - we can! Like many, many humans before us we can take this basic template and draw up detailed designs for our own God and his buttressing religion. For tens of thousands of years, in fact throughout the whole of human history, man has invented a personal God or more usually, several Gods or Spirits that they feel comfortable with. We've had, and still have, hundreds of different religions. Even within the same religion people have held their own personal idea of who and what their God is. The effect of multiplying each main stream religion by the number of derivations or sects and then again by every adherent's individual take means we have had a myriad of personalised deities. We can continue this well-established trend - set the detailed criteria for a God we want, building on the broad contractual basis listed above. All our ancestors and contemporaries have done this sort of thing. But this time, we can work hard to get it right, with the help of a selected cadre of geniuses, all of them carefully programmed.

The God Commissioning Committee

This bunch of super-people will form a committee - a God Commissioning Committee.

The God Commissioning Committee's aim will be to work up the basic contract into a fully-fledged set of detailed requirements. The possible committee members will be carefully screened to ensure no rigid, narrow-minded extremists make the cut.

The committee will be required to ensure our God is imbued with a full set of attractive attributes that allow Him/Her (androgynous of course) to be a truly thoughtful; kind; benevolent; just; forgiving; comforting and - new feature - amusing deity. He will be a joke cracking, laughing God, that's essential. If He is judged to be too serious or solemn He will be subject to a fine, or up to six months community service. Fun loving will be His compulsory default state. In short, our God will be someone you can occasionally sit down with and enjoy a pint in a pub, a glass of wine in a trendy bistro or even a Cappuccino in Costabucks.

In effect, He will be a God with sufficient capability, attributes and resolve to keep everyone happy; on Earth as well as in heaven.

[Figure: Illustration of the new God demonstrating fun-loving nature, leading people in compulsory two laughs a day]

Incidentally, the type of heaven that individuals desire will be based on their personal choice. All recently departed persons (RDPs for short) will initially float, as a sentient spiritual essence, to a transit station. Here, they will be asked to browse a set of 3D holographic travelogues.

These will espouse the attractions of a variety of heavens. To get the RDP in the right mood Cliff Richard's song "We Are All Going on a Summer Holiday" will play in the background. The angel Ezekiel will offer advice and guidance to every RDP. He will use expertise gained from a months practical training course with a major travel company.

The RDP would choose from the 99 heavens available in the travelogues. These will include all the well-known ones like: the Vikings Valhalla; Buddhists Nirvana: Confucians Tian; Muslims Jennah or Paradise (although virgins will be banned, but Virgin TV and virgin olive oil allowed).

Then there's the Swarga Loka of Hindus and the traditional Christian heaven. The latter would be at the back, in the special offers section. As well as all these there would be lots of others to choose from. After confirming selection, RDPs will be immediately transferred to his/her heaven of choice. Later, to avoid endless tedium, all RDPs will be allowed to have temporary or permanent respite by spending time in alternate heavens to their original choice.

Some RDPs, who had not cut the mustard when pre-RDP, (i.e., despite Godly persuasion, they had been naughty people on Earth) will be automatically moved out of the transit station into the rehab centre. There will be no hell, just a rehabilitation centre that works.

After a suitable re-conditioning period the contrite and spiritually restored RDP will be shunted back from re-hab to transit and given license to choose his/her heaven.

Fred Satan will have a much curtailed and very minor role in human affairs. He will be reduced in rank, and become just an annoying little devil, one who can easily be slapped down.

Let's start the in-depth Godly design process in good old British administrative fashion, with lining up the God Commissioning Committee.

The committee's remit will be to consider the aim and broad requirement already indicated and develop it in more detail. They will be given one year to complete this task. Over the course of this year, with monthly meetings, and input from various sub-groups, our committee will draw up a detailed specification for a God, including his modus operandi. They will also produce an easy-to-read manual, a timetable of religious festivals or special observance days, a list of foods that should or should not be eaten, a dress code and a marketing plan. These would establish him as a serious Deity (not too serious of course. There must always be laughter). The marketing package will get Him and His message across to the whole world.

Once the whole process is put in train, with advertising on prime-time TV, and all media, an ever-increasing number of believers in our God will be recruited. This rising tide of belief will eventually reach Tsunami proportions. The mystic power generated by this mass belief will become so great our God will emerge as a reality - of sorts. Instead of the excessively humble religious maxim "thy will be done" it will be a case of "thy done be willed" (in old English vernacular).

Chapter 22

What else if not Religion?

Religious belief in some countries may be declining. This is certainly so for Christianity in Britain, as indicated by the British Social Attitudes Survey (BSA). Their report in 2013, based on 3,000 people interviewed, showed the following:

50.6% of the population regarded themselves as belonging to no religion in 2013, up from 47.7% in 2012. Only 41.7% defined themselves as Christian and just 16.3% as Anglicans, both lowest ever figures.
This marked decline in religiosity comes despite only 19.1% of respondents in 2013 saying that they had been brought up in a non-religious household
Just 24% of respondents saw Christianity as an important element of national identity in 2013, down from 32% in 1995 and 31% in 2003.
62.4% of the population never attends religious services and meetings, whilst merely 13.1% go once a week or more.

Worldwide, in 2019, the irreligious number between 500 to 750 million, according to sociologist, Phil Zuckerman. Other sociologists, Ariela Keysar and Juhem Navarro-Rivera say there are about 500 million definite atheists and agnostics, with China topping the league at 200 million non-believers. Non-belief appears to be on an upward trend. But maybe there will be a religious resurgence, because of the worry and fear generated by world-wide pandemics, like the COVID 19 virus, and through the growing impact of Climate Change. In times of major crisis, people desire to grasp at something they see as re-assuring and hopeful. Recovery of religious belief though, is not certain.

This begs the question, what else to follow/practice, if not religion?

Some alternatives to religion are: Agnosticism; Atheism; Humanism, modern Spiritualism, and Astrology. There are others, including Buddhism, which has had a airing in the philosophy chapter (20). Here's the AAHSA:

Agnosticism, these doubt God exists but don't have the absolute proof, so are not wanting to nail themselves firmly to the mast of atheism. There are various shades of agnosticism. Some may think the odds against there being a God are so great it's more than a million to one against his existence, but there is still a very slight chance. At the other end of the atheistic spectrum are those who are almost one of the faithful, but are just not quite sure enough to admit to a Godly belief;

Atheism, this is for people who have absolutely no doubt - He's not there. Atheists are certain sure that there is no God. They are people with no need for religion as a prop. Author John Buchan described them as: "An atheist is a man who has no invisible means of support."

Humanism

Humanists are focused on humans, not Gods of any sort. Some ancient Greek philosophers could be considered of a humanist inclination, particularly Socrates, with his denial of Gods and focus of high ethical standards. Basically, humanists want to help people and communities so that there is movement towards a better, more just society. Many Humanists might attach other labels to themselves. They could also be atheists, agnostics or secularists. What they do not have is a religious affiliation. Humanism is worldwide. It's prevalent in at least 40 countries. In the United Kingdom it is major: An Ipsos MORI poll, published in January 2007 for Humanists UK indicated that 36% of people - equivalent to around 17 million adults - 1 in 5 people - are in fact humanist in their basic outlook; despite they may not formally identify themselves as humanists. The UK has 90,000 formally signed up, with dues paid.

There are some well-known people running this body as at 2019: Chair of the Board, Tamar Ghosh (also Chief Exec. Of the Royal Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene), President, Professor Alice Roberts (evolutionary biologist, author and TV broadcaster); Vice-President, Professor Jim Al-Khalili (theoretical physicist, author, radio and TV broadcaster); Vice-President, Professor A C Grayling (philosopher and writer, regular on radio and TV), and Vice-President Shappi Khorsandi (stand-up comic, performing in theatre, appearing on radio and TV, author).

Humanists UK

Humanists UK, here's what they say they want:

A world where everyone lives cooperatively on the basis of shared human values, respect for human rights and concern for future generations;
To help non-religious people be confident in living ethical and fulfilling lives on the basis of reason and humanity. This is inclusive and well, humanitarian.

Education features very strongly on the Humanists agenda. They've campaigned against faith schools, saying: "The majority of the evidence ... points towards their being an unfair and unpopular part of our state education system which the majority of people in Britain want them phased out.", adding "All pupils in all types of school should have the opportunity to consider philosophical and fundamental questions, and that in a pluralist society we should learn about each other's beliefs, including humanist ones". They opposed the teaching of creationism launching a campaign in 2011 that schools should: "Teach Evolution, not Creationism." Later, the Department for Education changed the funding system for free schools so that government cash could be withdrawn if the school taught creationism as an established scientific fact.

Teaching myths as truth is not good educational policy, so the DfE is to be commended. It's hard to find either any science or facts that give support to creationism. It may be though, the story in Chapter 18a of God's creation plan, which Gabriel so strongly opposed, did come to pass! Those dinosaur bones were cunningly planted (with the emphasis on 'con'), and the space candles - they must have been gi-normous. However, these thoughts are stretching credulity beyond credibility into no-no space.

"If religion were true, its followers would not try to bludgeon their young into an artificial conformity; but would merely insist on their unbending quest for the truth, irrespective of artificial backgrounds or practical consequences."

HP Lovecraft, US SF author 1890-1937

Apart from being for the teaching of evolution, Humanists UK has also campaigned against faith schools saying: "We want pupils from all different backgrounds educated together in a shared environment, rather than separated according to the religious beliefs of their parents. On Religious Education they've said: "We think it's vital that every young person learns about the different religions that are common in the UK today, as well as humanism. We work to ensure that such education is critical, objective, and pluralistic."

Not surprisingly, Humanists UK also supports secularism; where Parliament is separate from religious organisations. The National Secular Society has similar intent.

All these aims demonstrate Humanists UK are promoting an inclusive society where everyone's beliefs are respected but not imposed on anyone else. These are worthy aims and ought to be supported by all who want a free and equal society.

A great early Humanist was Margaret Knight. While in her third year at Girton College Cambridge Margaret said that she found the "moral courage", finally to at last give up the religious beliefs she had been uncomfortable with for a long time. She explained this defining moment in her book: "Morals Without Religion (1955)", writing "...a fresh, cleansing wind swept through the stuffy room that contained the relics of my religious beliefs. I let them go with a profound sense of relief, and ever since I have lived happily without them."

On the radio, BBC Home Service, 1955, Margaret argued intelligently that children's moral education should be uncoupled from religious education saying: "I am not out to destroy the Christian convictions of people in whom they are deeply implanted and to whom they mean a great deal. And I am sure that nothing I say here will have the slightest effect on believers of this type. But what I do want to argue is that, in a climate of thought that is increasingly unfavourable to these beliefs, it is a mistake to try to impose them on children, and to make them the basis of moral training. The moral education of children is much too important a matter to be built on such foundations." This caused a bit of a controversy with conservative Brits at the time.

Buddhism

The several varieties of Buddhism, have the aim of helping people reach nirvana (see Chapter 23, 8 Philosophy). Zen Buddhism is unusual. It requires people to focus inside themselves, looking for inner truth, and eventually becoming Buddha. Zen claims we all are Buddha.

Modern Spiritualism

Varieties of spiritualism have been common throughout the world and throughout human history, most usually in the form of shamanism and animism. These two are both associated with nature and spirits and are more fully described in Chapter 5. Modern Spiritualism is largely of an American location - the National Spiritual Association of Churches (NSAC), USA. Although it's said to be 'modern' one of its doctrines is Confucius 'golden rule'. Confucius was a Chinese philosopher who expounded his wisdom 2,500 years ago. The Golden Rule says 'treat others as you would yourself.'

The NSAC has 8 other principles including reference to prophecy and healing through use of mediums. These are people who claim to have physic abilities. Other, non-proven, but claimed aspects of modern spiritualism include clairvoyance, levitation, ectoplasm, the gift of tongues and communication with the spirits of the dead. Mediums, usually women, are the conduits for these attempted spiritual events.

Emanuel Swedenborg was a Swede who was both a theologian, with religious belief, and a medium. He is seen as the father of Modern Spiritualism.

[Figure: Medium Eva Carrière with a light between her hands]

One medium, the French woman Eva Carrière (1886 to 1943), was famous in her time. She managed to pull the wool over the eyes of Arthur Conan Doyle but not Harry Houdini, what would Sherlock Holmes make of his originator being hoodwinked? Eva's séances were highly erotic. She often appeared nude, perhaps to put off balance her male séancers, and distract them so they would not notice they were being duped.

Astrology

From the New York Post, Sally Brompton says to those Aries people: "This is a time to be on the move, physically and mentally. Even if you are unable to wander far from home there are still plenty of things you can do to stretch your body and expand your mind, so use your imagination and find ways to improve yourself", finally, from Pakistan Today, those under Virgo receive this advice: "Virgo is a 'difficult' sign. Virgoans are very mind oriented; they are constantly analysing, thinking and critiquing. They enjoy bettering themselves and those around them. Sometimes they even succeed (in the former). They are the busiest of all zodiac signs, although it is not always clear what they are busy at."

Some people pay attention to their horoscope, many treat them as a bit of fun and not to be taken seriously.

Wicca

This is a modern pagan religion, tracing some of its nature focused, partly shamanistic practices, to ancient times. The followers have no temples, or specific buildings in which they worship. They gather in groups, called covens of 10 to 15 members. They engage in witchcraft, various rituals and practice magic, using their "Book of Shadows". Two of their main deities are a female Goddess and the male, horned God. A key Wiccan sect is known as Wiccan Rede. Its ethical code says: "If it harms none, do what you will." Wiccans are mainly to be found in Great Britain and the USA, but also in continental Europe. One estimate put their number at 5 million, worldwide.

A Holistic Approach

Some people may take a holistic approach: embracing into one whole bits of: Humanism; Zen or other Buddhism; meditation; yoga and spiritualism (not like Eva!), maybe some of these if not all. There is a multitude of guidance available from gurus of various sort. These tell how to live a life, to achieve either or all of these: a fulfilling one; content one; happy one; active one, but not necessarily a religious one. The guidance works if you believe it.

The above are some of the alternate beliefs to main stream religions, and as shown there's also a growing number of non-believers. Often, people of all these different beliefs and non-beliefs have a common, basic 'goodness".

Non-Believers are bad, according to the Bible in Psalms 14 and 53

Does the Bible celebrate or welcome people like this - NO! Even Good...

Goodness and community spirit are at odds with the cruel, wholly mistaken Psalm 14 of the Bible. This says people who don't believe in God are filthy, corrupt fools, entirely incapable of doing any good.

A later Psalm, 53 re-emphasises these points: From KJV: "The fool hath said in his heart, there is no God. Corrupt are they, and have done abominable iniquity: there is none that doeth good." Corrupt fools? Incapable of doing good? What does the evidence say?

What's Good about the good

As seen earlier, many non-religious people could be described as Humanists, that is, those who have a care for other people and do good works. This is analogous to some religious people, of the non-fundamentalist sort. Many religious people, of every religion, are not rigid, fundamentalists. In fact, some are at the opposite end of the religious spectrum holding on to a gentler belief concept. Of course, there are many levels of religious zealotry between those two poles. But let's focus on just the lower end of these two extremes. These are closer to the views and actions of the best of non-religious people.

Very anti-fundamentalist religious persons are characterised by their respect and toleration of others outside their faith. They help others, no matter what alternate beliefs they may hold, and do much good for their fellow man. Typically, they obey the rules and laws of their society, despite this may be of a secular nature. They have tolerance and engage amicably with those of a different religious persuasion. Even atheists and agnostics are accepted with equanimity. In this way these "goodies" contribute to, and help build a just and thriving society. This is in contrast with the negative and sometimes destructive impact of their more ardent, narrow minded and fundamentalist brethren. These latter tend to believe there is only one way, their way. They will seek to impose their ways and may even use violence to achieve their goal. The goodies are able to live their loving religious good are people with a Tolerant, Democratic Faith. They could be initialised as the TDF crowd.

The TDF Crowd are a broad church

The application of gentle goodness by the TDF is unaffected by adherence to a particular religion. The same societal advantages are gained from these people's goodness whether they are TDF Christians; Jews; Muslims; Hindus; Buddhists or others, even of no faith at all. What do TDF's do? Well, this is wide ranging. Common to all is the application of charity to help the less fortunate in society. They are community minded and community active.

The TDF Crowd are a broad church

pages.text:
For Christian denominations, at least, it also involves these type of community activities, based at a church location, but without imposing Christianity:

Holding dinners, coffee mornings, teas, for anyone who wants to come
Putting on other social and community events that may involve choirs, music playing, theatrical performance, plant swaps or sales, and talks on a wide variety of topics;
'adopting' elderly single people, regular visiting them and taking them to events.

Typically, these actions will not involve any form of preaching, praying or moralising.

There are numerous examples, the world over, of individual religious groups conducting forms of community and charitable work. Just one example is from Cambridge, England. Here, in 2019 and 2020, churches of all types got together to provide regular beds for homeless people. This was rotationally, over the winter period from November to March. The homeless were given clean linen, washing and toilet facilities and a meal and were not preached at or required to pray.

These simple, humanitarian acts, are usually not directly related to a particular belief. On other occasions they may be encouraged by the religion itself, with a hint of a better afterlife for the good deeder. This is one example of TDF in action.

For themselves, the disciples of TDF can feel a sense of personal satisfaction from their ethical behaviour and application of community spirit. They also gain personally from their faith and belief. Their religious belief gives them a calm confidence, a certainty and assurance. They can look forward to life eternal; of a type of their religious choosing. This latter mind-set is particularly helpful when death is near. The TDF follower can visualise meeting up with deceased family and friends in a new and wonderful beginning, rather than just a vacuous end.

TOLERANCE CONDEMNS PERSECUTION OF OTHERS.

TDFs can be found in followers of every faith and of no faith at all. Their good deeds can be both composite and individual. Many philosophers have outlined the essentials of such behavior, generally saying we have empathy towards others and treat them fairly.

Of course, there is the alternative, an encouragement to selfishness by philosophers such as Ayn Rand and Bernard Mandeville, but the majority of philosophers advise, in essence, look out for others, 'don't be selfish'.

These 'goody' behaviors can be found in the heavily stripped-down, core instruction, of almost every religion. The TDF crowd demonstrates them, and they are at the heart of non-religious Humanism.

Several psychological studies show that people are generally inclined to be kind and helpful to others. Neuroscience research also backs this up (Christov-Moore & Iacoboni, 2015). The tendencies are not absolute imperatives. Studies also show that urgent self-interest can overwhelm the kindness tendency. These tendencies, of all people of all and no faiths, are the building blocks of the type of ethical behaviour most approve of. They can be encouraged to establish firmer moral attitudes that do not require any religion as a guide, and be prepared to ask difficult questions about any claim of certainty over required forms of behaviour.

All need to have some education to lead them along this path. In their formative years children ought to be taught to have more open minds in schools free of association with a particular religion.

Let's have more TDF's, either of the religious or humanist variety. Their aims and work are supportive of their fellow man and are ethically centered.

It was that great ancient Greek, Socrates, who laid immense emphasis on the importance of ethics and morality, so perhaps TDF's ought to be labeled "Socratists'. That's a thought!

figures.caption: Chart showing Earth's five ice ages across geological time. Columns show millions of years ago, the geological periods (Quaternary, Neogene, Paleogene, Cretaceous, Jurassic, Triassic, Permian, Carboniferous, Devonian, Silurian, Ordovician, Cambrian and the Precambrian), a curve of global average temperature, and the ice ages: Ice Age 1, Huronian (2,400 to 2,100 million years ago); Ice Age 2, Cryogenian "Snowball Earth" (720 to 635 million years ago); Ice Age 3, Andean-Saharan (460 to 420 million years ago); Ice Age 4, Karoo (360 to 260 million years ago); and Ice Age 5, Late Cenozoic (34 million years ago to now).
Image of the above table

figures.caption: Diagram showing the greenhouse effect and human contributions to climate change. The illustration shows Earth with arrows indicating radiation absorbed, reflected, and escaping at the edge of atmosphere. Various sources of greenhouse gases are depicted including: deforestation, oil and petrol engines, CFCs, fossil fuels, and radiation absorbed by greenhouse gases and the atmosphere/Earth. Text labels point to different processes: "escaping radiation," "reflected," "absorbed," "absorbed by atmosphere and Earth," "absorbed by greenhouse gases," and "deforestation."
figures.credit: Original artwork by the author.
